## CHAPTER 5: THE LOCAL 405 ALLIANCE

The hydraulic hiss of the loading bay doors announces my arrival before the heat does. Local 405 Union Hall has never been what anyone would call pristine—two decades of arcane machinery modifications have ground their mark into every surface—but tonight there's an urgency to the chaos.

I step through the threshold into controlled pandemonium.

Argon torches throw their brilliant white-blue hellfire across catwalks fifty feet overhead, where Dwarven machinists in welder's masks work on armor plating for trauma-ambulances that look like they've been in more fights than paramedics should ever see. The clang of hammers on metal echoes off concrete pillars thick enough to survive anything short of a full-cascade collapse. Somewhere deep in the bowels of the building, a Telluric generator thrums with that particular vibration that makes your teeth ache and your fillings hum.

The smell hits me next. Diesel exhaust from vehicles idling in the outer staging area mingles with burnt flux and the acrid tang of ozone where raw tellurium has been worked too hard, too fast. My nose wrinkles despite years of service in worse conditions.

But I don't come here for the ambiance.

My eyes find the Arcane Iron-Lung immediately because it's impossible to miss—a brass-and-glass monstrosity that takes up the central third of the main garage floor. The machine gleams under industrial floodlights, its polished surfaces reflecting dancing shadows from the welding torches above. Hissing pistons rhythmically expand and contract, maintaining the pressure differential Danny needs to live another day outside sterile medical facilities that would bleed him dry before morning.

And there he is.

Nineteen years old, trapped behind reinforced glass, reading some battered paperback like this is just another Tuesday. The book looks familiar—one of those noir detective novels he used to quote at me during stakeouts when we were still pretending the world made sense. His dark hair falls across his forehead the same way it did back in Newark when he was fresh out of training and convinced he could save everyone.

I stop fifteen feet from the lung, suddenly uncertain about my legs. Bram notices first, of course. The Dwarven master-machinist straightens from where he'd been checking pressure gauges on the brass casing, wiping grease onto overalls already decorated with enough oil stains to chart a century of work.

"Core compressor holding steady at ninety percent," Bram barks in that gravelly North Jersey accent that sounds like someone grinding rocks into powder. "Kid's breathing easy." He gestures toward the lung with a wrench the size of my forearm. "Been awake since six PM. Wouldn't take sedatives until he heard you were coming."

Danny's head snaps up from his book. Even through the distortion of thick glass, I can see his smile spread across his face like dawn breaking over the Passaic River. He presses one hand against the interior surface, right at chest height.

"Hey, Cole."

His voice comes through external speakers, metallic and filtered but undeniably him. There's something wrong with the phonetic processors—they always sound like they're transmitting from underwater—but Danny never complained. Never asked for anything better than what kept him alive.

"You died again." It's not an accusation, more like an observation delivered with that smartass tone that got us both kicked out of half the precincts between here and Gary. "Getting real tired of paying for flowers, you know. Two hundred bucks last time. Rose arrangements are expensive as hell in this economy."

I walk forward, each step feeling heavier than the last. My frost-cobalt coat leaves condensation trails on the concrete—automatic temperature regulation activating without conscious thought because trauma makes you cold even when you're standing in an inferno. When I reach the lung, I place my hand exactly where his touches the glass from inside.

The brass is warm. Alive with residual energy from the Telluric generator that powers everything, keeps oxygen flowing, maintains pressure differentials that would crush human lungs in seconds flat.

"I'm sorry," I say quietly, watching our hands align perfectly through the barrier. My palm cools the metal, frost patterns spreading outward in crystalline fractals. "Last time. I promise."

Bram snorts from somewhere behind me, but he doesn't interrupt. The Dwarf has been around long enough to recognize when promises matter more than probability. We built this machine together back in 2000, after Newark taught us what happened when you ran out of options. His hands were on every weld, his expertise in tellurium mechanics keeping the theoretical stable enough for field deployment.

Danny's eyes search mine through layers of reinforced glass and the distance that no amount of technology can bridge. There are questions there, concerns about whatever fresh hell brought me back from wherever death kept dropping me these days. But there's also something else—the absolute certainty that if anyone could survive it all, it would be me.

"You look like shit," he adds helpfully, still smiling. "When was the last time you slept?"

"Before I died," I answer honestly. "Doesn't count if you wake up somewhere else, right?"

The joke lands wrong—I can see it in how his expression flickers—but Danny covers with another quote from whatever noir paperback currently occupies his attention. "'Dead men don't sleep, they just stop breathing.' Pretty accurate considering your resume lately."

A metallic clang echoes across the garage as one of the welding teams finishes securing armor plating to an ambulance chassis. Molten sparks rain down like a miniature meteor shower, forcing nearby machinists to scatter. Someone shouts directions in a language that predates Old English by several centuries—Dwarven, probably, though half the Union speaks it fluently while the other half pretends they don't understand.

Then the heavy rolling doors at the far end of the garage shudder.

Not the vibration of vehicles outside. Not wind or weather or any natural occurrence. The entire corrugated steel structure rattles under impact—once, twice—a fist-sized dent appearing where steel meets steel.

"OPEN THE SLOTTING DOOR, KOVACS, BEFORE I TEAR IT OFF THE HINGES!"

The voice booms across the cavernous space, each syllable delivered with enough force to rattle loose tools from their pegboards. Every head turns toward the sound, welders abandoning torches mid-strike, the ambient noise of industrial labor grinding to an abrupt halt.

Bram's hand moves to something holstered at his hip—not a weapon exactly, but close enough when Dwarves decide they're done playing nice. His eyes find mine briefly before shifting to survey the exits.

"Well," Danny's voice crackles through speakers, somehow managing to sound amused despite the situation, "looks like you brought company."

* * *

The warehouse doors groan on rusted hydraulics as they roll upward, spilling neon-soaked rainwater into the concrete pit below. I step forward, my boots tracking water across the floor, and the air hits me first—wet asphalt and diesel fumes layered over something earthier, muskier. Ozone crackles somewhere in the back, mixing with the acrid tang of gun oil.

Then *they* emerge from the shadows.

Grimjaw leads them out, all seven feet two inches of scarred green hide and chrome-reinforced jaw. The metal catches the sickly orange glow filtering through the broken skylights above, making him look half-mechanical, half-nightmare. Behind him, a dozen more Orcs materialize—their forms broader than normal human builds, hunched slightly under the low ceiling, their leathery skin marked with tribal scars that seem to shift in the bad light.

They're carrying crates. Big ones. Wooden, unmarked except for scuff marks and rust stains. The first one drops with a wet *thud* that echoes off the corrugated walls, followed by another, then another, until six identical containers sit arranged in a rough circle around the center of the warehouse space.

"You brought the whole damn family reunion, Cole." My voice cuts through the ambient noise—somewhere a generator wheezes, keeping this place lit against whatever darkness has claimed most of the district beyond these walls.

Cole doesn't turn immediately. He's already at the Crown Vic, its matte-black paint drinking in the darkness like spilled oil. His fingers trace the hood's edge as he nods toward Grimjaw. "The Commander knows we don't do anything small anymore."

Grimjaw works his jaw, the chrome grinding audibly as he settles an unlit cigar between yellowed tusks. When he speaks, it's like tectonic plates grinding together. "Voss has a private army of High-Spire suits and corporate mercs locking down the perimeter. We push through the front, it's a meat grinder." He spits, the wad landing near my boots. No malice in it—just matter-of-fact contempt.

I walk closer, studying the crew gathering around the car. Dwarves I recognize from the BATC rolls—I've got files on maybe half of them. Short-barreled shotguns slung across their backs, bandoliers heavy with ammunition. And the Orcs... Christ, they're *massive*. Not just tall but thick, the kind of muscle that comes from hauling freight through the Sludge sewers for decades.

"We aren't pushing through the front," Cole says finally, straightening up. The tactical map on his tablet glows red against his face. "We're going to drive these trauma-ambulances straight through their arcane barricades."

"Arcane barricades." I repeat it flatly, trying to parse what exactly he means by 'trauma-ambulances' when there are no ambulances in sight. "Cole—"

"Bram!" Cole calls out without looking at me.

A stocky figure detaches from the group around the crates—a dwarf with a gold tooth that catches the light as he grins. He kicks open one of the containers with obvious pride, the wood splintering inward.

Inside, nestled in custom-cut foam, are hundreds of shells. Massive things, each one etched with glowing runes that pulse with sickly purple energy. Depleted bismuth, I realize after a second. Heavy enough to punch through brick, packed with enough kinetic force to crater concrete.

"Special order from the Reyes connections in Macau," Bram announces, running a hand over the nearest shell reverently. "Hollow-core design. We hit their wards hard enough, the resonant frequency will cascade through the entire network. One shot, Commander. That's all we need."

I stare at the shells, then back at Cole. Around us, Grimjaw's sandhogs have positioned themselves around the perimeter, not threatening but... ready. Waiting for orders they'll follow because Cole liberated them from something worse than death in those sewers.

"Pylon #4 at the Old Mint," Cole says quietly, zooming in on the map. The red glow intensifies, showing buildings I recognize from my patrol routes, streets I've walked a hundred times under different pretense. "That's where Voss is consolidating his power. High-Spire has already moved half their assets into the surrounding blocks. By tomorrow morning, this whole sector goes corporate-locked."

"And you're planning to stop it by turning that mint into rubble." It's not a question.

"We're planning to stop it by stopping *him*." There's steel in Cole's voice now, the same edge I remember from the briefings about the Millennium Breach. "Voss opened that breach, Mara. Every nightmare that's crawled out of the Sludge since 2000? His fault. Those suits think they can contain it with money and magic. They're wrong."

Grimjaw shifts his weight, the chrome in his jaw clicking. "We go tonight. Three hours until moonrise. The tide turns, the marsh waters flood higher, covers our approach from the east." He pulls the cigar from his mouth, examines it without lighting it. "You want war with High-Spire? Tonight, they get it."

The warehouse feels smaller suddenly, pressed in by the weight of what we're discussing. Outside, rain continues its relentless assault on Neon Hollow, each drop another second ticking away toward whatever comes next.

I look around at all of them—Cole with his tactical certainty, Grimjaw with his brutal loyalty, Bram with his pride in destructive innovation, and beyond them dozens more metahumans ready to march on a corporate fortress because one man decided enough was enough.

"What makes you think," I ask slowly, "that I'm going to let you do this?"

Cole finally meets my eyes, and there's something old there, something that remembers when we were both just trying to survive the Breach instead of deciding how to end it. "Because you're the only person in North Jersey who still knows the difference between right and legal, Commander. And Voss crossed that line three years ago. You know it. I know it." He taps the map. "Question is whether you're willing to do something about it before the whole city drowns in what he's unleashed."

The gold tooth catches the light again as Bram grins wider. "And hey... worst case scenario, we make enough noise that even the Council can't ignore it anymore."

I should arrest them. Should call in tactical support, lock down this location, process every last one of these metahumans for weapons violations alone.

Instead I find myself asking: "How many vehicles?"

* * *

# THE MILLENNIUM BREACH

## THE TEMPLE OF STEEL

The PalmPilot's screen bleeds green numbers across my palm—17:34:11. Seventeen hours, thirty-four minutes, eleven seconds since Cole's team rolled out into that storm. Since I watched their taillights disappear down Route 280, swallowed by curtains of rain that looked like liquid mercury under the orange sodium lights.

I'm three levels above the ground floor of a parking structure on 9th Street, leaning against a concrete pillar that smells of piss and old motor oil. The wind whips through gaps in the rusted chain-link fencing, carrying with it the chemical sweetness of the Passaic River and something worse—the acrid bite of ozone where reality wears thin. Where the grid cracks leak through.

My white-lilac wards are screaming at me. They've been screaming since I jacked this PalmPilot off that dead High-Spire officer back in Newark. Her blood was still warm when I took it, still steaming in the October cold, mixing with the puddles of rain and oil on Sub-Station Seven's concrete floor. The memory makes my teeth ache.

The wards taste wrong now. Polluted. That ash-gray static has wormed its way into every glyph, every sigil woven around my spine, my heart, my third eye. It feels like swallowing battery acid mixed with burnt cedar—sharp and bitter and somehow sweet, the way only true corruption can be. Seventy-two hours since Sub-Station Seven blew, and I still can't scrub the stench from my magic. Can't wash away the smell of wet charred wool that clings to everything touched by that breach.

Below me, Pylon #4 rises like a tombstone carved from steel and desperation. The Old Mint squats in the middle of a six-block radius that Marcus Voss has turned into his personal hunting ground. The Telluric grid runs thick here, so dense you could choke on it, pulsing beneath asphalt and foundation stone with all the sickly green light of an infected wound. And Voss sits at the center of it, siphoning power, building his army, preparing for whatever comes next.

I know what comes next. I read it in the PalmPilot while I waited for the convoy to reach the outer perimeter. The BATC's final solution to the Passaic anomaly: nuclear option. Thermobaric warfare. Burn everything inside a two-mile radius and hope whatever opened the breach gets incinerated along with Cole's team, along with half of Kearny, along with any chance we had of understanding what we're actually dealing with.

They're going to glass this entire section of Neon Hollow unless Voss is dead by 0600 hours tomorrow morning.

The PalmPilot buzzes against my palm—a new message scrolling across its cracked screen:

*COVENANT FORCES HOLDING AT PYLON PERIMETER. HEAVY LOSSES. REQUEST IMMEDIATE AIR SUPPORT.*

I don't have air support. I have one pistol—my father's .38 Special, hollow-point rounds loaded with salt and blessed iron—and a set of wards that are currently trying to eat their way out through my skin because they taste too much like ash-gray static and burnt things.

Below me, movement catches my eye. A figure detaches from the shadows near the Old Mint's main entrance. Too far away to make out details, but I can feel him—the pressure change in the air, the way reality bends around certain kinds of power. Metahuman. One of Voss's lieutenants probably. They've been circling like vultures since Cole's convoy breached the outer wall an hour ago.

My hand moves to the .38 at my hip. The metal feels warm despite the rain-soaked cold, warm from the wards wrapped around it, around me, desperate for something clean to burn with.

Seventeen hours until sunrise.

Fifteen hours until the bombs fall.

I need to get down there. Need to find Cole before whatever he's planning to do goes sideways—which is when things always go wrong in this job. When the easy plan becomes suicide.

I slip the PalmPilot into my jacket pocket and start moving, descending through layers of concrete and rust toward ground level, toward the temple of steel where Marcus Voss keeps his court. Each step sends sharp pains through my calves—too long standing still, too little sleep, too much adrenaline keeping my heart hammering against my ribs like it wants out.

The rain hits harder as I reach street level, driving horizontal sheets of water that sting like needles against my face. Somewhere in the distance, gunfire erupts—not the controlled staccato of military weapons but the wild chaos of a firefight gone to hell. Cole's team maybe, or just some other poor bastards caught in the crossfire between Voss's metas and the Covenant's desperation.

I pull up the hood on my jacket and head east, following 9th Street toward the Old Mint's perimeter fence. The sidewalk is deserted except for puddles reflecting neon signs advertising liquor stores and check-cashing places, all the usual monuments to Neon Hollow's particular brand of decay.

Two blocks away now. Close enough to see the glow of the Telluric grid pulsing beneath Pylon #4 like a living thing, close enough to taste copper on my tongue from the wards burning through my system. My white-lilac magic has started to crack, little fissures of gray-black static bleeding through the protective glyphs, eating at my concentration, making everything look slightly wrong, slightly off-center.

Another message on the PalmPilot:

*CMD MARA VANCE. ABORT MISSION. REPEAT. ABORT MISSION.*

Not happening.

I tuck the phone away and keep walking, one hand on the .38, one hand holding what's left of my wards together with sheer stubborn will. The Old Mint's fence looms ahead—a twelve-foot barrier topped with concertina wire, set into concrete foundations reinforced with something that glows faintly green when you look at it just right.

There's a gap about thirty yards south where someone's already torn their way through, metal cutters having done their work on three of the fence posts. An invitation or a trap, hard to say which.

I choose the gap.

The rain gets worse as I step onto what used to be a parking lot but now looks more like a battlefield—trench lines dug in mud, sandbags stacked around makeshift fighting positions, spent shell casings glittering like junk jewelry in every puddle. Somewhere inside this hellzone, Cole is either dead or about to do something monumentally stupid.

My boots squelch through mud that smells of blood and cordite, each step taking me closer to Pylon #4's main entrance. Ahead, silhouette movement near an old loading dock—the same figure I saw from above, still circling, still watching for targets.

The wards scream louder now, reacting to whatever power signature radiates from that metahuman. Ash-gray static spreads across my vision like oil spreading

---

## CHAPTER 6: THE TEMPLE OF STEEL

The sodium lights overhead flickered like dying stars, casting everything below in sickly yellow. Water sluiced through cracks in the parking garage ceiling, pooling around my boots as I descended the rust-eaten stairs. The air tasted of ozone and stale Marlboros.

Mara waited by a workbench cobbled together from scrap steel, her leather coat darkening where rain still dripped from her hair. She held up the PalmPilot like a dead bird—bloodstained plastic casing, cracked LCD screen showing nothing but static now that its owner was meat.

"You brought them?" Her eyes flicked past me to the shadows.

I stepped aside. Fidget emerged first, all five-foot-nothing of Gnome muscle packed into a grease-stained mechanic's jacket. His fingers never stopped moving, already pulling cables from his rucksack. Behind him, Shiv and two other Razor-Wire Elves materialized—optical-camo tattoos making their faces shimmer in the bad light.

"Got something for us, sweetheart?" Fidget's voice ran together, syllables bleeding into each other like melted wax. He dumped his gear on the bench, an IBM ThinkPad that had seen better days around 1998, all its guts exposed and wrapped in copper heat-sinks that glowed faint red.

Mara placed the PalmPilot down without ceremony. "It's locked tight. BATC encryption suite. Corporate-grade."

"Corporate-grade." Fidget snorted, already cracking open the device with a jeweler's screwdriver. "That's cute. They think those firewalls mean something when you're not hitting them straight-on." His hands moved faster than should be possible, fingers dancing across keyboard keys that lit up green one by one.

Shiv leaned against the concrete pillar, arms crossed, optical-camos rippling across his forearms in slow waves. "You know what you're asking here, Vance. Internal Affairs isn't just standing guard at the Old Mint. Thorne's got them running sweeps every twenty minutes. Thermal drones overhead. Ground teams with enough hardware to glass a city block."

"The frequency brokers told me the convoy moves tonight," Mara said flatly. "Voss or someone close to him is making the call."

"Yeah? Well the Telluric Pylons don't give a fuck about your informants' timetables." Shiv pulled a crumpled data-chip from his jacket, tossed it onto the bench. "Internal Affairs layouts. Updated this morning. Every entrance, every ventilation shaft, every goddamn maintenance tunnel. It's a fortress, not a building."

The ThinkPad let out a high-pitched whine as Fidget hardwired the PalmPilot directly into its motherboard. Exposed circuit boards sparked once, twice, then settled into a steady blue glow.

"There we go. Oh yeah, there we fucking go." Fidget's grin split his face wide enough to show too many teeth. "Bouncing signal off cell towers... wait, wait... off pirate radio relay... got it. Holy shit, he's moving heavy. Three armored Victors, two trauma-buses, and what looks like a mobile command center bringing up the rear."

Mara's head snapped toward the screen. "Trauma-buses?"

"Can't hear that?" The third Gnome—couldn't remember if she'd introduced herself—had her ear pressed against a Sony MiniDisc player hooked into the rig. She rewound, played back. Audio crackled through tiny speakers: "Code Black on all medical transport. Repeating, Code Black on all medical transport. Containment protocols Alpha-Niner initiated."

Shiv pushed off the pillar. "Containment protocols? What are they hauling that needs—"

The ThinkPad screen flashed red. Solid, pulsing red that drowned out everything else.

Fidget's hands froze over the keyboard. "What the..."

"Heavy vehicle one just stopped," another Gnome read off numbers cascading down the screen. "Lat-long coordinates match Pylon Four. Wait—fuck—armored Victor Two is breaking formation. Moving to intercept civilian traffic control. Third vehicle still in transit but decelerating."

"Telluric arming sequence," Mara breathed. Her hand went to the pistol at her hip—not the one Thorne knew about, the backup piece strapped inside her boot. "They're not transporting anything. They're initiating."

Shiv grabbed my arm. His optical-camos flickered, trying to hide his expression. "Vance. Look at me. You know what happens when Telluric gets armed with Internal Affairs already on-site. That's not a raid. That's a kill-box. We need to abort. Now."

But Mara was already moving toward the stairs, the PalmPilot forgotten on the bench where Fidget had left it half-disassembled.

"They've begun arming," she called back, voice echoing off wet concrete. "If we don't stop this at Pylon Four, there won't be an Old Mint to storm anyway. The whole neighborhood goes up."

The rain hammered harder now, each drop hitting the waterlogged floor like gunshots.

* * *

The rain hammers down harder now, each drop a tiny nail hammered into the city's coffin. I can taste copper in my mouth—not blood, just the metallic tang that always comes when the magic wants something. Wants *me*.

From the rooftop of the old textile mill, I watch them arrive.

Three black '99 Crown Vics first, moving like oil across water through Neon Hollow's industrial guts. Their headlights cut through the downpour in smeared yellow blades. Then the ambulances—retrofitted '89 Fords, the kind they used for transporting high-value assets before the Breach turned everything inside-out. Those things shouldn't still be running. But Voss has a way with machinery. A way with people too.

The convoy pulls into the loading bays of the Old Mint, tires hissing against wet concrete. Red taillights bleed into puddles the color of arterial spray. My fingers twitch around the grips of my hex-revolvers, the ash-gray static crawling up my forearms like hungry insects. The sensation makes me want to scream.

*Fifty-three seconds*, I think. That's how long it took for the Orphans' fire to consume those 314 commuters on the Lincoln Tunnel train back in 2005. Fifty-three seconds of watching faces melt and bodies blacken while the children screamed themselves hoarse in the next car over. I saved thirty-seven kids. Burned three hundred and fourteen souls to do it.

I can smell charred wool even now.

The High-Spire officers emerge from the vehicles, their movements too fluid, too precise. Tailored suits hiding kinetic-dampening armor beneath—probably Tier-4 protection, the kind that stops anything short of dedicated anti-materiel rounds. Their faces are sharp and alien under the Mint's sickly yellow security lights, features too perfect, smiles too knowing.

There are twelve of them. Maybe thirteen.

My magic burns in my veins like swallowed lightning. Blue-black iron-gall residue drips from my fingertips, sizzling as it hits the rain-soaked iron of the fire escape. Each drop is a tiny sacrifice, a promise of violence. I've got enough wards prepped to turn this whole block into a deathtrap if I play it right.

But there's no playing anymore. Not really.

I accept that I'm not walking away from tonight. Haven't been since I made the choice to come here, to follow Voss's trail down through the marshlands and across the Skyway. Taking him down—that's all I have left. All I've *earned*.

The boots on wet metal behind me nearly make me jump. Combat boots, rhythmic, approaching fast across the fire escape. I don't turn around. Don't need to.

"Mara," comes the voice, smooth as poison. "Did you think we wouldn't know? Did you really imagine you could slip past our sensors?"

I finally turn, hex-revolvers already drawn, the air crackling with barely-contained magical pressure.

He's standing maybe fifteen feet away on the fire escape, one hand resting casually against the railing. High-Spire Elite, his suit immaculate despite the weather. Behind him, two more officers materialize from the shadows, their weapons—some kind of energy pistols that hum with that distinctive resonant frequency—already aimed at my center mass.

"My dear," he says, that smile never wavering, "you're under arrest for crimes against the Accord. For the murder of 314 civilians. For unauthorized magical deployment in a Tier-2 restricted zone."

"I burned those people to save children," I say, voice steady even though my heart's trying to tear itself out of my chest. "And you Elves can take your Accord and shove it."

His expression doesn't change. "Then this ends now."

* * *

The cold bit through my jacket like hungry teeth.

I stood in the shadow of the rusted water tower off Passaic Avenue, watching the thermometer on my phone's screen drop from forty-three to thirty-eight in the span of two minutes. That wasn't normal October weather. That was *hex-work*—the kind that made my fingers tingle with recognition, blood-memory of the forge, of pouring iron that remembered every soul it'd consumed.

"Boss." Rico's voice crackled in my earpiece, tight and controlled. "You seeing this?"

"Seeing it," I muttered, eyes tracking the temperature indicator. "Someone just dropped a serious weight-class spell three blocks north."

The Old Mint rose against the sickly orange glow of Neon Hollow, its crumbling Victorian façade a monument to broken promises. Pylon #4 sat embedded in its eastern wall like a tumor, pulsing with corrupted white-lilac energy that stank of ozone and worse things—things that made my metallic taste buds recoil.

"We moving?" That was Santos, positioned near the docks. My team had fanned out around the perimeter while I took the high ground, looking for any sign of Mara Vance. She'd gone dark after her message: *They're coming for me. For us. Don't let them take the core.*

I didn't know what that meant. Still don't, looking back. But I knew she was scared, and that was enough.

My phone vibrated. Text from an unknown number: A photo showing Mara pinned beneath an overturned dumpster, surrounded by six figures in tactical gear. The lead one wore a long black trench coat that somehow stayed pristine despite the alley's grime. Elven features. Cold gray eyes.

Beneath the photo: COORDINATES. TIMER (0:03:28...)

"Move now," I said into the comm. "Rico, left flank. Santos, right. No hesitation, no holding fire when we breach. These are High-Spire IA—"

A gunshot cracked through the night. Then another. And then the sound of automatic weapons firing in rapid succession, punctuated by the sharp *crack* of kinetic shields shattering.

Mara's voice, barely audible even through my enhanced hearing: "File this under 'go to hell,' Thorne."

The temperature dropped another five degrees.

I was already running down the water tower's maintenance ladder, boots hitting rusted iron with bone-jarring impacts. My metallurgy hexes flared hot-cold, blood-iron locking into frost-cobalt mode. Each heartbeat sent waves of killing intent radiating outward—I could feel the cold seeping into my bones, could taste copper on my tongue as my body prepared for what came next.

This wasn't justice anymore. This was survival.

The alley opened before me like a wound in the city's flesh—brick walls slick with rain, puddles reflecting neon signs from three streets over. The stench hit immediately: gunpowder, blood, and that distinctive acrid burn of corrupted core energy.

Four IA officers remained standing, their rune-etched MP5s trained on Mara's position. One lay dead near the dumpster, his chest caved in. Another's leg was shattered, knee blown out at an angle that made even me wince.

And there—in the center of it all—stood the elf from the photo. Vane Thorne. His coat rippled in wind that didn't exist, perfectly tailored despite the chaos around him. He held something in his hand, and even from fifty yards away I could see white-lilac light leaking between his fingers like trapped lightning.

"Compliance was always your failing, Vance," he said, his voice carrying that unsettling corporate detachment. Calm. Measured. Like he was reading from a script written in someone else's blood. "You're a rogue asset, and your depreciation is scheduled for tonight."

Mara spit blood onto the pavement. Her left arm hung useless, but her right still clutched some kind of device—her corrupted core, maybe? It pulsed with unstable energy, flickering between white and purple.

"You can file this under 'go to hell,' Thorne," she rasped.

The temperature dropped again. Ten degrees in ten seconds. Ice formed along the edges of the puddles.

Thorne raised his hand, and gravity *bent*.

The dumpster groaned as invisible force pressed down on it. Mara screamed—not from pain, but from the weight bearing down on her ribs, on her lungs. The metal began to buckle.

She had maybe thirty seconds before her sternum gave way.

Thirty seconds before they extracted whatever they came for and left her corpse in the garbage.

I raised my piece—a modified .45 with bismuth-copper rounds—and fired three shots at the officer nearest Thorne. Two missed. One caught him in the shoulder, spun him around.

But it wasn't enough. Would never be enough against High-Spire assets.

The elf turned those gray eyes toward me, and I felt the full weight of what stood between us. Not physical—something deeper. Older. The accumulated malice of every corporation that'd ever carved up North Jersey like a slaughterhouse cut.

He smiled.

Then everything went sideways.

A sound like thunder and tearing silk split the night. Something massive tore through the alley from the north end—depleted-bismuth slug, the size of my forearm, trailing smoke and heat-distortion. It hit the IA officer standing next to Thorne and kept going, punching through brick wall behind them, taking half his torso with it.

The sudden absence made everyone freeze for one heartbeat. Two.

And then the cold hit like a wall.

Forty degrees. Thirty-five. Thirty.

Ice crystallized across my skin, frost forming in my beard, my eyebrows. But underneath—the blood-iron hexes burned hotter than ever, frost-cobalt locking into place with lethal finality.

"Contact!" someone shouted. "North perimeter! Multiple—"

The temperature dropped to twenty-eight degrees.

Someone was coming. Someone who could make the air itself freeze solid.

I looked at Mara, still pinned under that crushing dumpster, her hand moving toward the corrupted core clutched against her chest.

Thorne's eyes flicked between me and something behind me, calculation running across those elven features like a computer processing threats.

The core pulsed once. Twice.

Mara's lips moved: *Sorry Cole.*

She began to press down on whatever mechanism held her core stable.

And I knew—with absolute certainty—that when she released it, we were all dead.

Every last one of us.

The question was whether whoever just saved our asses would get here in time to matter.

## CHAPTER 7: THE SLIVER OF JUSTICE

The clinic smells wrong—too clean, like disinfectant trying too hard to cover up something rotten underneath. I watch from my corner spot while Cole makes his ritual. The Polaroid trembles in his fingers, yellowed edges catching the overhead fluorescents that hum like angry hornets.

Danny's nineteen in the photo. Alive. Breathing. Before the black iron got into his lungs, before the Syndicate's Telluric Core Compressor turned him into a brass-and-glass experiment buried six feet under Sub-Station Seven.

"You know what I'm thinking?" Cole doesn't look at me when he speaks. His revolvers sit on the makeshift altar—a stainless steel tray—but he's already checked them twice. Blood-iron chambered, alchemical solvents wiped across every trigger assembly until they gleam. "I'm thinking this raid won't scrape a single molecule of that shit out of Danny's system."

Grimjaw shifts his bulk against the wall, his seven-foot-two frame making the medical supply closet feel smaller than it already is. His voice scrapes like concrete grinding against pavement: "Then why we doing this?"

Cole finally looks up, and there's nothing soft left in those eyes. "Because the sliver of justice is better than no justice at all." He taps the Polaroid once, reverent. "Won't bring back the dead. Won't fix the broken. But maybe—maybe—we can make sure whoever did this remembers what it feels like to bleed."

Bram Kovacs emerges from the shadows near the autoclave, his Local 405 Dwarven machinist rig clanking with heavy metallic purpose. Each piece of gear has been custom-fitted to account for the heat tolerances, the pressure dynamics of rune-worked ammunition. He hefts his shotgun—something between practical and obscene in its modifications—and racks a round that echoes through the clinic like a death knell.

"Tolerances are tight tonight, Reyes," Bram says, his accent thick as molasses. "Don't overheat the barrel, or it'll take your hand off." He's talking to Grimjaw, who's been fidgeting with one of the bismuth slugs, turning it over like a prayer bead. "These hex-rigs don't forgive mistakes."

Grimjaw grunts something that might be acknowledgment. The bismuth slug disappears into his weapon's chamber with a soft click-click. "Got them loaded. Let's go crack these corporate suits open."

The Motorola Razr on the counter starts shrieking—police scanner feed, intercepted through some Gnome hacker's black market software. Dispatch calls crackling through: "...multiple armed suspects approaching Old Mint perimeter... request tactical support..."

Cole moves fast then, snatching up both revolvers, tucking them into his shoulder holster while grabbing pre-cut charges from a medical tray someone's emptied out. "That's our cue."

We pile toward the exit, past stacks of expired medical supplies and equipment someone liberated from Jersey City Medical Center. The van's waiting outside—a battered, reinforced transit vehicle that's seen better days but still runs when you kick it just right.

I slide the side door open, feeling the weight of what's coming settle over my shoulders like a coat made of lead. The night air hits me first: humid, thick, tasting of Passaic River mud and ozone from the skyway's electrical grid.

"Commander." Cole's standing in the open doorway now, one foot already in the van. His eyes lock onto mine. "Whatever happens at the Old Mint tonight—"

"The mission completes," I finish for him. It's not optimism. It's doctrine.

He nods once and climbs aboard. Grimjaw follows, his massive frame folding into the reinforced back compartment with surprising grace. Bram Kovacs brings up the rear, shotgun cradled against his chest like a baby he's preparing to baptize in blood.

The engine roars to life beneath us—not pretty, but loud enough to wake the dead. Our driver jams the accelerator forward without ceremony, and we're moving before anyone can change their mind about this insanity.

Through the windshield, the Old Mint rises against the neon-drenched sky of Neon Hollow. Windows dark except for the telltale glow of rune-etched security lights. Chain-link fence approaches fast—

The van doesn't slow.

Metal screams as we tear through the barrier, chain links snapping like gunfire. Tires screech across wet pavement, and then we're inside the perimeter, engines howling, headlights blinding anything trying to hide in the shadows.

That's when we hear it.

*Crack-crack-crack.*

High-Spire MP5s, rune-etched barrels singing that distinct, echoing death-song that means professional operators are waiting for us. The sound ricochets off the Old Mint's stone walls, multiplying until it sounds like an entire army has decided tonight is when they end our story.

Cole's already pulling his revolvers, checking chambers by touch alone while his eyes stay locked on the windshield. "Contact."

Grimjaw yanks open the side door even as we're still moving, bismuth slugs ready, his roar cutting through the night: "Then let's give them something worth remembering!"

* * *

The gantry sways under my weight as I crouch low against the rusted iron railing, peering down through the phosphorescent haze that clings to everything in this godforsaken industrial graveyard. My breath comes sharp and shallow, each exhale crystallizing into needles of frost-coal that tinkle against the metal grating beneath my boots.

Below, maybe thirty feet straight down, Mara lies pinned beneath an overturned dumpster—its twisted iron frame smoking where it scraped across concrete. Blood pools around her in a widening halo of black, absorbing the sickly yellow light from the sodium arc lamps that flicker like dying stars along the loading dock walls.

"Commander," Grimjaw's gravelly voice crackles in my earpiece, "targets acquired. Three tangents, northeast corner. Two more moving up from the eastern alley."

I don't respond. Can't. The sight of Mara has driven all words from my throat. Her usual silver-white aura has gone gray—not the clean ash-gray of exhaustion, but something corrupted, tainted. Dark veins pulse through it like rot spreading through living flesh. Whatever she did to close that breach, whatever price she paid, it's written in the desecration of her magic.

One of Vane Thorne's hunters circles the dumpster, its movements too smooth, too fluid for human physiology. Enhanced. The bastard's been upgrading his pack again.

"Target the kinetic-shields first," I whisper into the Nextel, my voice carrying that same frost-chilled quality as the air around me. My blood-iron magic responds instinctively, reaching out to taste the condensation forming on every surface—a hundred tiny ice crystals beginning their slow crawl toward the railings, toward the support beams, toward anything metal within reach. "Bram, lay down suppressing fire on the Crown Vics. Keep them pinned in those blind spots."

A burst of automatic rifle fire erupts from Bram's position, the muzzle flashes painting the darkness in staccato bursts of orange and white. The two hunters near the alley entrance scatter, their shield generators sparking as rounds glance off the shimmering barriers.

"Grimjaw..." I shift my weight, feeling the gantry protest with a groan of tortured metal. "...you're with me. We're taking the hard way down."

"You're insane, boss. That's a three-story drop, and you're—"

"I know what I am." My fingers grip the railing until my knuckles go white, the cold biting deep enough to numb. "Synchronize targets. When I give the word, you take the southeast flank. No quarter."

The rusted grating beneath my feet suddenly screams in protest as I step forward, then sideways, then onto nothing but open air. For one heart-stopping moment, I'm falling—three stories of pure vertical descent with only the wind screaming past my ears and the distant wail of sirens echoing through the marshes beyond Pulaski Skyway.

My blood-iron magic flares violent crimson as it engages, creating a localized gravity-dampener that makes the fall feel like being sucked down a drain. The ground rushes up faster than physics should allow, faster than sanity should permit. I twist mid-plummet, drawing both pistols from their holsters in one fluid motion.

Vane Thorne stands over Mara, his back to me, hands raised in some arcane gesture that sends ripples of distorted space-time radiating outward. He hasn't noticed me yet—a fatal miscalculation on his part.

I fire three rounds into his back before he can react.

The first two punch through whatever defenses he managed to raise, red blooms spreading across his black coat like spilled wine. The third catches him center-mass, and I watch the life go out of his eyes even as his body continues the motion of turning toward me.

Grimjaw's assault rifle roars into action behind me, the heavy caliber rounds tearing through the remaining hunters with wet, organic finality. Their shields collapse in sequence, each pop accompanied by a brief flash of violet light.

I land hard enough to crack pavement, my knees buckling under the impact. Pain lances through my legs, up my spine, but I force myself upright anyway. Vane Thorne lies sprawled at my feet, his corrupted magic dissipating like morning fog, revealing the human wreckage beneath—middle-aged, scared, dying.

"Mara!" I drop beside her, sliding my hand under her shoulder. The moment I touch her skin, I feel the wrongness of her corruption like an electric shock. "Mara, look at me!"

Her eyes flutter open, silver-gray meeting mine. Blood trickles from the corner of her mouth.

"It's done," she whispers. "Commander... it's done."

But looking at the gray rot consuming her aura, I know it's not done at all. Not by half.

Behind us, Grimjaw's voice cuts through the aftermath: "Boss! Movement on the catwalk!"

I spin, pistols raised, frost-coal gathering around my fingers in preparation for another desperate gambit.

* * *

The world fractured into crystalline shards as something immense slammed down behind me, each impact reverberating through bone and asphalt alike. I felt the temperature plummet—my breath crystallizing before my lips in clouds of desperate relief.

"CONCENTRATE FIRE ON THE HUMAN! BREAK HIS WARDS!"

Thorne's voice cracked for the first time, that corporate veneer finally shattered by whatever nightmare had just descended on his kill zone. I couldn't look away from the iron dumpster pinning me, its weight absolute and crushing. Blood pooled beneath my ribs where splinters had found their mark, hot copper flooding my mouth.

Then the impossible happened.

He walked through their fire like it wasn't there.

Cole's boots hit ground zero of the hex-gun barrage, frost spreading outward from each footfall in geometric patterns of perfect preservation. The air itself screamed as it flash-freezed, each bullet that struck his wards exploding into harmless snow instead of tearing through flesh. His right hand came up, fingers splayed, and two IA hunters simply... stopped. Their kinetic shields flashed once—a soundless, blinding pulse—and then they were statues, cracks spiderwebbing across ceramic armor before both suits shattered into glittering dust storms.

"The fuck?" someone whispered from the line.

Grimjaw landed second, a thunderclap of displaced air and crumpling metal. The Crown Vic's hood buckled under his mass, aluminum screaming protest as he rolled off it smooth as water. That depleted-bismuth sledgehammer—still carrying the ghost-weight of fifty tons despite being half-empty now—swung in a lazy arc that caught a Hex-Aggression specialist across the shoulders. The impact sound was wrong: wet meat and shattering bone compressed into one terrible moment.

The Razor-Wire snipers opened up from their perches, but their rounds weren't meant to pierce wards. They were meant to sever limbs and puncture vitals. Not that it mattered.

Cole moved. Three steps through withering fire, each one leaving hoarfrost in his wake, the alley's temperature dropping so fast I could feel frost forming on my eyelashes. The dumpster pinning me groaned—metal shrieking as his hands closed around its edge.

"Vance!"

His voice cut through everything else. Deep. Stable. Real in a way that made the last three years feel like a fever dream I was finally waking from.

My eyes found him. Found those amber-gold eyes burning behind cobalt-blue flames that danced along his skin like tattoos come alive. His left hand was extended toward me even as his right tore the dumpster free, throwing it aside like trash.

"You look like hell," he said simply, kneeling beside me. Close enough that I felt the radiant heat bleeding off his wards. Close enough that the frost spreading from his knees began devouring the blood pooling beneath my ribs, cauterizing wounds I hadn't known were mortal until this second.

I couldn't speak. Couldn't breathe past the shock hammering my heart against fractured ribs. He was *there*. Alive. Whole. Standing between me and extinction while bullets sparked harmlessly against walls of frozen air.

"Why?" The word scraped out raw. "You're supposed to be dead."

"I am." A grim smile, teeth flashing white against the blue fire consuming his face. "Bram's been keeping score. Apparently 'dead' is negotiable when you owe someone a debt."

Behind him, Thorne was screaming into his comms, trying to call down orbital strikes, but Cole didn't spare him a glance. Those golden eyes stayed locked on mine, watching me with an intensity that burned hotter than any ward flame.

"Hurt bad?" he asked, like we were having coffee somewhere normal. Somewhere safe.

Before I could answer, before I could process the question, our hands touched.

His palm found mine, skin-to-skin, no buffer, no distance. And the world went white.

Not the clean white of snow or the sterile white of hospitals. This was something else entirely—raw power flooding through the point of contact, racing up my arm in waves of molten recognition. My white-lilac flame answered immediately, that core of me that had been tamped down, suppressed, locked away since 2005. It surged upward, desperate and starving for connection.

The fusion was violent. Beautiful. Catastrophic.

Frost met flame, ice met inferno, and where they touched they created something new: ash-gray static dissolved into nothingness as lilac-white fire consumed every last trace of charred wool stench clinging to my soul. My trauma—those memories of burning alive in an alley almost identical to this one—crackled once and then *scorched* clean from existence.

I gasped, arching off the ground as the 4th-Law reaction built between us. Cole's hand tightened around mine, his other arm bracing across my chest to keep me grounded while reality itself tried to tear apart at the seams around us.

"What the fuck did you do to yourself?!" His voice was strained now, barely human past the rumble of active wards. "You reworked your entire foundation! Mara, what—"

"Needed," I managed, forcing words through the pain and pleasure of it all. "To survive without you."

But even as I said it, even as my flames poured into him and his frost poured back into me, I knew. He'd never left. Not really. Just been waiting for someone to figure out how to call him home.

And now he was here.

---

## CHAPTER 8: THE COVENANT OF ASH AND LILAC

The bullet took me in the shoulder—not where I'd been aiming, but close enough to make my arm go numb. I went down hard against wet asphalt, the rain immediately soaking through my leather jacket. Through the rain-distorted view between two Crown Vics, I could see them surrounding the substation entrance: six Spire operatives in tactical gear, their weapons humming with that distinctive arcane resonance.

Then I saw her.

Mara stood in the doorway of Sub-Station Seven, backlit by the flickering emergency lights within. She looked like something dug up from a mass grave—hair plastered to her skull, her oversized hoodie hanging off one shoulder, revealing the ugly purple-green bruising that mapped her ribs like some sick constellation. But it was her eyes that stopped me cold. That ash-gray static I remembered from before she'd gone dark, now consuming everything. The glow of her corrupted wards pulsed around her in erratic waves of battery-acid yellow and sickly green.

"Fuck," I breathed, tasting copper on my tongue.

She didn't see me yet. Couldn't see past the fog of whatever the Weave had done to her mind. One of the Spire shooters raised his rifle, and I watched that muzzle-flash in slow motion as he sent a full-auto burst toward her chest.

Time compresses when you're running out of it.

I was already moving before my conscious brain caught up. My frost-cobalt magic flared hotter than it ever had—cold-burning ice that crystallized across every surface it touched. The bullets froze mid-flight, suspended in glittering crystalline prison-air. But I couldn't hold them long; the strain made my vision white at the edges.

So I did what I do best.

I threw myself between Mara and those frozen bullets.

They shattered against my back, each impact feeling like someone driving railroad spikes through bone. I crashed into Mara hard enough to knock us both backward, tumbling into the substation's entrance as hex-fire scorched the doorframe where we'd just been standing.

"Cole?" Her voice cracked like old leather.

"Still here." Blood ran warm down my spine. "Still annoying."

Her hands were on my face, fingers trembling so hard they vibrated against my skin. Those ash-gray eyes searched mine with desperate, feral intensity. "You're dead. I saw you die. I felt it when you died. Felt it tear through my chest like—"

"I know." My voice came out rougher than intended. "But you're looking right at me, aren't you?"

The sound of boots on wet pavement grew louder. Shouting. More shots.

I pulled Mara deeper into Sub-Station Seven's gloom, dragging her behind cover—a concrete pillar thick as a sequoia trunk. My shoulder screamed where the bullet had gone clean through muscle. Warm blood soaked my jacket, but adrenaline kept the worst of the pain at bay.

"What are you doing here?" she whispered, still holding onto my collar like I might evaporate if she let go. "Why did you come back? After what I—I killed those people, Cole. Killed them all. The Weave showed me everything. Every drop of blood. Every scream."

My frost-cobalt magic pulsed around us in protective spikes, their crystalline surfaces reflecting the emergency lights into fractured rainbows. But beneath that cold-burning surface, something else stirred—the deep hearth-coal warmth I usually kept buried. The part of myself I'd locked away after Newark, after watching too many people burn.

It bled into her.

I felt the exact moment it happened—the way her breathing changed, the sudden intake of air that wasn't quite a gasp. Her pupils dilated until there was almost no color left except for thin rings of brown. The ash-gray static in her mind went *silent*.

"Jesus," she breathed.

"The real one or the comic book version?" Despite everything, despite the blood and the gunfire and the Spire shooters probably breaching the door right now, I managed something close to a smile.

Her wards ignited.

Not with that battery-acid yellow or sickly green. Not with the suicidal self-destructive fury they'd possessed before. Instead, pure golden-lilac fire wrapped around my frost-cobalt spikes—a cascade of impossible beauty that shouldn't have been possible according to any law of thermodynamics or arcane physics.

The stench of charred wool evaporated instantly, replaced by fresh cedar and white-lilac—scents so clean and bright they hurt to breathe.

Mara's hands flew to her chest where her corrupted wards had burned for three years. Now they blazed with that same golden-lilac radiance, but different. *Cleaner*. Like someone had taken a filthy window and washed it until the glass gleamed.

"What did you do?" She stared at her hands like they belonged to someone else.

"I didn't do anything." I pulled her tighter behind cover as more shots rang out, hex-fire scorching concrete where we'd been half a second before. "You did this yourself. Been carrying it inside you all along."

The weight lifted from her spine—I could see it happen, watch her shoulders drop an inch as some massive burden simply... vanished. Her breathing steadied. Color returned to her face faster than should have been physically possible.

"You're alive," Mara said again, but differently this time. Wonder instead of denial. "You're actually alive."

"Yeah, well." I grimaced as I shifted position, sending another wave of blood down my back. "Try not to make it a habit of killing me off prematurely, okay? Bad for my reputation."

She laughed—actually laughed—and the sound was like breaking glass in reverse, each shard reassembling into something beautiful and whole.

Then she stepped out from behind our cover.

"No!" I grabbed for her arm, missed.

But what I saw made every word die in my throat.

Her golden-lilac wards expanded outward in a kinetic dome, growing larger by the second—a hemisphere of pure protective energy that caught the incoming barrage of High-Spire hex-fire. The impacts lit up the night like a fireworks display: bursts of emerald-green and crimson-orange detonating against that lilac barrier without even cracking its surface.

Mara stood at the center of it all, arms raised, eyes closed, her hair floating in a wind that came from nowhere.

She looked like she'd been born for this moment.

"Get ready to run," she said without opening her eyes, voice steady in a way I hadn't heard since before Sub-Station Seven had taken everything from her. "When this breaks, we move fast. There's someone I need you to meet inside."

The dome pulsed brighter, bright enough that the Spire shooters outside staggered backward, weapons smoking.

I pulled myself to my feet despite the screaming agony in my shoulder, frost-cobalt magic crystallizing across my knuckles. "Who?"

"The thing that's been living in Sub-Station Seven." Mara's smile would have been more comforting if it wasn't quite so sharp around the edges. "And trust me when I say—you're going to want to

* * *

The first round goes hot between my revolvers as Mara's fingers dance across reality itself—pure white-lilac flame licking from her palms like living light. We're moving together now, some fundamental frequency locked between us that transcends thought. My boots hit the wet asphalt in rhythm with her breath, two pistons in a machine built for killing.

"Two on the left! Heavy armor!"

I don't need to look. Her voice cuts through the chaos with surgical precision, all tactical shorthand learned from years of corporate security detail in places that no longer exist. The mercenaries in those high-end kinetic suits are trying to flank us, smart enough to recognize we're the real threat. They raise their assault rifles, but they're already dead—they just don't know it yet.

Mara's hex-blast slams into the lead suit. The lilac fire wraps around the armor plating like hungry serpents, and suddenly the man inside is screaming through his helmet. His partner stumbles back, shield generator sparking and dying. That's my cue.

The frost-cobalt rounds burn cold downrange. No hesitation. No remorse. Just the perfect weight of iron and the righteous anger that's been building since Voss put his hands on what was mine. Both men drop before they can process that their shields are gone. Blood hits the pavement—that copper smell mixing with ozone and the acrid tang of melting circuit boards.

"Reloading!" Grimjaw's voice rips through the night, that brutal Orcish bark cutting through everything else. The thunder of his shotgun has been our baseline percussion, keeping the reinforcements pinned at the mouth of the alley while Bram covers the other angle. I catch sight of the Dwarf—his face hidden behind his breathing apparatus, both barrels smoking as he works the pump action like he's been doing it since before steel was forged.

"They're running!" Grimjaw laughs, and there's something beautiful in that sound—genuine joy at watching High-Spire corporate security scramble over themselves to escape the slaughter we've brought to their doorstep. "Look at 'em! All those pretty suits don't mean shit when you're bleeding out!"

The third wave comes hard—a mixed unit of mercenaries and Elven retainers Voss must have pulled from whatever pocket dimension he keeps them in between jobs. Their formation is textbook, but textbooks don't account for Mara's improvisation or my complete lack of fucks to give.

"Incoming!"

I pivot right, revolvers tracking the first wave of elves. They move like water, all graceful lethality and enchanted blades that probably cost more than this entire block of warehouses. Doesn't matter. My frost-cobalt burns cold enough to freeze magic itself, and two more bodies join the growing collection painting the asphalt red.

Mara's on the left flank now, her flames creating a wall of disorienting light that sends the remaining elves stumbling into each other. Their white-gold armor melts under her assault, kinetic shielding popping like soap bubbles. She doesn't even look back as she coordinates with me:

"Six o'clock! Heavy weapons!"

There's a technician operating some kind of mobile railgun setup, trying to get a bead on our position. I can see his targeting reticle painting us in crimson. Can feel the way the air compresses around the projectile as it builds charge.

My revolvers speak before he can fire. Double-tap center mass. The man's chest explodes outward in a spray of blood and bone fragments, his expensive equipment shorting out as the rounds punch through circuitry and flesh alike.

"Target down!" Mara calls out, already moving forward. "We're breaching the doors!"

She's right—the loading bay entrance to the Old Mint looms ahead, massive steel construction designed to handle military vehicles and probably worth more than anything inside. The mercenaries who haven't fled are making a stand there, forming a defensive line behind makeshift barricades welded together from shipping containers.

Grimjaw lays down suppressing fire, his shotgun tearing chunks out of the barriers while Bram provides covering arcs. We move as one unit—Mara's hex-blasts softening the defenses, my bullets punching through the gaps she creates, both of us feeding off each other's momentum like we were built for this exact scenario.

The doors themselves are impressive—hydraulic mechanisms and enough steel to withstand a siege. But nothing's perfect, and where there's mechanism there's weakness. I spot the access panel, half-hidden behind corroded piping.

"Cover me!" I shout, breaking formation long enough to slam my shoulder into the maintenance hatch. It gives way with a screech of protesting metal, spilling out a cascade of wires and hydraulic lines. My fingers find the emergency override—a big red lever that's probably illegal on three different continents—and I yank it hard enough to feel something tear in my rotator cuff.

The doors groan open, revealing darkness beyond.

That's when I see him—Vane Thorne, backlit by some interior light source, his face twisted in something between fury and calculation. He's already moving backward, his coat billowing dramatically as he raises one hand toward what looks like an ancient runestone mounted on the wall.

"Cole! No!"

But Mara's warning comes too late. The stone pulses once—brilliant blue-white lightning arcing across its surface—and then Voss is gone, swallowed by shadows that seem deeper than they should be. Behind him, secondary blast doors slam shut with a finality that makes my teeth ache.

Bram stalks forward, shotgun leveled at those doors. "Telluric mine. Fresh charge."

"We need to—"

The ground beneath our feet hums with accumulated energy. Whatever Voss just armed is big enough to level half the block if we breach those doors conventionally. Grimjaw spins around, breathing hard inside his helmet:

"He's using us for bait now. Sinking son of a bitch thinks he can wait us out."

I look at Mara, catching her eye over the barrel of my revolver. There's blood on her face—whether hers or someone else's I can't tell—and her flames have dimmed to barely visible embers dancing between her fingers.

"I'm not waiting," she says quietly. "We're going through."

* * *

The mine detonated inside our ward like a star collapsing into itself.

For one frozen heartbeat, I felt the weight of it—a thousand tons of compressed Telluric energy trying to tear through our combined magic. My forearms screamed where white-hot power surged from my core, mixing with Mara's pristine white-lilac radiance. Her hands were clasped against my chest, fingers digging into my ribs hard enough to bruise, but I barely noticed. The air crackled and hissed inside our containment sphere, reality bending around us like fabric stretched taut over a drumhead.

Then it was over.

A muffled *thump* rippled outward instead of an explosion. The Telluric charge had nowhere to go but back into itself, consuming its own destructive potential in a feedback loop we'd created together. Mara stumbled backward, breathing hard, her face pale except for two spots of color high on her cheeks. Behind where she'd been standing, the floor showed a perfect circle of scorched concrete, black and glassy at the edges.

"Jesus Christ," she whispered.

I didn't answer. Didn't have breath to spare. My focus narrowed down to a pinpoint as I reached out with blood-iron sense, feeling for the lock mechanisms in those secondary blast doors. There—three of them, massive steel bolts sunk deep into reinforced frames. They gleamed red-gold in my inner sight, almost alive with potential energy waiting to be shaped.

My knuckles whitened around nothing as I gripped them in mind rather than hand.

The first bolt groaned, metal screaming as I twisted it counterclockwise. Hydraulic fluid hissed. The second gave way easier, already compromised by age and neglect. The third took everything I had left—not just strength but will, poured into the molten iron of its construction until I felt the threads strip, the mechanism tear free from its housing with a sound like ripping canvas magnified a thousand times.

Steel shrieked.

The doors swung inward.

Beyond them lay darkness so complete it seemed solid, a wall of absence that swallowed even the emergency lighting bleeding through cracks in the ceiling. But underneath that emptiness ran current—copper-thick Telluric power humming through busbars retrofitted into architecture older than the grid itself. The Old Mint. Pylon #4's heart. Voss was in there somewhere, waiting.

I grabbed Mara's wrist—not gently—and pulled her with me across the threshold. "Bram, Grimjaw! Hold the perimeter. Nobody gets in or out." The Nextel crackled against my hip as Bram's gravelly voice responded: "Copy that, Reyes. We'll turn this alley into a meatgrinder. Go get Voss."

The doors slammed shut behind us with a finality that made my teeth ache.

We stood alone in cathedral-sized silence punctuated only by the distant drip of water echoing off unseen surfaces. My hearth-coal ward still pulsed around us both, mixing now with faint traces of white-lilac where our magic had touched during the containment. It felt... different somehow. Not separate anymore but braided together, two colors wound around each other until you couldn't tell where one ended and the other began.

Mara pressed closer to my side, her hand finding mine in the dark. Her fingers were cold.

"Can you see anything?" she asked quietly.

Yeah. I could see everything—or at least enough to make out the vast industrial space opening before us. The Old Mint's original vaulted ceilings stretched away into shadow, reinforced concrete arches that would have looked right at home in some forgotten European monastery if not for the glowing copper busbars snaking between them like veins carrying poisoned blood. They pulsed in time with something deep below, rhythmic and hungry.

And standing at the far end of it all—maybe fifty yards away across open floor—I saw him.

Voss.

He wasn't moving. Just standing there in a posture that suggested either meditation or death, hands hanging loosely at his sides. But even from here I could feel the distortion around him, space warping under the weight of what he'd become.

"Cole," Mara whispered urgently. "What is that smell?"

I breathed in carefully through my mouth because yeah—the air tasted wrong down here. Like burnt sugar mixed with ozone and underneath it something organic and rotting. Flesh left too long in heat maybe. Or corpses.

"Stay behind me," I said.

We started walking toward Voss, our footsteps echoing off surfaces too far apart to be walls—these must have been loading bays once upon a time, spaces designed for heavy machinery and pallets of precious metals waiting to be minted into currency. Now they just waited empty except for dust and the copper busbars growing thicker as we approached, until they formed something almost like pillars supporting nothing but their own weight and the terrible pressure of Telluric energy flowing through them.

The closer we got, the harder it became to ignore how quiet everything was.

No drip of water anymore. No hum from the busbars. Even our footsteps seemed muffled now by something that might have been distance or might have been the way reality bent around Voss's presence.

Mara squeezed my hand three times—our old signal from the South Side: *I trust you.*

I squeezed back twice: *Trust yourself more.*

Then we were close enough to see his face.

And I wish we weren't.

---

## CHAPTER 9: GHOSTS OF THE GRID

The Old Mint looms over us like a cathedral dedicated to sin itself. Our tactical flashlights cut thin fingers through the darkness, illuminating dust motes that drift lazily in air thick with the scent of decayed currency and ancient machine oil. The beam catches copper busbars rising from floor to ceiling—twisted serpents of metal that pulse with a faint green luminescence from Pylon #4's Telluric core below.

"Jesus," Cole mutters beside me, his breath visible in the cold. His frost-cobalt eyes scan the impossible architecture surrounding us. "This place..."

I know what he sees. I see it too—the way the industrial space opens into vaulted chambers that shouldn't exist in any structure meant purely for minting coins. This is something else. Something darker. The shadows here don't behave like normal shadows. They pool in corners where light should reach them, they cling to vertical surfaces as if gravity has no claim on their movement.

"This was Julian Sterling's pride," I say quietly, my voice swallowed by the vastness of the space. "Before Elias Morvain tore it down to build his empire. Or maybe..." I pause, running my hand along one of the busbars, feeling the faint vibration of charge building beneath tons of concrete and steel. "...maybe Sterling built this knowing Morvain would come."

Cole looks at me sharply. "What are you talking about?"

But I can't answer him yet because the architecture itself is speaking to me. Those soaring ceilings supported by iron pillars thick as redwoods—they're designed to make whoever enters feel small. Insignificant. Like ants scurrying through the ribs of some great sleeping beast. It reminds me of the Morvain Estate, though that house wore its opulence openly while this structure hides its grandeur behind rusted doors and forgotten entrances.

"I hate this place," I whisper, surprising myself with the venom in my own voice. My reflection fragments across the copper surface before me—dozens of Maras staring back with different expressions. Some angry. Some afraid. All haunted. "I hate everything it represents."

The Telluric core pulses again, stronger now, and somewhere far below us something metallic groans in response. The green glow intensifies momentarily, casting our shadows long and distorted against walls stained with a century of grime.

"What did they do to you?" Cole asks gently.

I laugh bitterly, the sound echoing strangely off the vaulted ceiling. "Everything. They did everything." 

I start walking deeper into the structure, following corridors that branch off from the main chamber like arteries. Each step echoes. Everything echoes here except for what matters most—that silence inside me where my real thoughts live.

"Elias and Malvourne..." The names taste like ash on my tongue. "They built me for this. They put the weight of Sub-Station Seven on my spine before I was even born. I'm just a product of a bloodline I never chose."

My hand trembles as I hold up my flashlight, illuminating more busbars, more iron pillars, more evidence of ambition so vast it could only end in ruin.

"Do you know what it's like?" I continue without waiting for his answer. "Knowing every decision you've made has been filtered through their designs? That every victory belongs to them because they engineered your bones to carry its weight?" I turn to face him fully now, letting him see whatever expression is written on my face. "I spent years hating myself, Cole. Years convincing myself that I deserved Sub-Station Seven because maybe... maybe if I'd been stronger or smarter or different somehow..."

The words catch in my throat but I push forward.

"...maybe I wouldn't have been such a perfect weapon for them."

The Telluric core builds its charge beneath us—thrumming like a heartbeat or a countdown. Dust continues its slow dance through our flashlight beams. And somewhere in these cathedral shadows forged by men who measured their legacies in corpses and chaos, Cole stops walking.

He turns to face me fully, and when he does, something extraordinary happens—the frost-cobalt in his eyes melts away entirely. Just... gone. Leaving behind only raw, human empathy that catches me off guard with its intensity.

"Mara," he says simply.

* * *

I watch her face as she sits there, shoulders curved inward like she's trying to contain something that wants to explode outward. My Zippo clicks open, shut, open again—the metal warm from my palm, a mechanical prayer I don't even realize I'm performing anymore.

"You want to know why we do this?" The words come out rougher than I intend, gravel scraped across concrete. "Why I drag you into the muck when every instinct screams to walk away?"

The marsh air tastes like rust and diesel fuel. Somewhere in the darkness beyond Sub-Station Seven, something metallic groans—a freight train maybe, or just the earth settling its bones. I can feel the Telluric radiation pressing against my hearth-coal magic like a fist against a door, and my heart beats steady, steady, holding it back.

"The answer isn't pretty." I flip the Zippo again. Click. Click. "You think about your 314 deaths, right? Every single one of them. You carry that weight."

Mara's head lifts slightly, her eyes finding mine in the half-light filtering through the station's grimy windows.

"Danny's still in that Arcane Iron-Lung, Mara. Still breathing the same sludge that killed all those commuters. Eight hundred thousand gallons of poison, and he swallowed some of it before I got him clear. Now he's got black iron growing in his lungs like trees, roots choking him from the inside out." I press my free hand against my chest, feeling the blood-iron hexes sewn into my vest, their familiar weight. "Every breath he takes is harder than the last. Every day, I wait for the phone call saying they couldn't save him."

I step closer, close enough to see the individual strands of silver threading through her dark hair.

"We're both weapons, you and me. Forged in trauma, quenched in black iron and ancient magic we never asked for." My voice drops lower, raw edge gone smooth as obsidian. "What we do—this revenge, this violence—I'm not gonna lie to you and say it matters. Killing Voss won't bring back your 314 victims. It won't cure Danny. Won't scrape the iron out of his lungs or undo whatever hell you've lived through across however many lifetimes you're carrying."

The Zippo clicks shut one final time. I slip it into my pocket and reach up, pulling the canvas strap of my tactical vest—a gesture that grounds me, reminds me what I am when everything else tries to dissolve into nightmare.

"But here's the thing." I lean forward just slightly, holding her gaze. "This sliver of justice? The one we might carve out with our bare hands if we have to? It's all we have. We didn't choose our bloodlines, Mara. Didn't ask for the magic that runs hot in our veins or the ghosts that haunt our footsteps. But we *do* choose who we point the gun at. We choose whether we're victims or something more."

My hand moves to rest on the hexes over my heart, feeling them pulse in time with my heartbeat—that steady rhythm that keeps the Telluric radiation from boiling my bones to ash.

"Is it enough?" I shake my head slowly, once. "Never. It's never enough. There's always another monster waiting in the dark, another wrong that needs righting, another price to pay. But 'never enough' is still better than nothing at all."

I take another step closer now, close enough that she could reach out and touch me if she wanted to.

"So yeah, I drag you into the muck. Because someone has to stand between the predators and their prey. Someone has to be the monster the monsters fear." My voice softens, barely above a whisper now. "And if that someone has to be us—you, with your 314 deaths weighing on your soul, me with Danny's iron-lungs counting down every second—I'll take that burden gladly."

The marsh falls silent around us, even the distant groan of metal ceased. In this moment, there's only us and the weight of what we carry, the choice we've made to carry it anyway.

Mara reaches out then, her fingers hesitant at first, then firmer as they settle over the blood-iron hexes on my chest. She can feel it—the steady, unbroken rhythm of my heart, the heat radiating outward in waves that keep the darkness at bay.

"We're tied together now," she says quietly, and I know she feels it too: the threefold cord woven between her deaths and my duty, between Danny's lungs and our shared refusal to let the world stay broken.

* * *

The ash-gray static finally died.

One moment it was there—a constant whisper behind my eyes, like nails scraping across bone—and the next, silence. True silence. I could feel Cole's magic winding through mine now, not fighting it but supporting it, two currents finding their natural balance after years of turbulence.

I opened my eyes.

Golden light—warm, real, *ours*—poured from our joined hands, casting long shadows across the vault floor. The Pylon hummed above us, indifferent to what had just transpired below its foundations. Outside, I could still hear the muffled crack of gunfire, shouts, the chaos we'd left behind when we descended here. But in this moment, in this dark space beneath the grid, time seemed to hold its breath.

Cole's hand was warm against mine. Not fever-hot anymore. Just... human. He looked different somehow—not softer exactly, but less haunted. The perpetual tension in his jaw had eased.

"Penance, revenge, and a sliver of justice," I said quietly, watching our combined light play across the ancient brick walls. The words came unbidden, pulled from somewhere deep. "That's what we've been carrying."

He didn't look surprised that I'd spoken. His green eyes met mine, clear for the first time since I'd known him. "The Threefold Cord." A slow nod. "It holds us together—or tears us apart. Depends on whether you're willing to share the weight."

"And you are?"

His thumb brushed over my knuckles once, twice. The gesture was almost reverent. "I am. If you can forgive your mother's bloodline enough to stop blaming yourself."

My throat tightened. How did he—I glanced down at our joined hands, understanding flooding through me. The psychogenic bleed hadn't just stabilized; it had become something else entirely. We weren't just linked anymore. We were transparent to each other in ways that should have terrified me but instead felt like coming home.

"I spent so long hating what she made me," I admitted, voice rough. "What the BATC forged me into."

"Not just the BATC." Cole's expression was gentle but honest. "Your father too. That genetic cocktail they used—it was never going to create anything ordinary."

"No." I laughed bitterly. "Just another weapon for the arsenal."

"Mara." He waited until I looked up again. "You stopped being anyone's weapon the moment you chose to come after Voss instead of reporting him. You could have let someone else handle this. Should have. But you didn't because deep down, you knew only you could stop him—not as a commander, not as an Aegis, but as the daughter who understood exactly what he was capable of becoming."

The golden light flared brighter between us.
