Outside, the sounds of combat grew more distant, or perhaps we simply couldn't hear them anymore. Our combined magic had created a pocket of reality here, separate and whole. I wanted to stay in it forever. Wanted to exist in this moment where forgiveness tasted like lilac and copper, where holding his hand meant holding onto my own humanity.

Then the proximity alarm shrieked.

Electronic and harsh, it cut through our sanctuary like a knife. Marcus Voss's voice echoed over the Old Mint's PA system: *"Did you two lovebirds finish bonding? I've got your friends cornered on Sub-Level Three. Tick-tock, Commander."*

Cole moved instantly, pulling me toward a dark doorway that led deeper into Pylon #4's abandoned minting offices. His hand gripped my arm—not rough, but urgent. The golden light extinguished as our magic pulled inward, defensive now rather than radiant.

"There's something you need to know," he said, urgency threading through every word as we ducked into what must have been some kind of counting room. Paper littered the floor, yellowed with age. Frost-cobalt spread from Cole's fingertips across the walls, creating a sound-dampening field. "Before we face him. Something about why he really came back to Neon Hollow."

I caught his eyes in the dim light filtering through the frost. Whatever he was about to tell me, it wasn't good. The way his jaw had tightened again, the fear flickering through those green depths—

"What is it?"

---

## CHAPTER 10: THE WATCHING PARTY

The oak door slams shut behind us with a thunderous crack that echoes through the abandoned minting office. I jam the iron deadbolt home—old magic, older than the concrete walls themselves—and twist the hex lock into place. The mechanism groans, and blue light traces along the seal like angry veins.

"Don't move," I tell Mara, already sweeping the perimeter. My boots crunch over broken glass from some dead executive's Panasonic Toughbook, its screen spider-webbed and dark. Dust hangs thick in the air, disturbed by our entrance, catching the weak emergency lights strung overhead. Everything smells like rust and old money.

She's breathing hard, one hand pressed to her shoulder where the bullet caught her. Not deep—I saw it graze—but bleeding enough to matter. I yank my trauma kit from the vest, toss it onto the mahogany desk beside ledgers stamped "1997 PROPERTY OF FEDERAL RESERVE." The wood is scarred with cigarette burns and coffee rings, somebody's forgotten battle station from before everything went sideways.

"You're gonna feel this," I mutter, ripping open an alchemical antiseptic pack. The Gnome stuff reeks like burning copper and hospital disinfectant mixed together. Mara flinches as I douse the wound.

"Fuck!" She hisses through clenched teeth.

"Voss is locking down the core. We have less than ten minutes before he arms the Pylon." I don't look up from the field dressing, packing gauze against the bleeding. My hands are steady. They always are when there's work to do.

"I know," she says. "Cole..."

But I'm not ready yet. Instead, I focus on the sterile technique, the procedure. Wrap the bandage tight around her shoulder, make sure the seal holds. Anything to keep from saying what needs to be said. The revolvers click as I reload them mechanically—left cylinder, right cylinder, count the brass, check the powder. The familiar weight settles back into my palms.

There. Done. No more excuses.

I look at her finally, really *look* at her, and I see my own fear reflected in her eyes. She knows something's coming. Something bad.

"We need to move," Mara insists, already reaching for her weapon.

"No."

The word comes out harder than I mean it, but she stops. The gravity of it makes her turn back, study my face. Whatever she sees there makes her blood run cold—I can tell by the way her color drains.

"Sit down."

It's not a request.

She sits, slow and careful, lowering herself onto the edge of the desk. Her hand finds one of the ledgers for support. The leather creaks under her weight. Outside, I hear Voss's machines humming through the walls—the core waking up, hungry and ready.

"The truth," I say, because that's where this has to start. "About why I'm alive. About who pulled me out of that warehouse three years ago when you all thought I was dead."

Her breathing stops. Completely.

"You're going to hate me when I'm finished."

* * *

I pull the modified Nokia from my jacket pocket, its black chassis scarred with burn marks and custom-welded antenna arrays. The screen glows sickly green in the half-light of Sub-Station Seven, scrolling text that would look like gibberish to anyone without the key.

"BATC's algorithms can't see this," I tell Mara, keeping my voice low even though we're alone in the maintenance tunnel. "Too primitive. Their satellite grid looks for standard communication patterns—cell towers, WiFi nodes, fiber optics. This network operates in the gaps. The seams."

She leans closer, her reflection doubling on the display. The text continues its endless crawl:

`[WATCHER-7] STATUS VERIFY: PULASKI SKYWAY SENSOR GRID ACTIVE`
`[WATCHER-12] MOVEMENT ALERT: THREE UNITS CONFIRMED BOUND FOR KEARNY MARSHES 0400 HRS`
`[ARCHON-NODE] AUTHENTICATION PENDING: REYES-CODE OMEGA`

"The Gnomes didn't build this network for fun, Mara." I swipe through screens with practiced precision. "It was commissioned. Financed. Every move BATC makes, the Watching Party sees it."

The fluorescent tube overhead flickers, casting everything in stutter-step shadows. The frost-ward hums its constant warning against the cold creeping up from the tunnels below—the old blood-magic still keeping our breath from fogging in air that should freeze lungs solid.

"They've been orchestrating this shadow-war for years." My thumb hovers over a menu option labeled `ARCHON-PROTOCOL`. "Waiting for the right moment to strike Elias and Malvourne."

Mara's eyes narrow as she studies the scrolling feed. Her fingers trace the air above the screen, following lines of code that make no sense to anyone outside the arcano-theory circles. She knows something about this encryption. I can see it in how her breathing changes—shallow, calculated.

"This is High-Spire syntax," she says quietly. Too quiet. Like she's afraid someone might hear us discussing it. "This cryptographic structure... I thought it went extinct during the Purge. Who the hell is running the Watching Party?"

I let the question hang in the damp air between us. The pager's antenna array catches interference from somewhere deeper in the station—a distant radio transmission bleeding through frequencies that shouldn't connect. Static crackles through hidden speakers, the ghost of voices speaking words just beyond comprehension.

"Does it matter?" I finally answer. "They saved my life when Elias's assassins put eight bullets through me on the South Side. Extracted me before the meat-wagon could arrive. Patched me up in some forgotten medical facility underneath Hackensack. Kept me alive while my body learned to reject the damage."

My hand unconsciously moves to the scar tissue at my side, feeling the raised welts where medical tech that predates BATC by decades stitched my guts back together.

"The Gnomes are their field agents—they're the ones running these transponders, maintaining the network." I toggle the display again. New text appears: `PASSED-AUTH: WATCHER-CODE OMEGA GRANTED FULL ACCESS`. "But the Watching Party? They're something else entirely. Strategic minds playing a game that spans years, decades maybe. They know things about the Breach that Malvourne would kill to learn."

The pager beeps—three sharp tones that make Mara flinch. An incoming message:

`[ARCHON-NODE] ALERT: YOUR PRESENCE REQUIRED NEON HOLLOW 2300 HRS`
`[ARCHON-NODE] BRING THE MACHINIST. WE HAVE SOMETHING TO SHOW YOU`

"What the hell is Neon Hollow?" Mara asks, but she's already reaching for her weapon—a compact pistol that looks absurdly small in her grip.

"A place you don't want to visit," I tell her, pocketing the pager. "But apparently we don't have a choice."

I stand, joints protesting after too many hours cramped in this maintenance tunnel. The frost-ward pulses once—warning or acknowledgment, it's hard to say—and then settles into its rhythm again. Somewhere above us, through layers of concrete and rebar and abandoned infrastructure, the world continues its oblivious march toward midnight.

"We've got four hours," I say. "Plenty of time to prepare."

Mara holsters her pistol with practiced efficiency. Her eyes are still fixed on where the pager disappeared into my jacket.

"High-Spire syntax doesn't just come back from extinction, Cole." She meets my gaze, and there's fear there—not of death or danger, but of knowledge. Of what knowing might cost. "Someone preserved it. Trained people in its use. That kind of infrastructure requires resources, protection, intelligence networks..."

"And?"

"Whoever they are, whatever the Watching Party represents—they're not street vigilantes like you." She steps closer, voice dropping to almost nothing. "They're playing chess while everyone else thinks it's checkers. And if they've been waiting years to make their move..." 

She doesn't finish. Doesn't need to.

The transponder beeps again: `ACKNOWLEDGE OR DENY`.

I pull it out, thumb hovering over the screen. Mara watches as I type a single character: Y.

`[ARCHON-NODE] CONFIRMED. EXPECT US.`

The message disappears. The screen goes black. In the sudden darkness before the green glow returns, I swear I see something reflected in Mara's pupils—a flash of light from deep within the tunnels below, like distant headlights emerging from water.

Or maybe it was just the flicker.

Either way, we have an appointment in Neon Hollow at eleven PM sharp.

And whatever waits for us there has been planning this moment for longer than either of us can imagine.

* * *

# THE WATCHING PARTY

The silence hits me first—not the comfortable kind, but the suffocating void that follows when the world decides to stop making sense. My frost-cobalt ward still hums around us both, a thin blue shell keeping the worse parts of this place at bay while I try to find the words that won't tear her apart.

Mara stands there, breathing hard, her hands still smoking from whatever she did to those elves. Her eyes are wide, pupils dilated in the red emergency lighting that bleeds across every surface like old blood. The mahogany desk behind her casts shadows that look too long, too hungry.

"They're alive," I say quietly. The words feel wrong in my mouth, like I'm speaking someone else's language. "Both of them."

Pylon #4 groans above us. Dust rains down from the ceiling in lazy spirals, each particle catching the crimson light. Somewhere deep in its core, something massive shifts—metal against metal, the sound of impossible weight adjusting itself.

"Lysandra didn't die in the fire." I watch her face as I speak, cataloging every micro-expression because I know what's coming. "And Elena didn't die in the clinic fire either. It was all staged. They faked their deaths to escape the Visible Heads."

The floor trembles. Not much, just enough to make my teeth ache.

Mara doesn't move. Doesn't breathe. She's carved from ice and shock, her white-lilac wards flickering around her fingers like trapped moths trying to remember how to fly.

"The Watching Party isn't some random collection of survivors," I continue, harder now because softening it would be cruel and I've never been accused of being cruel when the truth needs telling. "They're organized. Coordinated. And they've been running the resistance from the Undercity for years. Every safe house, every contact point, every piece of intelligence that's made it through the lockdown?"

I take a step closer, close enough to see the way her hands are shaking.

"It came from them."

The silence stretches until I can hear the blood rushing in my own ears. Pylon #4 shudders again, more violently this time. A crack spiderwebs across the concrete wall behind Mara, spreading like a frozen river.

"My mother is alive?" The words come out strangled, barely audible over the grinding of stressed metal. Her voice cracks on the last syllable.

"Yes."

"Elena Reyes. My mother." She repeats it like a mantra, like if she says it enough times it might become real in a way that doesn't hurt. "She's been... what? Hiding? Coord—" Another tremor cuts off her words as something deep below us detonates with a sound like God's fist slamming into stone.

The lights flicker. Die. Come back weaker than before.

And then we hear it—a voice booming through speakers I didn't even know existed, filling the Old Mint with such absolute authority that my ward flares bright blue in response:

"You've given me no choice, Reyes."

Marcus Voss.

"I'm sealing the blast doors. Pylon #4 is locked down. Your little reunion ends here."

The floor lurches beneath our feet. Warning klaxons begin screaming somewhere distant, their wails bouncing off cavern walls until they're everywhere at once.

"But I believe in fairness," Voss continues, and there's something almost cheerful in his tone that makes my stomach turn. "So I'll give you this: I'm releasing the Ogre-Kin thralls from containment. All twenty-three of them. Venom-bound and hungry. Let's see how well your mother's training holds up when the Undercity tries to digest you both alive."

The shaking intensifies. Concrete dust fills the air, coating everything in gray powder. Mara stumbles backward against the desk, her wards flaring brilliant white-lilac for just a moment before the ash-gray static tries to choke them again.

"The copper vat is still active," Voss says. "Find it. Survive. Maybe you'll earn the right to meet the women who abandoned you both."

The line goes dead.

And beneath us, in the deepest chambers where light has never touched and life should not exist, something begins to move.

---

## CHAPTER 11: CHAPTER 11

I taste copper in my mouth again—the old familiar burn when adrenaline spikes hard enough to make you feel like your own teeth are trying to tear through your gums from the inside. The smoking ruin of what used to be Voss's High-Spire strike team spreads across thirty meters of cracked concrete, the bodies still steaming where the thermic charges went off. Elven tech doesn't stop burning right away. It cooks.

"Contact!" Cole's voice cuts through the acrid smoke behind me—sharp, controlled. His rifle's already tracking movement somewhere in the upper galleries. I don't turn around. Can't afford to break visual on the primary gantry above us.

Voss is there. Of course he fucking is.

Marcus Voss—Visible Head #2 of Biological Asset Tracking Corporation—stands at his terminal like some kind of armored god, the bespoke suit catching the sodium-vapor glare in sickly yellow highlights. His fingers punch keys with the casual confidence of a man who owns every room he walks into. And right now? This whole godforsaken Old Mint is his room.

The stolen PalmPilot in my pocket vibrates so hard it feels like someone's jammed a cell phone against my hipbone, buzzing bone-deep. The encrypted display scrolls past numbers that mean nothing to anyone without the right decryption key—which I definitely have after we pulled it off that dead High-Spire lieutenant back in the pulaski skyway standoff last week. The override code flashes once, twice, then locks.

*CLANG.*

The sound hits before my ears even register it—a physical thing that slams into my chest and rattles my ribs. Foot-thick steel, reinforced with rune-etched titanium alloy, dropping from overhead. Four separate blast doors, each one big enough to swallow a transport truck, slamming down over the extraction tunnels.

We're sealed inside the smelting cavern now.

"Vance!" Cole's close enough that I can smell the sweat under his tactical vest. "Commander!"

"I know." My voice comes out steady. No tremor. Not even a hint of what used to shake through my words back in 2005 when the Breach first came tearing through Neon Hollow and turned my whole precinct into meat-paste and screaming ghosts.

Above us, Voss's voice booms through the PA system—that corporate smoothness layered over something colder underneath:

"You street-level roaches think a few dead Elven suits makes this a victory? You're in BATC territory now."

The PalmPilot bucks again in my pocket. The biological signature reader's going haywire—massive heat blooms registering across all fourteen lower holding pens simultaneously. Something's being released down there. Something big enough to spike readings through three meters of reinforced concrete and another two of active lead shielding.

"Cole," I say, still not turning around, still tracking Voss's position on the gantry, "you reading those bios?"

"Fuck yes I am." His rifle shifts angle—now covering both the upper galleries AND the floor grates. Smart. "Commander, those numbers are wrong. That much mass displacement would mean—"

"—something that eats BATC High-Spire strike teams for breakfast and comes back asking for seconds." I finally turn to face him, meeting his eyes just long enough to make sure he sees mine: cold, clear, professional. "We hold this position until backup arrives or we go down fighting."

The sodium-vapor lamps flicker. Power draw's spiking—something massive is drawing juice from the lower levels' generator array.

*HISS.*

That sound shouldn't be possible. Hydraulic release mechanisms are supposed to be silent—smooth enough that you don't even notice them operating. But what echoes up from beneath our feet isn't smooth. It's angry. It's hungry.

The steel plates of the floor grate buck upward with a screech of tortured metal.

* * *

The grates explode upward in a shower of twisted metal shrapnel. I drop flat as the first one comes through—the thing is nine feet of corded muscle slicked in black venous fluid that steams where it hits the smelting floor.

"Apep's teeth," Cole hisses beside me. His MP5 comes up immediately, the rune-work along the barrel glowing faint orange in the low light.

The Ogre-Kin doesn't even flinch when the rounds impact its chest. *Plink-plink-plink*—spent casings ping against concrete like coins dropped down a well. The bullets carom away uselessly off subdermal plating, leaving only shallow dents in grayish flesh that weeps that same viscous black sludge.

Two more emerge from the ventilation shaft, then three more. Six total. Each one moves with that wrong, jerking momentum—a puppet on strings visible only to some godless master.

Voss's mercenaries open fire. Automatic rifle reports echo through the cavernous space, but the Ogre-Kin wade forward like walking siege engines. One merc—wearing tactical armor and carrying what looks like an FN P90—is grabbed by a massive hand. The fingers close. There's no sound except wet tearing fabric and the crunch of bone before the thing drops two halves onto the ground.

"Shit! Shit!" Another merc throws himself backward into cover behind a support pillar, but he's already too slow. An Ogre-Kin is on him, those dead eyes reflecting nothing but hunger, venom dripping from its mouth in thick cords that sizzle on contact with the floor.

The chemical reek hits me then—not just sewage anymore, but something else underneath. Something ancient and hungry wearing a skin of corrupted flesh.

Cole fires again, full auto now, red tracers stitching across the nearest Ogre-Kin's torso. Still nothing. The thing keeps coming, each footfall shaking the ground.

Grimjaw slides into position beside Cole, his rotary shotgun already cycling. "Boss, these ain't standard muscle!" He pumps the fore-end, chambering rounds the size of my thumb. "Voss pumped 'em full of that deep-drain drek. They're meat-puppets!"

I see it then—the cybernetic control-collar bolted into each neck. Thick as a man's fist, bristling with diodes that pulse in sickly green rhythm. The chains connecting them to... somewhere below. Somewhere darker.

"The collars!" I shout over the gunfire, pointing. "Target the collars, not center mass!"

*Clack-clack*—empty magazines hit the concrete. Someone's out.

Grimjaw's rotary barks, buckshot hammering into an Ogre-Kin's shoulder in a spray of red and black. The thing staggers sideways, roaring, and for a moment I think we have a chance—but then it straightens, reaches down, and rips the torn muscle apart with its bare hands before tossing the ruined limb aside like garbage.

"Can't get through the plating!" Cole sweeps his MP5 up, trying again. The runes flare brighter now—some kind of ward-work, maybe, against venom or corruption. Still ineffective.

Another merc goes down, crushed under an Ogre-Kin's boot. The wet crunch makes my stomach turn even as I raise my sidearm and open fire at the blinking diodes on the nearest thrall's collar.

The first shot sparks off steel. The second hits a diode dead-on.

The effect is immediate. The Ogre-Kin freezes mid-lunge, those black eyes widening in something almost like surprise. Then the body goes slack, collapsing forward onto the concrete with enough force to crack the foundation beneath it.

"Yes! Collars!" I pivot, firing twice more at another one. One round misses—they're moving faster now, learning. But the second catches the diode, and that Ogre-Kin drops too.

Two down. Four still coming.

One of them veers toward Grimjaw's position. The orc sandhog works the pump-action again—*clack*—and fires point-blank into the collar. The Ogre-Kin's head snaps backward, servos screaming, before it topples over.

Three down. Three left.

The lead one—the first through the grate—locks those dead eyes on me. It's covered in black sludge from neck to waist where the fluid has pooled in folds of skin. When it opens its mouth, I can see teeth corroded green.

And then it does something I don't expect.

It reaches out to where the forklift sits parked twenty feet away. Just grabs it. Two tons of industrial machinery lifted like a baseball bat.

"MARA!" Cole screams.

I dive sideways as the forklift hurls toward where I was standing. Metal crashes against concrete so hard the entire substation shudders. Sparks shower everywhere where the impact tears through electrical conduits overhead.

My shoulder hits the ground hard enough to knock the wind from my lungs. Above me, an Ogre-Kin is already closing in, reaching down with hands that could tear me apart.

The diodes on its collar pulse in rhythmic green.

I have maybe three seconds before it gets me.

* * *

The forklift screamed through the air, its engine howling like something dying. I didn't think—couldn't afford to think. My body moved on pure instinct, muscles coiled and driving me forward until I stood between Cole and Grimjaw, palms extended toward the hurtling metal death.

For three years, my wards had been ash-gray static. Choked. Corrupted by whatever poison the Breach had dumped into this world. Every time I'd tried to raise a shield, it felt like trying to breathe underwater—the magic thick and suffocating in my throat, turning to lead before it ever left my fingertips.

Not now.

White-lilac fire erupted from my hands so fast my vision whited out for a heartbeat. Hearth-coal threads twisted through the prismatic energy, burning cold and clean. The forklift hit the arcano-kinetic barrier hard enough that I felt it reverberate through my entire skeleton, up my arms, rattling my teeth. But it held. Held like God's own promise.

Metal shrieked—a sound of tortured steel—and the forklift crumpled against the shield, folding in on itself with a series of sickening *CRUNCH* sounds. It dropped to the deck plating like discarded scrap, sparking and smoking but harmless as a child's toy.

I gasped, tasting fresh cedar on my tongue instead of rust and decay. The burn in my lungs was clean. Pure. Alive.

"Commander!" Cole's voice cut through the ringing in my ears. His frost-cobalt aura had kicked in, the temperature around us plummeting until my breath misted in front of my face. He'd already shouldered his primary weapon and brought up the secondary, bolt locked and ready.

My eyes were glowing violet—I could feel the light pouring from them even without looking at my reflection. The ward still stood between us and the approaching Ogre-Kin, swirling with that same pristine white-lilac energy. No corruption. No contamination.

Behind the lead Ogre's charging form, I saw it clearly now—the consciousness trapped behind those venom-clouded eyes. Panic. Agony. A mind screaming inside its own skull while the thrall-collar forced this body forward into combat.

"They're not collateral damage," I said, breathing heavily. The words came out strained, my voice pitching higher than normal when magic ran hot through me. "Cole... they're victims."

The lead Ogre-Kin raised both massive fists overhead, drool and black bile streaming from its mouth. The red LEDs on its control collar blinked in sequence—synchronizing with the others. Seven more of them lumbering forward through the smog-choked cavern, each one moving with that horrible puppet-like jerkiness.

"Copy that." Cole racked the bolt on his secondary weapon, frost-crystals forming along the barrel. "Grimjaw! Tell Bram to load the heavy biz."

The Dwarf-Drake didn't need translation. His comm unit crackled as he barked orders upward toward the catwalks. Above us, I heard the heavy *CLACK-CLACK* of something big being loaded into position—a familiar sound if you'd ever heard Bram Kovacs work with custom machinery.

I held the ward steady, feeling sweat beading down my spine despite the cold. Each Ogre-Kin was easily thirteen feet tall, their bodies scarred and reconstructed by whatever twisted surgery had turned them into living weapons. The collars around their thick necks pulsed with that sick crimson light, cutting through the industrial smog like lighthouse beams pointing toward doom.

From the catwalk above, I caught a glimpse of movement. Bram's silhouette against the dim lighting, working the bolt action on something that definitely wasn't standard issue equipment.

---

## CHAPTER 12: CHAPTER 12

The thunder arrives before I see it—a sound like God tearing apart sheet metal that rattles through my chest cavity and sets my teeth on edge. My ears ring instantly.

"Contact!" someone screams. Maybe me. Maybe Grimjaw's boys.

Bram doesn't ask twice.

The anti-materiel rifle coughs its rage, and the world becomes violence. The first depleted-bismuth slug catches the nearest Ogre-Kin square in what passes for his neck—that thick column of muscle and bone between the steel collar and his shoulders. The impact is catastrophic. Metal shrieks. The collar explodes in a shower of molten sparks that rain down like dying stars onto the concrete below. The Ogre-Kin staggers backward, both hands flying to his throat, and makes a sound I'll hear in nightmares—the wet, gasping wheeze of a man whose airway just became Swiss cheese.

"Three down, Cole! Keep 'em in the pocket!"

Bram's voice crackles through the Nextel radio, all South Side grit and mechanical precision. I don't look at him—can't afford to take my eyes off the chaos—but I can picture him there, hunched over that monstrous rifle, one eye squeezed shut behind the scope, his finger dancing that lethal dance between restraint and annihilation.

More shots. The cavern lights flicker from the electrical storm each impact generates. The second Ogre-Kin takes it in the shoulder, the collar there detonating into fragments that tear through the air like angry hornets. He crashes down hard enough to crack the floor, and I catch a flash of his face before he falls—a momentary glimpse of clarity breaking through whatever venom-fog Apep wrapped around his brain.

"GRIMJAW!" I roar, and the orc is already moving, his massive frame weaving between the thralls with a brutal grace that speaks to years of street fighting in worse places than this. He slams one disoriented Ogre-Kin aside with a forearm to the chest, the impact sending the big bastard sprawling into another. "DOWN! STAY DOWN OR I BREAK YOUR FUCKING NECK!"

The gutter-Orcish translation comes automatic, guttural and threatening. Grimjaw doesn't wait for compliance—he shoulder-checks the nearest Ogre-Kin, using two hundred pounds of dense muscle as a battering ram. Bones crack. Something crunches. The Ogre-Kin drops without another word.

The third shot goes wide—I see Bram's muzzle flash light up the darkness and track the slug's path as it screams past an Ogre-Kin's head close enough to part his hair. "Shit! Shit! Cole, they're scattering!"

But we'd planned for this. The herding pattern Grimjaw's boys laid out, driving the thralls toward the center of the chamber where Bram has clear line-of-sight. One of the freed orcs—still shaking off the mind-control but regaining focus fast—suddenly wheels around, all seven feet of him turning toward the gantry above like he's smelled fresh meat.

Marcus Voss freezes mid-gesture on that catwalk, the ritual circle beneath him still glowing that sickly green that tastes of copper and decay. For just a heartbeat, our eyes meet across the cavern's width. His face pales.

"Bram!" I'm running now, boots slipping on blood-slick concrete as I burn toward the next cluster of thralls. "High target! The gantry!"

The fourth shot is pure artistry—impossible precision under impossible conditions. The depleted-bismuth slug traces a perfect arc through the air, catching the support cable anchoring the gantry to its mounting point. Steel wires scream as they part, the sound like a thousand violins being shredded simultaneously. The gantry lurches sideways.

Voss shrieks.

The freed Ogre-Kin let out a roar that makes my spine vibrate. It's rage incarnate, vengeance given voice, and it echoes through the chamber like the birth cry of something ancient and terrible. Two more join in—the ones Grimjaw knocked down are back on their feet, and whatever mental chains Apep forged have shattered completely.

They turn as one toward the swaying gantry, toward Marcus Voss scrambling to keep his footing as the whole structure groans and bends at an angle that shouldn't be physically possible. Their fists clench. Their jaws open.

And then they *charged*.

* * *

The Ogre-Kin are tearing the gantry apart like it's made of matchsticks.

I can hear the groaning metal two levels below me, the scream of stressed alloy as those massive, clawed hands wrench support beams free. Below them, Voss's corporate guards—all that expensive security—are scrambling, their expensive tactical gear worthless against creatures built in the crucibles of some other world. Bullets ping off thick hide. Grenades barely make them flinch.

Good. Let them have a distraction.

My combat boots hit the first steel stair tread, and I feel the cold gathering in my core—the same cold that lives behind my eyes when I'm really pissed, when I remember Danny Martinez's last breath rattling through sludge-black lungs. The frost-coal magic responds instantly, crawling up from my sternum through my throat, coating my teeth with crystalline winter.

Not the time to hesitate.

A corp-sec lieutenant spots me on the stairs, his rifle coming up with practiced efficiency. He's got the good armor, the kind that stops bullets, maybe even the first few blows from something supernaturally strong. But he doesn't know about men like me yet. Doesn't understand that we're outside whatever playbook his military contractors gave him.

I don't even slow down.

Three steps before his muzzle aligns with my chest, I exhale—not air, but pure winter. The frost-hex hits him square in the chestplate, and I watch his eyes go wide as ice spiderwebs across every visible inch of skin. His body goes rigid, and he topples backward onto the grating with a sound like dropping a side of beef.

*"Stay down, suit,"* I say to his frost-covered corpse. *"You don't get to die for him today."*

The emergency strobes are still flashing red, painting everything in bloodlight. Each pulse illuminates the chaos below—Ogre-Kin tearing through security barriers, guards trying to establish fallback positions, the massive central vat of molten Telluric copper roaring like a trapped dragon, its heat making the whole structure shimmer.

My Nextel crackles at my hip. Mara's voice cuts through the static: *"I'm taking the east flank, Cole. Box him in."*

Smart girl. Voss thinks he's safe because he's surrounded by loyalists, but loyalty has expiration dates when Ogre-Kin are chewing through your support columns.

I hit the second level landing, boots crunching on frost I left behind. The cold is automatic now, reflexive, just like breathing or blinking. It's been three years since I figured out what I could do, since that night in the Kearny marshes when something went wrong during a summoning ritual and decided to make me its permanent home instead of its temporary host.

The trade-off was simple: I got magic that freezes things solid, and in return, I stopped being able to feel anything warm. Not in the usual sense. My heart beats, blood flows, but it's all running through ice-cold veins. Sometimes I wonder if I died that night and this is just... echoes. Ghosts wearing my face.

The third stairwell is clearer. Whatever guards were positioned here scattered when they heard the Ogre-Kin breach. Smart. Survival instincts over corporate loyalty—there's hope for some of them yet.

But not enough hope. Not nearly enough.

Danny Martinez was nineteen years old. Nineteen. Lived his whole life in Newark housing projects, never had a chance to breathe air that wasn't thick with industrial runoff. Then 2000 rolls around, and Voss Chemical needs human test subjects for their new sludge formula—the stuff they're planning to pump into the Passaic River once they get the permits sorted. Promised those families jobs, benefits, medical care. Lied about every single word.

Danny ended up drowning in his own lungs, lungs filled with black iron byproduct, and there isn't a court in the state that'll touch it because Voss owns half the judges and most of the politicians besides.

That's eight hundred thousand gallons of poison sluiced directly into the system. That's hundreds of kids like Danny who never got to be twenty, or thirty, or old enough to know what they were missing out on.

I can't undo any of that.

Can't scrape that black iron from Danny's dead lungs. Can't make him breathe again. Can't bring back anyone else Voss killed in his pursuit of profit margins and patent protection.

All I can do is climb these stairs. All I can do is hunt the man responsible. All I can do is freeze whatever pieces I can reach until he's nothing but a corpse cooling on the same concrete where he buried other people's futures.

Is it justice? No. Justice would mean punishment fitting the crime, would mean reparation, would mean the world making things right. What I'm doing won't fix anything. Won't heal anyone. Won't even really hurt Voss's bottom line—not permanently.

But it's something. A sliver of reckoning in an unjust world. And sometimes, when you're standing at the edge of the abyss, a sliver is all you've got left to work with.

My hand finds the reinforced door handle at the top of the stairwell. The heat radiating through the metal is intense—must be fifty feet above that copper vat now, close enough that I can feel my skin tightening against the dry air. Behind me, below me, the sounds of combat continue. Mara's voice crackles again over the Nextel: *"He's moving toward the observation deck."*

Of course he is.

Voss thinks he can hole up somewhere safe, call for backup, wait this out. He doesn't understand yet that there are no safe places anymore. That every door between here and wherever he thought he could hide has already been unlocked by men like me.

I kick the reinforced door open and step out into the blistering heat directly above the roaring molten copper smelting vat.

The primary oversight catwalk stretches before me, a narrow steel bridge suspended over hell itself.

* * *

The catwalk groans under my boots as I step forward, the metal already hot enough to singe through the rubber. Forty feet below, the vat churns like hell's own gullet—molten Telluric copper glowing orange-bright, hungry. The air shimmers and wavers with heat that makes my eyes water, skin crawling even with the frost-cobalt armor humming across my shoulders.

Voss stands at the center, backed against the suspension cable like a rat in a cage it built itself. His expensive suit is sweat-darkened, hair plastered to his skull. The mask he wore at those corporate meetings has cracked clean down the middle. What's underneath isn't human anymore—not really. Just ambition curdled into something wrong.

"Stop right there." His voice cracks on the words. He's holding something I've never seen before—a prototype hex-weapon, blocky and heavy-looking, wires running up its grip like exposed veins. The thing hums, an unstable whine that sets my teeth on edge.

I don't stop walking.

"You think you're a hero, Reyes?" Voss's sneer slips, revealing fear underneath. "You're just a South Side mechanic playing in the big leagues."

The catwalk shifts beneath me. My shadow stretches long in the orange glare, the frost-cobalt aura flaring bright along my edges. "I stopped being a hero the day my brother coughed up his first pint of sludge, Voss. I'm just the bill collector."

He brings the weapon up—not toward me, but toward the main suspension cable supporting this entire walkway. "I drop this cable, we both burn."

My boots keep coming. The heat presses down like a physical weight, each breath scalding my throat. I can smell my own hair starting to singe, the rubber soles of my work boots sticking slightly to metal hot enough to cook meat.

"Do you know what Telluric copper does to flesh?" Voss's finger twitches near the trigger. "It doesn't just melt—it *transfigures*. Turns bone into glass. Makes organs weep copper tears."

"I've seen it happen," I say flatly. "Saw a kid from the projects fall into the Passaic back in '03. Took three days for them to scrape him off the riverbed. He'd crystallized solid."

Voss's gun wavers. Sweat rolls down his temples. The hex-weapon whines louder, some kind of feedback loop building. Sparks crawl along its barrel like angry insects.

"Last chance." His voice isn't nearly as confident now. "Back off or we both die."

The catwalk creaks dangerously under my next step. Behind Voss, I can see the cable he's threatening—a thick braid of steel and something else, something that glows faintly with containment wards. If that goes...

I'm ten feet away when he panics.

His finger slams down on the trigger.

---

## CHAPTER 13: CHAPTER 13

I step out onto the east side of the catwalk, my boots finding purchase on the metal grating even as my perception expands beyond this moment. The Weave flows through me like liquid starlight, and I can feel every component in Voss's hex-weapon—a weapon that's killed more people than he'll ever admit, that's torn apart families in the Undercity while he sat in his penthouse sipping champagne.

My hand extends forward, palm up.

The white-lilac energy that coils around my fingers isn't just magic—it's precision. It's years of training at the Academy, decades of combat experience, every lesson Master Chen tried to drill into me before the Breach turned us all into something else. The telekinetic vise closes around the hex-weapon with surgical exactness.

Inside that gun, the stabilized mana core begins to misfire. Once. Twice. A third time.

Then it *screams*.

The firing mechanism fuses into a lump of slag, polymer melting into a single molten mass. Voss's eyes go wide behind his glasses as he tries to drop it, but his tailored gloves are already burning through. He screams, a high-pitched sound of pain and disbelief, and flings the ruined weapon away. It clatters against the catwalk plating, still glowing orange-red where the fire had been contained within its housing moments before.

I walk forward.

My wards shimmer around me—not the desperate, half-formed barriers I'd thrown up during my worst days, but layered protections that smell of cedar and burn cold as winter wind. They shield me from the intense heat radiating up from the copper vat below, its heavy churning providing a rhythmic counterpoint to the chaos above.

When I look at Voss, I don't see the Visible Head anymore. Don't see the man who controls shipping routes and smuggling operations across three states. 

I see what he is: a cornered rat in expensive clothing, his empire built on the bones of people who never stood a chance. His power was always an illusion—a house of cards waiting for someone to breathe on it.

"I was," I say, my voice cutting through the sizzle of evaporating sweat on my skin—heat that would have boiled off anyone else standing this close to the vat, but which barely registers against my wards. "But Cole reminded me how to forge something new out of the scrap."

Voss stumbles backward along the catwalk, his pristine suit now scorched, his perfectly styled hair disheveled. The confidence that carried him through every negotiation and backroom deal has evaporated like water on hot metal.

"Vance..." His voice cracks. "Elias said you were *broken*."

"I am," I agree calmly. My eyes find Cole across the expanse of the catwalk. He's there, solid, real—my anchor in this nightmare. "Broken open. That's different than shattered."

I look back at Voss, and beneath the fear in his eyes, I see something worse: understanding. Recognition that this isn't going to end with threats or bribes or promises.

He's calculating odds that no longer exist.

"He's yours," I tell Voss simply, and mean it in multiple ways.

The catwalk groans under our weight as we face each other—the hunter and the prey, separated by maybe fifteen feet of iron grating and decades of accumulated evil.

Voss's hand moves with desperate speed toward his belt, fumbling for a secondary holdout blade I'd already cataloged three seconds ago with my expanded perception.

He makes his choice then—not wisdom, not strategy, but pure animal terror pushing him toward a suicidal rush at Cole.

My wards flare brighter, cedar scent sharpening into pine needles, and I ready myself to intercept.

The catwalk shudders.

And Voss launches forward with a scream that echoes off the warehouse walls.

* * *

The catwalk shudders beneath our weight, metal groaning like something dying. I keep Voss pinned against the rail, one hand fisted in his lapel—expensive fabric that reeks of ozone and old money. His other arm flails uselessly, grasping at air thick enough to taste.

"Please," he gasps. "Anything."

Below us, the vat bubbles with sick orange light, each pop and hiss a promise of what's coming. Copper smoke rises in greasy columns, catching in my throat. I lean closer until his breath fogs my face. Frost spreads from where my fingers grip him, crystalline patterns racing down the black armor plating, freezing sweat into tiny icicles on his temple.

"I know about the Arcane Iron-Lung," I say quietly. My voice carries over the industrial chaos around us—the hydraulic whines, the generator hums, the distant scream of sirens approaching Sub-Station Seven too late. "Brass and glass construction. Spec'd for maximum efficiency. Fits a child's lungs perfectly, doesn't it? Allows them to breathe through eight hundred thousand gallons of chemical sludge while their bodies slowly dissolve from the inside out."

Voss's eyes go wide. The color drains from what little skin shows below his receding hairline.

"The specs came through Pylon Five," I continue, watching frost crawl across his collar. "All those contracts you signed off on in your climate-controlled office. Every kid who choked on copper vapor, every lung that turned to jelly—you authorized it. You made it possible."

"You don't understand!" He struggles weakly against my grip. The railing bends another inch under his weight. Metal screams. "The company needed that waste processing! It was cost-efficient!"

"My brother Danny wore one of those devices." I'm not shouting. There's no need. The words cut deeper than any yell could. "He was seven years old when they fitted him with it. Spent three months breathing poison because someone like you decided profit margins mattered more than kids' lives."

Behind Voss, Mara stands silhouetted against the control panel lights, her hand resting on the termination switch. She watches me with those old, tired eyes—not judging, just waiting.

"Offshore accounts," Voss sputters. "I can give you access codes. Everything. Gnome telemetry, encryption keys, operational data for—"

I shake my head slowly. "I'll take those myself."

His face twists with desperation. "Pylon Five! Elias! I can give you both! Full network access, authentication protocols, everything!"

"See?" A cold smile touches my lips. Frost spreads wider across his suit. "You're learning. But this isn't about information."

Voss begins to pray then—a garbled mess of corporate jargon and empty apologies that blur together into meaningless noise. I let him finish, counting the seconds in my head until the sirens grow close enough that even a man like Voss might hear them coming for him through all the industrial hell.

When he finally runs out of words, I recite the Threefold Cord:

*"One: Penance. For every breath stolen from a child's lungs."*

The frost on his collar thickens, spreading down his chest now, numbing whatever warmth remains in his heart.

*"Two: Revenge. For every parent who held their dying kid while copper vapor burned through their throat."*

Voss sobs. Actually sobs.

*"Three: A Sliver of Justice."* I lean in so close our foreheads nearly touch. My reflection stares back at me in his terrified eyes. "Because the system won't convict you. The courts won't punish you. You're too valuable, Mr. Visible Head #2. Too connected. So justice has to come some other way."

He struggles one final time, enough that the railing groans dangerously. His weight shifts. He slips another inch over the edge.

"The kids who didn't get to grow up," I say softly. "This is for them."

I look past him to Mara. She stands perfectly still against the control panel, bathed in amber warning lights. Our eyes meet. No words pass between us—none needed after everything we've been through together.

She gives me a single nod. Resolute. Certain.

It's time to end Visible Head #2.

* * *

The gantry didn't just break—it *shattered*.

I watched the metal crystallize into a spiderweb of fractures a split-second before Cole drove his frost-cobalt hex into the load-bearing joint. My kinetic blast caught it mid-fracture, the white-lilac energy spiraling through the weak points like lightning finding its path to ground. The catwalk screamed—a sound that cut through the industrial cacophony of the smelting cavern, sharp and final.

Marcus Voss's eyes went wide. For one frozen heartbeat, he seemed to comprehend what was happening. Then gravity reasserted itself with brutal efficiency.

"NO!" His voice cracked as the section beneath him tilted, then dropped away in a cascade of falling steel. He threw his arms out, fingers clawing at empty air where solid support had been moments before.

The fall lasted less than two seconds. Long enough for him to realize there would be no survival. Long enough for that mask of aristocratic contempt to twist into something primal and afraid.

He hit the surface of the Telluric copper vat with a sound like a thunderclap muffled underwater. The molten metal erupted in a geyser of orange-white fury, steam hissing violently as superheated liquid splashed against the sides. But it wasn't water—this was arcane-infused copper, conductive and hungry, and Voss vanished into it instantly.

His scream cut off mid-note, replaced by the sickening *hiss* of boiling vapor and the crackle of extreme heat.

Cole stood perfectly still at the edge, staring down into the churning vat. The surface began to smooth almost immediately, the roiling copper settling back into place over whatever remained of Marcus Voss. The man who'd orchestrated the Millennium Breach, who'd sold out humanity's future for power and profit, was now encased in permanent, living metal—a statue at the very heart of Pylon #4, forever conductive, forever bound.

"One down," Cole said quietly. "Three Heads left."

I walked to the edge, my white-lilac wards still holding, still smelling of cedar rather than ash. The adrenaline crash was starting to set in, my hands steady but trembling slightly. Below, the vat's surface had gone nearly calm again, dark and reflective.

Then I saw it.

A small object arcing away from the vat's lip, trailing droplets of cooling copper that solidified into black beads before hitting the steel grating. It bounced once, twice, then settled near my boots with a soft *click*.

The cybernetic neural-link module. Voss's.

Its green LED blinked steadily in the cavern's dim light, undamaged, pulsing like a tiny heartbeat. The emergency ejection system had triggered just before he hit the molten surface—the extreme heat must have activated the failsafe. All that remained of Marcus Voss in recognizable form was this blinking piece of technology.

I crouched beside it, studying the device. Inside its memory banks would be everything—access codes, contact lists, transaction records. The evidence we needed. But also warnings, traps, dead-man switches.

Behind us, sirens began to wail through the Old Mint's upper levels. High-pitched, insistent—the automated BATC response teams breaching security seals. We had minutes, maybe less.

Cole's head snapped toward the sound. "Time to go."

I reached out, then hesitated. My fingers hovered over the module's activation panel. One touch and we'd know what Voss had been hiding. One touch and we might trigger exactly what he'd designed to prevent capture.

The sirens grew louder.

"Mara." Cole's voice carried an edge. "We grab it on the way out or we leave it."

I made my decision. Clipping the module to my belt, I stood. "Move."

We ran for the Undercity access point as the first heavy footsteps of BATC tactical units thundered down from above.

---

## CHAPTER 14: CHAPTER 14

The air crackles with wrongness.

I'm crouched near one of the coolant vats—this massive steel thing still steaming like some industrial demon's breath—when I spot it. Voss's severed neural-link module, half-submerged in the oily surface. It's *sizzling*, actually sizzling, sending up these little puffs of vapor that smell like burnt hair mixed with that metallic tang you get when lightning strikes too close.

"Cole." Mara's voice cuts through the ambient chaos. She's already moving, her hands weaving those white-lilac streams of magic I've learned to recognize as her protective shit. "That's ICE-laced. Don't even think about touching it barehanded."

But she doesn't wait. Can't afford to. Her fingers wrap around the module, and the way they glow—that soft purple luminescence—I can see her grimacing through the pain. The thing must be cooking her digits, but she lifts it clean anyway, dripping black residue across the concrete floor. Iron-gall juice mixed with... fuck, is that spinal fluid? From Voss's neck-stump?

She tosses it my way. I catch it reflexively, hissing at the heat even through my gloves. There's no time to admire it though. I jam it into one of the insulated Faraday pouches stashed in my pack—one of Grimjaw's modifications—and seal it tight. Whatever frequency this piece of tech is broadcasting, it needs containment before it fries our brains.

The hiss of the coolant vat behind us intensifies. Mara straightens up, wiping her glowing hand on her coat and looking ceiling-ward where sparks are starting to rain down from the upper levels. That high-pitched whine—*plasma cutters*. Someone's burning through the blast doors.

"They're coming in hard," Grimjaw's voice rumbles from my left. He's got his rifle shouldered, scanning the darkness beyond our position. Bram materializes beside him, breath fogging in the cold air.

"High-Spire strike teams," Bram adds, voice flat as a graveyard tombstone. "I count four points of entry. They're coordinated." His eyes flick to me, then Mara. "My boys can buy you three minutes. Maybe four if we're lucky."

Mara doesn't respond verbally. Just looks at me with those eyes that seem too bright in the low light. Waiting.

I drop to my knees, yanking my modified Panasonic Toughbook from the pack—this thing's seen better days, held together with duct tape and prayers, but its frequency capabilities are second-to-none in the Undercity. I slam it onto an overturned crate, booting it up while my fingers fly across the keys.

"Need names," I mutter, already pulling up my broker list. These Gnomes don't work for free, and they sure as hell don't work fast unless you've got credit to burn. But Voss's neural-link module? That's leverage. Pure gold in the right markets.

The screen flickers to life.

* * *

The ventilation shaft coughs out two shapes that hit the concrete floor like bags of wet sand. Both Gnomes—Fizz and his partner who went by the handle Splice—were hunched over like question marks, their coveralls stiff with machine oil and what looked suspiciously like dried blood. The welding goggles they wore made them look like deep-sea creatures surfacing into hostile air.

"ICE is hot," Fizz announced without preamble, his fingers already dancing across a battered mechanical keyboard he'd pulled from somewhere inside his massive coat. "Sterling-Voss proprietary shit. This ain't your garden-variety BATC security."

I knelt beside the Panasonic Toughbook, watching its screen flicker to life with that familiar green-on-black terminal text. The Nokia transponder—a brick of a device held together with duct tape and optimism—began beeping insistently as Splice slotted it into the jury-rigged array of fiber-optic cables snaking across my workshop floor.

"Voss locked this down tight before he bought it," Fizz continued, his voice taking on that particular rhythm hackers get when they're half in and half out of the digital world. "Kill-switches everywhere. One wrong move and we're all having a very bad day."

Grimjaw had positioned himself near the door, his shotgun's weight making the floorboards creak. He didn't trust the Gnomes—not many people did—but right now they were our only shot at cracking through the BATC's defensive matrix.

"How long?" I asked.

"Not long enough if those Elves find us first." Grimjaw's voice was gravel and rust. "Already smell their cologne. Probably coming up the Pulaski right now in one of those blacked-out sedans."

Fizz's fingers paused for just a second, then resumed their assault on the keyboard with renewed fury. The Nokia transponder's beeping accelerated, creating a staccato rhythm against the Toughbook's mechanical whir. On-screen, lines of code scrolled past so fast they blurred:

[BATC-SECURITY v4.7] ACCESS DENIED
[HANDSHAKE FAILED: RETRY 1/3]
[SPOOFING MAC ADDRESS...]
[RETRY 2/3]
[CRACKING ENCRYPTION LAYER ONE...]

"You got company!" Splice barked, though he never looked up from his own terminal—a battered Dell laptop covered in stickers from defunct ISPs. "Three vehicles. Two north, one circling. Your boys at Sub-Station Seven are lighting up like a Christmas tree."

The workshop smelled like soldering iron and the cheap coffee I'd been brewing since yesterday afternoon. Oil stains on the concrete formed patterns that looked almost deliberate—almost like runes. The fluorescent lights overhead flickered, casting everything in shades of sickly yellow.

"Slotting the ICE now," Fizz announced, and I watched as his fingers became a blur. "Voss had this drek locked up tight. Give me a sec to spoof the handshake..."

The screen flashed white.

For one heart-stopping moment, I thought we'd triggered the kill-switch.

Then green text bloomed across the display like toxic flowers:

[ACCESS GRANTED]
[TRACE INITIALIZED]
[FOLLOWING DATA STREAM BACK TO SOURCE...]
[BYPASSING FIREWALL LAYER THREE...]
[CONNECTING TO BATC CENTRAL MAINFRAME...]

"Yes!" Fizz pumped his fist, nearly knocking over a jar of screws. "We're in! Oh shit, we're *deep* in!"

Numbers cascaded down the screen—coordinates, IP addresses, server logs that made my head hurt even trying to parse them. But underneath it all, something was rendering. A map. Topographical data. Neon Hollow spreading out in wireframe precision.

"Find Pylon #5," I said, my voice steady despite the adrenaline burning through my veins. "That's what we need. That's where Voss stashed the data dump."

Splice started muttering to himself, words in some programming language that sounded like Latin corrupted by machine code. His fingers flew across his own keyboard in sync with Fizz's, the two of them forming some kind of digital duet against Sterling-Voss's security architecture.

The Nokia transponder let out a final, triumphant beep.

The Toughbook screen went solid red.

My stomach dropped into my boots.

Then red bled away to green, and a 3D rendering of Neon Hollow materialized, complete with street names, building profiles, and—there—a blinking red cursor that locked onto a specific location near the Kearny marshes. Where the Passaic River curved around industrial ruins that hadn't seen legitimate use since before the Breach.

"There!" Fizz practically shouted, jabbing at the screen. "Pylon #5 is real! And Cole, buddy, you ain't gonna like where this thing is pointing."

I leaned closer, watching as more data scrolled past:

LOCATION: KEARNY MARSHES
COORDINATES: [REDACTED]
STRUCTURE: ABANDONED WATER TREATMENT FACILITY
SECURITY LEVEL: CRITICAL
NOTES: ACTIVE CONTAINMENT PROTOCOLS IN PLACE
WARNING: NEURAL INTERFERENCE DETECTED

"Son of a bitch," I breathed.

"That ain't even the worst part." Splice pushed his goggles up, revealing eyes that looked haunted despite their small size. "Look at the timestamp on this data dump. When Voss uploaded it."

Green text pulsed at the bottom of the screen:

[TIMESTAMP: 04/19/2008 - 03:47 AM]
[STATUS: COMPLETE]

Tomorrow. He'd uploaded it *tomorrow*.

Which meant we had maybe fourteen hours to get there, crack whatever security he'd layered around the facility itself, and pull the data before the BATC knew what hit them—and before whatever was guarding Pylon #5 decided we were an acceptable casualty in maintaining containment protocols.

Grimjaw's shotgun racking broke the silence.

"Elves are close enough to smell now," he said flatly. "We moving or we holding?"

I closed the laptop with a sharp click, already calculating angles of approach through Neon Hollow's industrial maze.

"We move," I said. "But we move smart."

* * *

The coordinates burned themselves into my retinas even as I slammed the Toughbook shut. Crown Spire. The fucking Crown Spire—where Morvain kept his throne in the clouds, where Lord Malvourne held court among the glittering towers that scraped heaven.

"Cole!" Mara's voice cut through the sudden chaos. "That's suicide! It's a fortress!"

I didn't answer. There was no time for answers.

The blast doors above us had given way with a sound like the world splitting open—a deep metallic *boom* that reverberated through bone and stone. Plasma fire cascaded down into our cavern, sheets of liquid light that turned everything bright as day for one terrible moment. The heat hit me instantly, a wall of force that made my skin tighten. Someone screamed. Someone else shouted orders I couldn't make out over the roar.

My hand found Mara's wrist—not her hand, too risky with the plasma burning overhead—and I yanked her toward the drainage culverts without looking back. Behind us, the crew scattered like cockroaches when the lights come on. Good. Disperse. Survive. That's what matters now.

"The Mother," I grunted, dragging her toward the rusted iron grate half-buried in mud and debris. "We need to warn her. If Elias is waking Apep..."

Plasma bolts stitched across the wall beside us, white-hot and hungry. One caught Mara's lilac wards with a crackling shriek—the protective hexes flared brilliant purple, deflecting the shot but leaving her exposed for a heartbeat. She stumbled. I hauled her forward by pure momentum.

Kicked the grate hard enough to feel it jar up my leg. Metal shrieked against concrete. The passage beyond yawned black, dripping with something that smelled like rotted meat and chemical burn.

"We don't have a choice," I said, because she needed to hear it even though we both knew it was death sentence talking. "Elias is waking Apep from the penthouse."

The grate fell inward. We plunged after it.

Stagnant water exploded upward as we hit bottom, soaking through immediately. Cold. The kind of cold that gets into bones and settles there like frostbite. Mara splashed down beside me, her glowing wards dimming in the oppressive dark—only mine and hers for light now, two small flames against an ocean of nothing.

Behind us, the sounds of pursuit: boots on stone, shouted commands, the crackle of plasma charges arming.

"Move!" I grabbed her hand properly now, calloused fingers closing around hers. Her skin felt too warm, fevered. Magic always ran hot when it worked too hard. "Deeper! Get deeper!"

The tunnel narrowed. Walled in by pipe and rust and the thick smell of old water. Each step sent ripples echoing ahead of us, bouncing off walls I couldn't see. My coal-light barely penetrated ten feet before being swallowed by the gloom.

And then—a sound that made every instinct scream *wrong*.

Chittering. Scraping. The wet click of teeth against stone.

We weren't alone in these tunnels.

Mara's grip tightened until her nails dug crescents into my palm. She didn't speak. Didn't need to. We both knew what lived in the splice-tunnels beneath Kearny. What hunted in packs. What tore apart anything that moved too slow or smelled too... human.

The chittering grew louder. Closer.

From somewhere ahead—and how far ahead was impossible to say in this darkness—a low rumble answered back. Not goblin. Something bigger. Something worse.

I pulled Mara faster, my lungs burning now, heart hammering against ribs like it wanted out. The Toughbook slammed against my spine with each stride, the coordinates still seared into my memory even without looking:

**CROWN SPIRE.**
**TOP FLOOR.**
**WHERE HELL BREEDS WITH MONEY.**

And behind us: the distinct sound of our pursuers hesitating at the tunnel mouth, their plasma weapons suddenly useless against what waited in the dark.

Their problem now.

Ours was what lay ahead—

The rumbling stopped.

Silence. Thick as tar. Thick as death.

Then movement from three directions at once. Fast. Hungry.

---

## CHAPTER 15: CHAPTER 15

The tunnel reeks of ozone and something worse—something biological that makes my stomach clench even behind the filtration. I lean against Cole's shoulder, and he doesn't shake me off this time. Good. Because if I let go now, I think I'll dissolve into the darkness around us like sugar in water.

"Easy there, Commander," Cole murmurs, one arm steadying my waist while his other keeps his MP5 low and ready. "We're almost to the sanctuaries."

Almost. That word tastes like rust.

The splice-tunnel spreads before us like a mechanical nervous system—thousands upon thousands of fiber-optic cables stolen from BATC mainlines, bundled together in jury-rigged conduits that hum with barely-contained data streams. Some glow faintly blue in the dark, pulsing like bioluminescent veins. Others are dead black, severed and weeping drops of resin that hit the concrete floor with wet *plops*.

"We need to move faster," I whisper, but even saying it exhausts me. The wards are screaming. They've been screaming since we left Sub-Station Seven, a constant high-pitched whine at the edge of my consciousness that makes my teeth ache. Every step feels like wading through honey made of broken glass.

"That way," Cole points with his chin toward a branching corridor where the cables split into different directions. Water drips somewhere in the distance—steady, rhythmic. The clicking sounds start up again. Multiple sources. Close.

Then they emerge from the shadows, and I have to fight not to trigger every defensive ward I've got loaded.

Goblins. Wire-runners. Six of them, maybe seven—I can't quite focus enough to count properly. Short, wiry metahumans with skin the color of old parchment and eyes that catch what little light there is and reflect it back in harsh yellow glints. They move with an unsettling economy of motion, each one holding electrified crowbars that crackle with contained lightning.

"Hold it right there!" The lead Goblin steps forward, scarred face twisted into something between a sneer and suspicion. His crowbar arcs between us like a miniature sun. "Corp-sec crawling all over the upper pipes, mechanic. You kicked the hornet's nest."

Cole's hand doesn't go for his weapon. Instead, he reaches into his pocket with deliberate slowness and produces a heavy iron coin, the Watching Party insignia etched so deep into its surface you could read it by touch alone.

The Goblin's eyes widen slightly. The others shift their weight but don't lower their weapons yet.

"I need passage to the clinic," Cole says, voice flat and certain. "Shadow Mothers owe me a favor. This woman needs medical attention that can't be traced."

There's a long moment where time seems to stretch. My wards are flickering now—not from any external threat but from my own fraying concentration. A pulse of cold blue light washes across our small group, and I hear one of the Goblins hiss.

Rix—at least, I think that's what Cole called him—examines the coin more closely, then looks up at me. Those yellow eyes bore into mine, and I see intelligence there, sharp and calculating. He's cataloguing every detail: my BATC uniform, the way my hands shake, the faint glow around my fingers where the wards are deteriorating.

"Payment first." His voice is guttural, accented in ways I can't quite parse. "Telluric copper. Pure shavings. Enough to grease three sensor grids."

Cole produces another item from his coat—a small leather pouch that he tosses to Rix with a practiced flick. The Goblin catches it, weighs it in his palm, then tears it open with his teeth. He sniffs the contents, nods once.

"Through the BATC thermal scanners won't pick us up," Rix says, already turning away. "But stay close. Step wrong, they'll have your heat signatures in seconds."

We move. Fast now. Following the wire-runners through passages that seem to shift and breathe around us. The cables overhead create patterns I almost recognize—they're routed according to some logic, some structure—but exhaustion makes it impossible to focus on.

My foot catches on an uneven section of concrete, and I go down hard. Pain lances up my ankle. My wards flare violently, not from any conscious command but from pure trauma response, flooding the tunnel with cascading barriers of cold blue light that reflect off the dripping walls like a thunderstorm trapped underground.

"Commander!" Cole drops to his knees beside me, one hand steadying my shoulder while the other keeps his weapon trained on the darkness ahead.

Rix stops, turns back with obvious irritation. But there's something else in his expression too—concern? Pity?

"We don't have time for this," the Goblin says, but he doesn't keep walking either. Instead, he crouches beside my other side without asking permission and looks into my eyes with an intensity that feels invasive. "You're bleeding out. Not physical. Wards are eating you alive."

I want to tell him he's wrong, that I'm fine, that we need to keep moving. But the words dissolve before they reach my tongue.

The ash-gray static is waiting at the edges of my vision again. Closer now. Hungry.

* * *

The tunnel floor rushes up to meet me, but it never connects. Arms catch me—strong, solid arms that know exactly how much pressure to use without hurting. Cole's grip is firm as iron around my waist, his chest against mine as he arrests my fall with effortless control.

My vision swims. Everything bleeds together—wet concrete walls, dripping stalactites of rust-streaked condensation, the faces of the Goblin crew watching with those unsettling amber eyes. Then there's something else. Something wrong.

*Smoke.*

I can't see it, but I *smell* it—that acrid burn of wet charred wool mixed with ash-gray static, like old newspapers catching fire in damp basement air. My nostrils flare involuntarily. Sub-Station Seven. That godforsaken place trying to drag me back down through time, through failure, through the memory of screaming commuters and burning flesh.

"No," I hear myself say, voice thin and distant. "No, no, no—"

Cole's hand cups the back of my head, pressing my face against his shoulder. The smell of him cuts through everything else—clean sweat, leather, and underneath it all that particular warmth of hearth-coal magic, like standing too close to a bonfire on a winter night. It's solid. Real. *Present tense.*

"Stay with me, Mara." His voice rumbles low against my ear, each word deliberate and measured. "You left the ash behind. You're here. You're breathing. We won."

His forehead presses to mine. Heat floods through the contact point—not just warmth but *certainty*, that frost-cobalt resolve that makes Cole who he is. It pours into me like water finding cracks in stone, forcing its way into every chaotic, tangled thread of my Weave where the static wants to take root.

My fingers clutch at his tactical vest, gripping the fabric hard enough to wrinkle it. The texture is real—I can feel every seam, every reinforced panel. This isn't memory or psychic echo. This is *now*.

"I'm here, Cole." My voice finds strength, pushes past the trembling. "I'm here."

The ash-gray recedes like fog burned away by morning sun. In its place blooms that pure white-lilac luminescence, brilliant and clean, filling my vision until there's nothing else. Cole's magic intertwines with mine—his blood-iron crimson threading through my violet like iron filings drawn to magnetism. Together they create something stronger than either alone.

Grimjaw watches from several feet away, arms crossed over his barrel chest. The Goblin chief's expression is unreadable—whether it's respect or concern or some combination I can't parse. Behind him, the rest of the crew maintains distance, their clicking conversation dropping to near-silence as they observe.

"You good?" Grimjaw asks finally, his gravel-and-sandpaper voice cutting through the tunnel's ambient drips.

I nod against Cole's shoulder before pulling back just enough to meet his eyes. His gaze holds mine steady, searching for any sign of regression. Finding none, the tension leaves his shoulders incrementally.

"Yeah," I say, straightening but keeping one hand braced against Cole's arm. "Just... needed a minute."

"Understood." Grimjaw jerks his chin toward the tunnel ahead. "Bunker's three hundred meters. Keep moving, keep quiet. Gnome security doesn't take kindly to surprise visitors."

We start forward again, Cole matching my pace without needing instruction. The dripping grows louder as we walk, water finding every crack in the aging infrastructure above us. Somewhere in the darkness ahead, light begins to glow—not the sickly yellow of sodium lamps but something cleaner, brighter.

The tunnel opens suddenly into vastness.

The bunker spreads out before us like a cathedral carved from concrete and steel. Overhead lights—fluorescent arrays mounted on industrial scaffolding—bathe everything in clinical white brightness that makes me squint after the tunnels' gloom. The air here smells different: sharp alchemical solvents cutting through antiseptic sterilization fluid, and underneath it all something almost comforting—fresh coffee brewing somewhere beyond our line of sight.

The floor is pristine polished concrete marked with yellow safety lines and caution tape. Workstations line the walls, most currently dark but clearly functional. In the center, raised platforms hold what look like research equipment covered in protective sheets.

"Gnomish design," Grimjaw mutters with something approaching pride. "Built this place themselves, before the Breach. Hasn't been touched since."

"Where are they?" I ask, scanning for signs of occupation. "Your people?"

"They come at night mostly. Daytime brings too many human patrols overhead." He gestures vaguely upward. "This deep, they can't hear us. But we don't push it."

Cole's hand finds mine, fingers lacing together briefly before releasing. Message received: *I've got your back.*

"Alright," I say, voice returning to its command tone now that the static has cleared completely. "We need to establish contact with whoever's running this operation. And then we need to figure out how the hell we're going to get to Sub-Station Seven without Marcus Voss's goons intercepting us."

"One problem at a time, Commander." Cole's smile is slight but present. "You just gave him terminal case of ego-death. Pretty sure he won't be coordinating anything for the next few hours while his consciousness reassembles itself."

"Good," I say flatly. "Because I'm not done with him yet."

* * *

The door hisses open.

I don't remember walking through it. The corridor behind us dissolves into static—white noise bleeding between dimensions—and then we're standing in a cathedral of technology that shouldn't exist beneath Neon Hollow's rust-slicked streets.

Banks of IBM ThinkPads glow like tombstones in a graveyard of old gods. Sony monitors line every wall, their green phosphorescent displays tracking BATC movements across the city in real-time. I can see our own heat signatures crawling through the network like parasites on silk. The hum of server racks fills my skull, vibrating through bone and filling the spaces where rational thought used to live.

"Commander Vance." Elena Reyes steps forward, her tactical gear stained with blood I recognize as her own. Behind her, kneeling beside what looks like an ancient mainframe jury-rigged with alchemical condensers, is a woman who makes me forget how to breathe.

Silver-streaked hair catches the blue-white light from the monitors. Eyes—violet eyes exactly like mine, but older, harder, carrying the weight of secrets that could crack continents—lift from a scrolling terminal display.

Mom.

My mother.

Lysandra Vance.

Alive.

The PalmPilot slips from my fingers. It clatters against concrete, and somewhere in the back of my mind I register the sound of plastic shattering, but I can't look away from her face. Can't process this as anything other than hallucination born from too many nights haunting the Kearny marshes, searching for ghosts in the fog.

She stands slowly, deliberately, and I'm moving before my brain catches up to intention. Three steps. Five. Seven. My legs are shaking so badly I barely make it across the room before my knees buckle.

Her arms catch me.

I bury my face in her shoulder, and the sobs that tear out of my chest sound like they're coming from someone else's throat—raw and desperate and six years late. She smells like ozone and old books and the particular scent of rain-soaked asphalt after a thunderstorm, and it's all I can do not to dissolve into nothing just to stay here, pressed against her, feeling her hand stroke my hair.

"Beautiful girl," she whispers, her voice thick with emotion but carrying that steel I remember from briefings when I was eight, watching her coordinate shadow-war operations through cracked satellite feeds. "You survived. You did so well."

I can't speak. Can only cling to her like she's the only solid thing in a universe gone liquid around us.

Over my shoulder, I feel her gaze shift. Feel the temperature drop by ten degrees as her attention focuses on Cole.

"You brought him." Her voice changes. The warmth bleeds out, replaced by tactical certainty that could carve through dimensional barriers. "Cole Brennan. The Cord-Bearer. You have the Toughbook?"

I force myself to lift my head, blinking tears away. Cole stands frozen near the doorway, his face pale beneath his tan, the IBM ThinkPad held like a holy relic he's afraid might shatter if he breathes wrong on it.

He nods jerkily, holding up the device.

Lysandra's expression doesn't soften. If anything, it hardens further as she gently extracts herself from my grip—I want to protest, to hold on tighter—but she guides me to stand beside Elena instead. Her violet eyes lock onto Cole with predatory focus.

"The coordinates for Pylon Five. The Crown Spire." It's not a question. "But to breach it..." She pauses, and I see something flicker across her face—regret? fear? Something ancient and terrible. "...we have to awaken something worse than Apep."

The server racks hum their hypnotic dirge.

Somewhere above us, three floors up, BATC patrols continue their endless rounds through Sub-Station Seven's corridors, oblivious to the abyss we're standing at the edge of.

And I realize with bone-deep certainty that whatever comes next will break us all.

---

# BOOK #14: THE FEATHERLESS HEART
### Grand Finale Trilogy Part 2 (U-2)

---

## CHAPTER 1: THE THREE WOMEN’S COUNCIL

The alternator of the 1989 Ford trauma-ambulance shuddered in the damp concrete belly of the Kearny marsh safehouse, its serpentine belt whining a relentless, rhythmic drone as it forced twelve volts into a daisy-chained bank of marine batteries. Through the wire-reinforced glass of the bay doors, the sodium-vapor lamps of the nearby truck depot threw long, jaundiced daggers across the floor, slick with puddle-runoff, brake fluid, and road salt dragged in from Route 7. The air was frigid, thick with the chemical burn of cheap diesel and the sharp, nostril-stinging bite of isopropyl alcohol, but underneath it all crawled something impossible.

It was the smell of late May in a garden that hadn’t existed since the towers took over Hackensack. Fresh-cut grass, melting frost, and an overwhelming, heavy sweetness: blooming white lilacs.

My hands wouldn't stop shaking. 

I’d spent seven years cataloging body bags for the Bureau of Arcano-Tactical Control, learning the exact density of charred elven cartilage and the greasy feel of soot from exploded railcars. I knew the weight of three hundred and fourteen commuter IDs tagged with yellow grease pencils, their owners shredded into meat and ash when the rail breach cracked the Midtown Direct line wide open. I carried the names of thirty-eight orphaned children like lead shot sewn directly into my ribcage, rattling every time I took a breath. I had lived under the ironclad assumption that my mother was just another unrecovered metric in the Spire’s classified casualty reports—pulped in some sub-basement purge before they paved over the old bio-clinics.

Yet she was standing five feet in front of me, leaning against the ambulance’s rusted fender.

Lysandra Vance wore an oil-stained Carhartt jacket two sizes too big, the cuffs rolled back to expose forearms mapped with jagged subcutaneous scarring—telltale tracks where corporate neural taps had been violently ripped from the flesh without dermal regenerators. Her hair was shot through with iron-gray, chopped unevenly at the collarbone, but the sharp line of her jaw and the cool, clinical slant of her green eyes were a mirror I had avoided in bathroom glass for nearly a decade. She held a suture needle clamped in hemostats, her fingers steady despite the bitter salt chill rolling off the meadows.

"You're breathing through your teeth, Mara," she said.
