The knife wound from the Newark docks, still pink and angry-looking. The burn scar from the substation fire in Kearny. Smaller things too, old things, faded white lines that tell stories I don't need to hear to understand.

His hands are steady as he unbuttons my tactical vest.

"Let me," he says quietly.

I let him. My fingers feel clumsy suddenly, useless. Nine years of armor and protocols and the weight of command, and here I am unable to undress because this man is touching my shoulders with a gentleness that feels like it could shatter something fundamental in my chest.

The vest drops. My shirt follows. Then my boots, which he kneels to untie with practiced efficiency—machinist's hands, made for precision work. When I'm down to just my underwear, he pauses.

"You're beautiful," he says, and there's no performance in it. No trying to be romantic or sweet. Just simple fact stated by someone who sees clearly.

I touch his face then, trace the line of his jaw. His stubble catches against my fingertips. "So are you."

He laughs softly, almost sadly. "Mara, I'm a wreck."

"No." My voice is firmer now. "You're the most real thing I've touched in fourteen years."

The gurney is narrow but we manage, tangled together in the heavy wool blankets we'd thrown off during our sleep hours before. His skin is warm against mine, fever-warm, and when our magic meets—white-lilac and hearth-coal—the medical car floods with light.

Not harsh. Not violent.

Perfect equilibrium.

Heat and cold dancing without consuming each other. Light that doesn't burn. The way opposite forces can exist in perfect balance if you just stop fighting them long enough to see how they fit together.

His scars are smooth under my palms. I map them all while he holds me like I'm the only solid thing in his universe. The knife wounds, the burns, the bullet grazes. Each one a moment he survived. Each one proof that death has tried and failed to take what was never meant to belong to it.

"Mara," he breathes into my hair.

"Yes?"

But there's no answer, just the sound of his heartbeat against my ear and the smell of cedar and clean sweat and something else underneath—like ozone after lightning strikes, that electric purity that comes from two magics recognizing their complement.

We move together slowly at first, finding rhythm without words. This isn't about performance or skill or any of the mechanics I've learned in briefings and training manuals. It's about two people who've walked through separate hells finally understanding that they don't have to walk alone anymore.

His hands are rough on my hips, calloused from wrenches and tools, and I grip his shoulders hard enough to leave marks. We're both marked already anyway—what's a few more?

The magic builds around us, pulsing in sync with our bodies. White-lilac threads through hearth-coal embers until I can't tell where one ends and the other begins. My frost-cobalt blood-iron keeps the medical car cool despite the heat we're generating, keeping everything in perfect balance.

I've spent nine years chasing ghosts and demons and monsters that wore human faces. I've burned out two command staffs and lost more agents than I care to count. I've carried ash-gray static in my veins since 2005, let it poison everything I touched.

This—this is the first pure thing I've felt in longer than I can remember.

Cole's breath catches. Mine does too. Then we're moving faster, harder, desperate suddenly in a way that has nothing to do with violence or revenge but everything to do with needing to prove to ourselves that this is real, that we're real, that we survived all those years just to find each other.

He says my name like a prayer when he comes, and I follow him over that edge into something that feels like falling upward. The magic peaks around us—brilliant white-lilac and burning hearth-coal filling every corner of the medical car—and then slowly, gradually, fades.

Not away though. Not gone.

Just settling into a soft, pulsing glow that will probably last until dawn.

We collapse together onto the narrow gurney, tangled in blankets and sweat-soaked sheets. The space heater might be dead but neither of us is cold. His heart hammers against my ribs while mine matches its rhythm beat for beat.

"Mara," he says eventually, voice rough from exertion.

"Hmm?"

"I've spent nine years looking for a sliver of justice." His fingers trace idle patterns on my spine. "I think I just found peace instead."

My eyes are heavy but I force them open to look at his face. He's watching me with an expression I haven't seen from him before—softened somehow, like the hardness that usually lives behind his eyes has finally relaxed.

"Keep both," I tell him. "We'll need them tomorrow."

A smile tugs at his mouth. "Always thinking ahead."

"Someone has to."

The magic continues its gentle pulse around us, keeping the temperature perfect. Somewhere in the distance—the sleeper cars maybe, or the depot beyond—I can hear the faint sound of voices. The 38 Orphans waking up. Danny stirring in the medical bay. The world starting its slow crawl toward morning.

But here, in this moment, we're suspended outside time.

Cole's breathing evens out first. Then mine does too. We lie there in silence, holding each other, while the soft glow of our combined magic casts shadows across the walls of the medical car.

I should get up. Should check on Danny, coordinate with the Orphans, plan our next move. Command never sleeps—that's what they taught me in Quantico.

But I don't move.

Instead, I close my eyes and let myself feel something I haven't felt since long before 2005: safe.

Far above us, miles of rock and steel separate us from the High-Spire penthouses where Elias Morvain waits for dawn. I cannot see it, but somewhere in those gilded rooms a Motorola Razr is vibrating insistently on a mahogany desk. A voice on the other end is saying words that will shatter whatever peace Cole and I have found.

*The vault is empty.*

*The Iron-Lung is gone.*

Morvain's finger hovers over the red execution key for the 60-Minute Lethal Geas Countdown.

But that's tomorrow's problem.

Tonight—right now—we sleep.


---

## CHAPTER 11: THE LEASH SNAPS

The hiss of the bellows was rhythmic, wet, and heavy, like an iron whale taking a drag off an unfiltered Camel. 

Every four seconds, the brass casing of the Arcane Iron-Lung expanded with a dull clank, drawing raw telluric bleed out of the ambient Kearny marsh air, scrubbing it through three stages of ground-glass charcoal, and forcing oxygenated ether into Danny’s shredded chest. Inside the polished cylinder, beneath the thick reinforced plexiglass port, the kid looked smaller than nineteen. His skin had that translucent, waxy sheen you only see on guys who’ve pulled forty-eight-hour shifts inside a boiler tank, or kids who had swallowed too much Syndicate byproduct. But his chest rose. It fell. He was breathing without drowning in his own blood.

On an overturned wooden crate beside the rig, an old blue Sony MiniDisc player was hooked up to a pair of battery-powered computer speakers. It was spinning a scratchy track from Chevelle, guitar riffs churning out in a thin, tinny hum that barely masked the low hum of the sodium-vapor lamps overhead. Next to it sat an IBM ThinkPad T42, its black plastic chassis scarred with flux burns, its thick screen glowing with green DOS-style telemetry curves patched directly into the lung’s pressure manifold.

Elena didn’t move. Her arms were crossed over her leather jacket, her knuckles white where she gripped her own elbows. The ambient yellow glare from the rafters carved deep shadows under her cheekbones. She hadn’t slept since we pulled the kid out of the reclamation pen down by the canal, and she smelled of burnt copper, salt spray, and stale diner coffee.

"Pressure's holding at twenty-two PSI," I said, keeping my voice low so it didn't rattle through the glass. I pulled a crescent wrench from my back pocket, tapping the brass collar on the primary bypass valve of the Telluric Core Compressor we’d cannibalized out of P-B2. The needle shuddered, settled, and held firm in the green. "The Syndicate upgrade took. The Ley-stabilizer isn't drifting. It’s feeding clean current to the diaphragm."

Elena exhaled, a long, ragged puff of vapor that caught the cold draft cutting through the depot’s corrugated tin walls. "For how long, Cole?"

"Long enough for his ribs to knit. Long enough for the alchemical burns to stop eating through his pleura." I tightened the locknut a quarter turn, feeling the clean bite of threads cut by union hands, not sweatshop slaves. "He’s tough, El. He took three lungfuls of black iron exhaust and still managed to keep the bypass lever pinned so the younger kids could crawl through the conduit. Most grown men would’ve melted from the inside out in thirty seconds."

"He shouldn't have had to," she whispered, her voice tightening like wire under tension. She stepped closer to the glass, her fingertips brushing the frosted edge where Danny’s breath condensed. "Look at him. He’s nineteen. He was supposed to be apprenticing at the machine shop on McCarter Highway next month. Now he’s bolted into an arcano-pneumatic tank in an abandoned rail barn, smelling like ozone and sterile gauze."

"He's alive," I said.

"Is that what we're calling it?" She turned to me, her dark eyes flashing with that raw, Reyes fury that always burned hottest when she was scared. "We pull him out of the fire, we patch the boiler, we slap some gauze over the rot, and we call it a win? What about the sludge, Cole? The residue in his bronchial tubes isn't going away. Every winter for the rest of his life, he’s gonna cough up black grease. He’s never gonna run for a bus. He’s never gonna take a deep breath of salt air off the bay without feeling that needle prick behind his breastbone."

I didn't answer right away. I wiped a smudge of machine oil off the ThinkPad’s trackpoint with the pad of my thumb, watching the vitals spike slightly as Danny shifted in his medically induced coma, then settle back down as the pneumatic rhythm lulled him under again. 

Outside, the distant rumble of the New Jersey Turnpike rolled across the mudflats—eighteen-wheelers hauling freight through the dark, diesel engines groaning against the grade of the Pulaski Skyway. Just ordinary commerce, grinding on while five miles away, the Four Heads were running occult taps into the municipal substations, bleeding the city dry to charge their batteries.

"You think I don't know that?" I said, my voice dead and quiet. I pocketed the wrench. "You think I’m standing here thinking we gave him a happy ending?"

She didn't back down, but her shoulders dropped an inch. "I'm just tired of counting scraps, Cole."

"Then don't count 'em. Just take 'em." I walked around the crate, stepping over the thick, rubber-insulated high-voltage cables snaking across the grease-stained concrete floor. I stopped right beside her, close enough to feel the cold radiate off her jacket. "We got the kid back, Elena. It ain't a clean slate. It doesn't scrape the black iron sludge out of his lungs, and it sure as hell doesn't resurrect the twelve men who got vaporized when Sub-Station Seven went supercritical two weeks ago. It is never enough. The math never balances out. You know that, and I know that."

She looked down at her boots, where the salt from the melting snow had dried into pale, chalky rings on the leather. "Then what are we doing here?"

"We got him back," I repeated, firm, leaning down so she had to look me in the eye. "It ain't whole, it ain't pure, but it’s a sliver of justice. And a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone. I’ll take that over the void any day of the week."

Elena swallowed hard. She reached out, her fingers resting lightly on the cold brass casing of the iron lung, right over where Danny’s heart was beating behind the metal. "A sliver," she murmured.

"Yeah. A sliver. It’s a wedge, El. You hammer a wedge into a crack in a foundation, and you hit it hard enough, the whole damn fortress comes down." I looked toward the darkened back corner of the depot, where our gear was staged—the shotguns, the ward-breakers, the heavy insulated cables, the maps of the marshland power corridors marked up in grease pencil. "We keep Danny breathing. We make sure the compressor doesn't fail. And then we take that sliver, we take every ounce of spit and vinegar this kid had left in him, and we march it straight up to Pylon Number Five. We end the Four Heads. We cut the wire at the root so nobody else has to sleep in a brass box."

For a second, the only sound between us was the tinny electric guitar from the speakers and the rhythmic *ch-chunk-hiss* of Danny’s air supply. Elena took a breath, slow and steady, letting the cold air clear her head. The fury didn't leave her eyes, but the tremor in her hands stopped. She nodded once. 

"Pylon Five," she said. "We burn it to the ties."

"To the ties," I agreed.

A sudden, violent racket shattered the quiet.

*BAM. BAM. BAM.*

It wasn't a polite knock. It was heavy, desperate fist-work pounding against the corrugated steel of the depot’s pedestrian entrance, accompanied by the shriek of metal on metal as someone threw their entire weight against the deadbolts.

Elena’s hand was inside her coat before the third strike hit, her fingers wrapped around the grip of her snub-nosed .38. I drew my heavy Kimber .45, thumbing the hammer back with a sharp, mechanical click that cut through the alt-rock hum.

"Cole! Elena! Open the fucking latch!" a high, reedy voice screeched through the seam in the doors, cracking with absolute terror. "Open it! They tracked the carrier wave! They're burning the exchange!"

"Digits," Elena hissed, dropping her aim toward the floor.

I lunged forward, throwing the dual slide-bolts back and hauling the steel door open three inches. 

Digits tumbled inside before the door was even halfway clear, hitting the concrete on his hands and knees. The gnome frequency-broker was barely four feet tall, draped in an oversized, oil-stained Carhartt jacket that dragged on the ground, his pointed ears twitching erratically beneath a dirty knit watch cap. Tucked under his left arm was a Panasonic Toughbook, its screen shattered, thick blue sparks arcing viciously from the cracked PCMCIA slot and scorching the nylon of his sleeve.

He scrambled backward toward Danny’s iron lung, his yellow eyes wide and wild in the sodium glare, chest heaving like a blown gasket.

"Shut it! Weld it! Seal it!" Digits shrieked, pointing a trembling, grease-blackened finger back toward the dark marshland outside. "The Head of Cables... Cole, he didn't wait for the shift change. He’s already at the transformer yards!"

* * *
The magnesium casing of the Panasonic Toughbook hit the scarred steel workbench with a hard, metallic crack that echoed through the drafty ribcage of the decommissioned railcar. 

Digits didn’t even bother to take his finger off the cracked touchpad. He hovered over the machine like a starving crow over roadkill, wrapped in an oversized nylon windbreaker from 2002 that reeked of rosin-core soldering smoke, damp wool, and the bitter, burnt-acid dregs of two-day-old diner coffee. The screen had a hairline fracture running from the upper left hinge down through the taskbar, dividing the Windows XP desktop into two distorted planes of gray and sickly neon green.

"Boss, you gotta hear this, these spire-suits are losing their damn minds," Digits spat, his words tumbling out in a fast, jittery street cadence, tongue practically tripping over his crooked teeth. His gnome ears, notched and scarred from old arc-welder pops, twitched forward under his greasy knit cap. "I caught their trunk line. Hit the repeater tower off the Pulaski Skyway right as they flipped the priority flag. Direct iDEN pull. Clear as a bell."

I wiped a smear of heavy gear oil off my knuckles with a rag that had seen better decades. Outside the rusted siding, the cold wind off the Hackensack marshes rattled the loose corrugated sheet metal of the yard shed, carrying that familiar North Jersey stink—low-tide mud, diesel exhaust from the turnpike overpass, and the sharp, dead-copper bite of stale thaumaturgy leaking out of the marsh substations. 

The heavy canvas curtain dividing the sleeper compartment scraped back on its steel rings. Mara Vance stepped through into the yellow wash of the bare incandescent bulb hanging from the ceiling beam. She looked like she hadn’t slept since Tuesday, her combat fatigues stripped down to a charcoal tank top and bruised collarbones, her BATC-issue sidearm sitting holstered low on her hip. The dark circles under her eyes were etched deep into her pale skin, but her posture was straight iron. When you spent fifteen years running tactical wet-work for the Bureau, you didn’t lose the edge just because your department had left you for dead in a Kearny ditch.

"Who’s on the line, Digits?" Mara asked, her voice raspy from dry air and cold tobacco. She didn't move past the edge of the workbench, her eyes immediately locking onto the blinking red spectrum analyzer on the Toughbook's cracked display.

"The top floor," Digits said, his stubby, calloused fingers hammering a keystroke. "Morvain and the tall-boy himself. Malvourne. They thought they had an air-gapped High-Spire channel routed through an auxiliary BATC microwave relay out of Secaucus. Clowns didn't realize the relay’s grounding rod was rusted through three blizzards ago. I picked up the bounce off an old taxi dispatch antenna."

He jabbed the spacebar.

The speakers hissed with static—the thick, rhythmic thrum of an encrypted cellular handshake. Then came the harsh, unmistakable double-chirp of an enterprise Nextel push-to-talk burst.

*Chirp-chirp.*

A voice spilled out of the laptop’s tinny speakers, wet and ragged with breathless panic. Elias Morvain. Even filtered through an eight-kilohertz voice codec, the bureaucrat's thin, patrician whine was unmistakable. 

"...telling you, the entire lower vault is cleared out!" Morvain was nearly shouting over the background drone of what sounded like an idling helicopter turbine. "The seals weren’t melted, they were bypassed with physical shims! Sub-Station Seven is totally empty. The manifests, the dry-storage casks, the containment ampoules—everything. The ward-breakers didn’t just breach the chop-shop perimeter, my lord, they butchered the whole floor team! The siege collapsed before the tactical units even cleared the toll barrier!"

Another *chirp-chirp* cut through the audio feed. 

When the response came, it didn’t have a trace of Morvain’s frantic tremor. It was smooth, slow, and chilled to near absolute zero. Lord Malvourne. Even through compressed digital radio waves, the corporate elf’s timbre carried that sickening, aristocratic cadence—the bored drawl of a creature who measured stock portfolios and human lives on the same balance sheet.

"Compose yourself, Morvain," Malvourne said, the tone as flat and polished as a marble headstone. "You sound like a vendor at an open-air market. Report the perimeter status. Is the auxiliary line intact?"

"No! Are you listening to me?" Morvain gasped, the rustle of synthetic silk audible as he shifted the phone. "The machine shop is burned to the bedrock. Reyes and that rogue Vance bitch pulled the entire crew out through the culverts. We have zero collars in holding. The third-shift union organizers we bagged last night? Gone. The strike committee’s families? Gone. We don't have a single hostage left to bring to the mediation table at dawn. The leverage is completely broken, my lord. If the Port Authority finds out the substation vault was bled dry of BATC reserves—"

"The Port Authority will find whatever ashes we permit them to sweep," Malvourne interrupted, his voice dropping an octave, slipping from boardroom arrogance into pure, unvarnished malice. There was no hesitation in him. No flicker of panic. Just the cold, mechanical calculus of an apex predator closing an unprofitable account. "The union vermin believe they have bought themselves an armistice because they hauled their meat out of the butcher’s freezer. They believe the board operates on human sentiment."

A heavy silence hung on the tape for two full seconds, punctuated only by the whistling wind outside our railcar and the faint click of Digits holding his breath. 

Mara’s hand dropped unconsciously to the grip of her pistol, her thumb flicking the thumb-break strap open without a sound. Her jaw was set so hard I could see the tendon jumping beneath the skin of her cheek.

"My lord?" Morvain’s voice came back, smaller now, stripped of its bluster, realizing too late what room he was standing in. "The contracts on those containment units... the collateral clauses are linked directly to the biometrics of the containment wardens and the shop floor stewards. If we default—"

"The leverage is gone. Burn the leashes. Let their chests cave in."

The command was delivered with the casual finality of a signature on a pink slip. 

"Wait," Morvain breathed. "All sixty-four of them? In the precinct cells? In the tenement blocks? The feedback will burn through the local grid—"

"Burn them," Malvourne repeated. 

The word *burn* hadn't even fully cleared the Toughbook’s cheap plastic grille before the audio shattered into a flatline squeal of dead static.

I opened my mouth to tell Digits to trace the IP termination, but the words died behind my teeth.

The air in the railcar suddenly inverted. The temperature plunged thirty degrees in the space of a single heartbeat, the moisture on the iron window frames instantly crystallizing into brittle, jagged needles of gray frost. The smell of cheap diner coffee and machine oil vanished, obliterated by an overwhelming stench of scorched copper and rotten bone marrow.

Then it hit me.

It wasn't a sound. It was an iron spike driven straight through the bridge of my nose into the soft meat of my brain. A deafening, ultra-high-frequency shriek tore through my skull, so violent and absolute that the yellow lightbulb overhead exploded in a rain of white-hot filament. My vision flared into pure, blinding static, my knees buckling beneath me as the concrete-hard railcar floor rushed up to meet my face.

* * *

The hum of the subterranean depot was the only thing keeping my head from splitting open: the low, vibrating drone of ancient diesel generators pumping through rusty conduits, the damp drip of marsh runoff seeping through forty feet of cracked concrete above us, and the rhythmic emerald glow of the command terminal on the battered IBM ThinkPad resting on an upturned grease drum. 

I was leaning over the rim of the drum, fingers sticky with motor oil and the lukewarm residue of diner coffee regular, watching the terminal trace a bypass loop through the regional BATC grid. Mara stood less than two feet away. I could feel the low-grade hum of her white-lilac weave radiating through the cold air between us—a faint, steady heat that smelled like crushed cedar and hot hearth-coals, anchoring the raw, jagged pulse of my blood-iron. 

Then the cursor froze.

A line of dead-black code printed across the screen, sharp and uncorrupted, followed by a hydraulic screech that didn’t come from the laptop’s speakers. It resonated directly inside the marrow of my clavicle.

"Cole—" Mara started.

The tripwire detonated.

It wasn’t an impact from the outside. It was an internal, systemic detonation—a corporate execution geas, sleeping in the hidden blood-debt ledger of our metahuman signatures, violently ripped awake. 

The pain didn’t radiate; it tore through my chest cavity like a rusted iron grate being dragged backwards through my lungs. My knees gave out instantly. I hit the oil-slicked depot floor hard enough to split the skin on my kneecaps, my palms slapping into the wet grit as all the air was vacuumed out of my trachea in a choked, gagging heave. Beside me, Mara dropped just as brutally, her hands flying to her throat as a ragged, strangled shriek tore through her clenched teeth.

"Ah—fuck—!"

My vision swam in a sickening strobe of pitch-black and oily iridescence. Beneath my Carhartt work shirt, something shifted. It wasn't muscle. It was hard, angular, and geometrically wrong. I grabbed fistfuls of my own collar, desperate to tear the cotton away, the heavy weave ripping under my grease-blackened fingernails as the fabric caught on jagged protrusions shoving upward through my skin. 

Beneath the raw flesh of my sternum, black bismuth was erupting. 

It didn't spread like an infection. It fractured like molten crystal cooling under impossible pressure, blooming in razor-sharp, right-angled stepped pyramids of iridescent pitch and toxic violet. The veins spiderwebbed out from my heart, thick as braided steel wire, dragging a blistering wake of blue-black iron-gall residue that sizzled and bubbled straight through my pores. The chemical stench was suffocating—scorched copper, battery acid, and the rotting, necrotic reek of corporate contract magic designed by pencil-pushing warlocks to liquidate human assets without leaving a paper trail.

Every pulse of my heart felt like it was slamming against an anvil. The bismuth lattice was constricting, wrapping around the left ventricle, biting deeper with each frantic contraction. 

My frost-cobalt blood-iron didn't ask for permission. It surged violently, answering the lethal intrusion with every ounce of survival instinct I had left.

The depot went instantly sub-zero. 

A sharp, deafening crack echoed through the chamber as the ambient air plummeted ten degrees in a single second. The puddle of brackish water around my knees flash-froze, the ice feathering outward in brittle white daggers. Moisture in the air condensed into falling flurries of frost, and on the grease drum above us, the LCD screen of the ThinkPad blossomed with crystalline ice, the green text obscured beneath a crust of flash-frozen condensation. 

My blood-iron fought like a cornered animal, freezing the peripheral capillaries, trying to build an ice-wall against the advancing corporate rot. But the geas had been hardcoded into our BATC files months ago—maybe years ago, buried under fine-print NDAs and blood-binding retention clauses. It had our exact genetic frequencies. The bismuth simply ground forward, crushing through the frost, fracturing my ribs with microscopic, audible snaps that made me cough a thick, sizzling spray of blue-black sludge onto the frozen concrete.

"Cole!" Mara choked out. 

She was curled on her side, her combat boots kicking uselessly against a rusted rail spur. The front of her tactical vest was already smeared with the same vile gall. Her hands clawed at her breastbone, her fingernails ripping red furrows through her own skin to get at the foreign geometric rot invading her chest. The black stepped veins were crawling up her neck, climbing toward her jawline like a collar of toxic iron. 

*Sixty minutes.*

The number wasn't spoken. It was branded directly onto my cerebral cortex by the spell’s telemetric payload—a cold, digital countdown hammering in rhythm with the bismuth vice. A sixty-minute hydraulic cycle. If the central circuit powering this kill-switch wasn't severed before the clock hit zero, the bismuth wouldn't just poison us. The crystalline lattice would snap completely shut, compacting inwards with the force of an industrial press, pulverizing our hearts, lungs, and mediastinum into a cupful of gray paste.

"Doc! Get the frag over here, they're crashing!" 

The roar shook the corrugated tin walls of the depot. Grimjaw’s massive combat boots slammed against the concrete, the heavy orc-make steel toes cracking the frozen slush as he sprinted out of the access tunnel. He skidded on the ice, his massive tusked face twisted in shock, his broad green hands hovering over Mara, terrified that touching her would snap whatever was keeping her alive. Behind him, the panicked clatter of medical crates echoed from the triage bay.

"Don't... don't touch it," I rasped, the words scraping out of my throat like crushed glass. I forced myself up onto one elbow, my arm trembling so violently the tendons felt ready to snap. Blood-gall dripped from my chin, hissing as it struck the ice between my hands. "It's... it's a closed loop..."

"The fuck is that?" Grimjaw barked, his voice rattling the low ceiling as he dropped to one knee, looking between the black bismuth tearing through my chest and the frost eating Mara’s tactical rig. "What did they do to you?"

"The contract..." Mara groaned, her back arching off the floor as a fresh spasm of geometric crystallization jagged across her ribs. "The BATC... master-override..."

I dragged myself an inch closer to her, my chest screaming as the frost-cobalt and her cedar-coal magic brushed against each other. The moment our field collided, the advancing bismuth hesitated—just a fraction of a millimeter, the raw heat of her white-lilac weave scorching the edges of the corporate crystal, while my frost blunted its razor-sharp tips. But it wasn't a cure. It was just a tourniquet on an amputation. The internal clock kept ticking, cold and relentless, sixty seconds already devoured by the dark.

I locked eyes with her through the haze of agony. The blue-black gall was running down my teeth, tasting of salt, rust, and burnt copper, but beneath the pain, the machinist in me saw the schematic. I knew where the master feed originated. I knew the only junction box in North Jersey with enough arcane bandwidth to broadcast an execution weave of this magnitude.

"Sixty minutes..." I managed to gasp out, clutching my chest to keep the ribs from separating, locking my gaze onto hers. "We have to hit the Pylon..."

Mara didn't look away. The agony was tearing her apart, but her jaw clenched, hard and unrelenting as industrial iron. Beneath the creeping black veins choking her throat, her eyes ignited—not with panic, not with pain, but with pure, undiluted white-lilac fire that pushed the necrotic static back from her pupils. 

She reached out, her trembling, blood-slicked fingers clamping onto the collar of my torn jacket, hauling herself up until our foreheads nearly touched.

"Then we better drive fast," she whispered.


---

## CHAPTER 12: TRIAGE AND TARMAC

The oil-slick damp of the concrete seeped right through the knees of my tactical cargos. My vision swam in pulses of greasy magenta, but I grabbed Cole by the heavy canvas collar of his Carhartt jacket and dragged him up with me, hauling his dead weight against the rust-scabbed steel of a bulkhead support.

He groaned, a low, wet sound torn out of his throat. His knuckles were raw, split against iron, and beneath the torn collar of his thermal shirt, the skin of his clavicle was convulsing. 

The black bismuth wasn’t just staining him; it was crystallizing. Angular, iridescent plates of razor-edged mineral were creeping out from the hollow of his neck like an invasive fungal shelf, blooming along the subterranean rivers of his vascular tree. Each time his chest hitched, the geometric facets clicked, shooting micro-fractures of pitch-black gall across his sternum.

"Look at me, Reyes," I rasped, my throat tasting of battery acid and scorched copper. "Cole. Eyes front."

His lids fluttered, pupils dilated until the brown was nearly swallowed by black. "Mara... chest feels like... somebody poured molten slag down the pipe..."

"It’s the Geas," I said, my fingers shaking as I tore open a foil packet with my teeth. The sharp, nose-stinging bite of isopropyl alcohol cut through the stagnant subterranean fug. "It’s kinetic-sympathetic. Every beat of your pump pushes the ink. The faster your ticker goes, the faster the cage locks shut."

On the floor between my boots, my black Motorola Razr lay flipped open, its cyan screen glowing weakly in the dirt. 03:14 AM. The digital seconds flicked past with cold, indifferent precision, a tiny stopwatch measuring out how much blood we had left before the bismuth petrified our ventricles into solid stone.

"Control your breathing, Mara. If you panic, the Geas accelerates."

My mother’s voice didn’t belong in a sunken rail spur beneath the Kearny Meadows, but there she was. Lysandra Vance crouched on Cole’s other side, her trench coat pulled back to keep the hem out of the stagnant puddle of runoff. Her hair was pulled into the same severe combat bun she’d worn during the ’99 Breach, though the silver at her temples had thinned. She didn't look like an aging woman; she looked like a retired field marshal calculating the tonnage of an incoming strike.

She pulled a bundle of dried Atlantic white cedar from her kit, touched a disposable Bic lighter to the tip until it flared orange, and blew it out. A column of pale, pungent smoke spiraled up, bitter and herbal, fighting a losing war against the heavy, copper-and-ink stench of iron-gall.

"Hold his shoulder down," Lysandra commanded, her voice dropping into the low, rhythmic cadences of the old Department bio-wards. "I’m locking his somatic perimeter, but the weave is ripping out from the center. He’s running at a hundred and twenty beats a minute. At this rate, the calcification hits his aortic arch before four."

"It's hardcoded, Mom," I said, my teeth clenched so tight my jaw clicked. "We can't break it here. We have to reach Pylon #5 and use the heartstop loophole."

"Then you’d better give him the hour to get there," she countered, her gray eyes fixing me with zero mercy. "Burn it back, Mara. Cauterize the line."

I spat blood onto the ties, took a ragged breath of the cedar smoke, and reached out.

I didn't use an arc-focus. There was no time for copper rods or glass capacitors. I pressed my bare right palm directly against the center of Cole’s chest, right over the junction where the bismuth plates were knitting together over his sternum.

Cole gasped, his back arching off the bulkhead.

"Easy," I whispered, though my own heart was hammering a frantic, suicidal rhythm against my ribs. "Easy, Reyes. Take it from me."

I reached down into the furnace behind my ribs, past the exhaustion, past the grit of three sleepless nights fueled by stale Wawa drip and adrenaline, and pulled up the white-lilac.

It didn't flare like normal fire. It bloomed under my skin first—pale, violet-hot, translucent as kerosene burning on glass. When it broke through my pores, it didn't scorch his flesh; it sank straight through the dermis, searching for the invasive frequency of the Geas.

The pain hit me through the sympathetic bridge like a high-voltage line snapping against bare bone. I saw what was inside him: the black script of the contract winding through his pericardium like barbed wire dipped in printer’s ink. The bismuth was feeding on his life-force, transmuting the sodium and calcium of his bloodstream into geometric slag.

"Breathe, Reyes," I snarled, forcing the flame deeper. "Don't fight the burn. Let it freeze."

I narrowed the lilac fire down from a blanket wash to a filament—a single, monomolecular thread of superheated kinetic will. With my thumb and index finger sinking into the metaphysical meat of the spell, I began to loop the flame around the base of his ascending aorta.

A tourniquet. Not a cure—you couldn't cure a Department death-sentence with field magic—but a ligature. A cold-fire choke collar to strangle the flow of the arcano-toxin before it could cross the threshold into his brain.

Cole thrashed violently, his heels kicking out, sending the Razr skittering three inches across the gravel. His teeth snapped together, foam bubbling at the corner of his mouth. 

"Hold him!" I yelled.

Lysandra leaned her entire weight onto his collarbone, her palms flaring with a muted, amber stabilization ward that hissed where it met his sweat-soaked shirt. "Hold the line, Mara! Don't let the fire drift into the vagus nerve or you'll stop his heart right here on the ballast!"

The smell was sickening. It wasn’t burning meat; it was the smell of hot lead, burnt cedar, and old, wet paper pulled from a flooded cellar. The iron-gall fought back. The black veins under his skin bulged, turning purple-black and rigid as steel cables, pushing against my weave. The lilac fire turned sickly, spitting white sparks that drifted down onto the wet ties, sizzling out in the grease.

"Down," I hissed through gritted teeth, my vision graying at the edges. "Stay down, you bastard."

With a final, savage push of intent, I knotted the lilac thread.

The reaction was instantaneous. The geometric crystallization on Cole's neck froze mid-bloom. The iridescent sheen dulled, turning into an inert, charcoal-gray crust. The frantic, hammering pulse in his carotid slowed, dropping from a panicked gallop to a heavy, sluggish thud.

Cole collapsed back against the bulkhead, his head rolling limp against his shoulder, chest heaving in slow, shuddering gasps. The black veins had receded half an inch, walled off behind a faint, glowing violet ring encircling his throat like a bruised choker.

I pulled my hand back. My fingers were curled into claws, trembling so hard I couldn't open them. The skin on my palm was pale, dead-white from arc-depletion, smelling faintly of ozone and scorched sugar.

On the ground, the Razr’s blue screen read 03:19 AM.

Five minutes. It felt like I’d spent forty-eight hours hauling pig iron out of a foundry trench.

"He's stable," Lysandra said, her fingers lingering on Cole's wrist, counting the pulse against her own stopwatch. Her voice had lost none of its steel, but the set of her shoulders dropped a fraction of an inch. "Sixty-two beats. The ligature will hold sixty minutes. Maybe seventy if he doesn't have to sprint."

"He won't have to sprint," I said, wiping cold sweat from my upper lip with the back of my sleeve. "He just has to walk. We get him through the Passaic drainage junction, we hit the base of Pylon #5, and we trip the ground wire. That's the only way to reset the loop."

I reached down, scooped up the Razr, and snapped it shut. The metallic click sounded absurdly loud in the cavernous concrete hollow.

Before I could shove the phone into my pocket, the floor shuddered.

It wasn't an arc-tremor. It wasn't the rhythmic thrum of the PATH trains running overhead toward Journal Square.

It was a deep, guttural, low-frequency mechanical violence—the deafening, unmuffled roar of a sixteen-cylinder diesel engine dropping into low gear, echoing straight out of the northern drainage tunnel. Dust drifted down from the ceiling bolts, speckling Cole's sweat-streaked face like gray snow, followed by the twin yellow blades of high-output halogen headlights cutting through the tunnel’s black mist.

* * *
The stench of burning flux, scorched transmission fluid, and dead low-tide mud from the Hackensack reached me before the noise did.

Then came the mechanical scream of straight-cut reverse gears and the pneumatic hiss of an overloaded air-brake system. The corrugated iron roll-up door rattled in its tracks as the monster backed into Bay Three. 

It was a nightmare on wheels—a Frankenstein hack-job built out of an old Newark municipal Ford E-350 trauma ambulance, wide-bodied and ugly, its cherry-and-white paint long since stripped down to mottled zinc primer and rust. Heavy quarter-inch boiler plate had been scabbed across the wheel wells, and across the snub-nosed snout sat a cow-catcher bumper forged from railway rebar and spiked angle iron. Arc-welding sparks rained off the rear quarter-panel in violent, spitting showers of white-hot magnesium light, illuminating the grease-blackened girders of the Local 405 depot.

Riding the driver-side running board like a harbor pilot bringing in an ironclad was Bram Kovacs. 

The dwarf was four-foot-two of solid, gristle-packed union stubbornness, stuffed into flame-retardant Carhartt coveralls that had seen twenty years of boiler rooms and lathe bays. His flip-front welding mask was shoved up over a forehead scarred by slag burns, his wire-bristle beard tied off in three neat rubber bands to keep it from catching the torch. He held an ungrounded stinger clamp in one heavy, gauntleted paw, trailing thick black rubber lead-cables across the oil-slick concrete.

"Cut it, you green bastard!" Bram bellowed, his voice like river gravel churning in an iron drum. "Cut the goddamn ignition before you shake the manifold studs out of the head!"

Inside the cab, a massive silhouette shifted against the cracked safety glass. The seven-foot frame of Grimjaw, our front-line breacher, killed the keyed starter. The 7.3-liter Navistar diesel shuddered, coughed a plume of thick, sulfurous soot toward the depot exhaust hoods, and dieseled twice before finally dying in a metallic tick of settling heat. 

The driver door popped open with a groan that sounded like a shipyard crane giving out. Grimjaw stepped down, boots crunching on dropped slag and metal shavings. A half-chewed, unlit White Owl blunt was clenched between his lower tusks, wet with saliva and reeking of artificial vanilla and stale ditch-weed. 

"Brakes are spongy, Bram," the orc rumbled, dragging the back of a calloused, slate-gray hand across his snout. "Pedal went halfway to the floorboards when I took the turn off Route 1&9. Thought I was gonna kiss the guardrail over the marsh."

"Because you drive like a blind steer with a lit cherry up its ass," Bram snapped back, dropping off the running board with a dull, heavy thud. He tossed his stinger onto a steel cart, wiping sweat from the deep crease between his bushy eyebrows. "She’s hauling three tons of surplus structural steel and six auxiliary battery banks. You don't pump the brakes like a teenage girl in a Civic, you downshift and let the drag do the talking."

I walked over, the cold draft coming through the depot door biting straight through my wool barn coat. My hands were shoved deep in my pockets, gripping my knuckles against the damp, salt-air ache that always crept in off Newark Bay around three in the morning.

"Is she going to hold, Bram?" I asked, looking up at the reinforced roof where two salvaged searchlight mounts had been crudely bolted above the light bar.

Bram spit a dark stream of tobacco against the nearest concrete pylon. "I bypassed the alternator governor and spliced a dual-manifold nitrous harness into the glow-plug taps. You drop the hammer, Reyes, and she’ll fly like an F-15 down the Pulaski. But you keep Grimjaw’s foot on the floor for more than fifteen seconds straight, and that block won't just overheat—the pistons’ll weld themselves to the cylinder walls and turn the whole crankcase into a puddle of molten scrap."

He kicked the front passenger tire—a heavy, ten-ply commercial tread reinforced with steel bands. 

"Suspension's shot to hell, but she'll take a rocket to the grill and keep rolling," Bram muttered, running a soot-blackened hand over the rough, overlapping bead welds along the cab armor. "Got the depleted-bismuth slugs loaded in the back. Forty boxes of three-inch magnums, wrapped in lead foil so your little magic toys don't cook off early."

Grimjaw grinned, his tusks gleaming yellow under the flickering sodium lights hanging from the depot roof. He patted the heavy iron ram-bar with a palm the size of a manhole cover. "Just point me at the spire-suits, Bram. I'll run 'em flat."

Behind the ambulance, the rear double doors creaked open. 

Elena was already inside the cavernous cargo bay, her slender frame silhouetted against the amber utility lights mounted along the ceiling. She had discarded her street coat, wearing only a gray thermal and a tactical chest harness, her breath pluming in the damp cold. In one hand, she held an ancient PalmPilot Tungsten, its monochrome LCD screen casting a sickly greenish glow over her sharp cheekbones as she repeatedly tapped the digitizer screen with an aluminum stylus.

Beside her, Digits was muscling wooden ordnance crates stamped with faded BATC logistics markings into the cargo runners, his wire-rimmed glasses sliding down his sweat-sheened nose. 

"Digits, tie those down with the ratchets," Elena ordered without looking up, her voice clipped, carrying that sharp edge she got whenever the leylines started humming out of phase. "If we hit the curb coming off the bridge and fifty pounds of consecrated buckshot loose-rolls into the batteries, we’re all going to heaven in a bucket."

"I'm securing it, I'm securing it," Digits huffed, his knuckles bloody from snagging an unground burr on the steel decking. He wrenched a yellow nylon strap tight, the ratchet mechanism clicking with rhythmic finality. "Though I’d like to note for the union minutes that hauling unregistered Class-IV munitions through Jersey City at four a.m. is generally considered a career-limiting maneuver."

I stepped up onto the rear bumper, peering over Elena’s shoulder. The screen of her PDA wasn't showing calendar appointments or contact lists; it was running a patched underground topographical map of the Kearny marsh substations and the deep aqueducts running beneath the Passaic River. A jagged line of corrupted pixels was pulsing along the lower third of the grid, jittering in sync with an invisible frequency.

"Fault lines are bleeding," Elena said softly, pointing the stylus at a cluster of crosshairs centered near the old industrial railheads. "The ambient resonance down in the Undercity has spiked forty percent in the last twenty minutes. The cold iron down there isn't grounding it anymore. It feels like... like grease poured on a hot griddle."

"The Pylons?" I asked, a tight knot forming in the pit of my gut.

"They're spooling up," she said, finally turning to look at me. Her dark eyes were bloodshot, rimmed with the deep shadows of three days without sleep. "The conduit isn't just leaking magic, Cole. It's pulling vacuum. Drawing raw power right out of the grid to prime the triggers."

Bram walked up to the open doors, wiping his hands with a kerosene-soaked rag that smelled sharp enough to clean carburetors. He looked at the fluctuating display on Elena's palmtop, his thick mouth setting into a hard, grim line.

"Then we're out of time to polish the chrome," the dwarf said quietly. "If those spires lock in, they'll turn everything from here to Hoboken into an ash heap."

Before I could answer, the depot's overhead warning horns tore the silence in two. 

It wasn't a standard fire alarm. It was the low, grinding wail of the Local's seismic trip-sensors—a mechanical klaxon salvaged from an old civil defense tower, wired directly to the bedrock probes five hundred feet down. The floor beneath our work boots trembled, a sharp, violent shudder that rattled the socket sets on the steel benches and sent a stack of empty oil drums tumbling across the far bay.

Across the yard, the lights dropped, flickering from harsh white to a dim, sickly brown as the regional grid groaned under a massive, subterranean draw.

Elena stared at the PalmPilot. The screen flickered, the monochrome lines scrambling into pure static as a high-pitched squeal tore through the ambulance’s radio receiver. 

"Cole," she breathed, her knuckles turning white around the stylus. "They're firing."

* * *

The underground maintenance depot smelled like thirty years of accumulated diesel sludge, ozone, and wet limestone. Above our heads, the ceiling trembled with the distant, rhythmic thunder of the Turnpike extension, each tractor-trailer shuddering down through the rebar like a dying pulse.

My ribs felt like someone had driven six-inch bismuth wedges between the intercostal muscle and twisted them with an iron wrench. Every breath was a rasp of crushed glass and metallic static. Across from me, Cole wasn’t doing any better. He leaned against the reinforced worktable, his big knuckles whitening against the grease-stained steel, his jaw locked so hard the tendons corded down into his throat. Beneath the skin of his collarbones, the iridescent, prism-sharp lines of the Geas flickered—a synthetic rot crawling inward toward his heart.

Lysandra stepped in close to me first. Her eyes were shadowed, rimmed with the frantic red of forty-eight hours without sleep, but her hands were steady as she reached out, catching my tactical vest by the shoulder straps. Her grip dug deep enough to bruise through the Kevlar.

"You don't let it take you, Vance," she whispered, her voice rough as unground coffee. "You hear me? You drag that bastard down, you break the seal, and you bring Reyes back in one piece. If you die out there in the marshes, I’m digging you up just to shoot you myself."

A sharp, humorless bark of laughter tore from my throat, immediately punishing me with a flare of agony behind my sternum. "I'll hold you to that, Lyse. Keep the sub-level sealed. If the Telluric alarms trip above five hundred milligauss, don't wait for us. You flood the secondary bulkheads and burn the conduit."

"Not happening," she said, though we both knew she was lying to keep from breaking. She stepped back, her chin coming up with that stubborn, hard-nosed Newark cop posture she’d worn since our first year in the bureau.

Beside her, Elena stood by the massive, rumbling cylinder of the vintage iron-lung rig they’d dragged out of the old county infirmary stockpile. The bellows heaved with a wet, mechanical sigh—*chhh-clack, chhh-clack*—cycling ambient arcanum through charcoal filters to keep the boy's lungs from filling with his own curdled blood. Elena had one hand flat against the viewing port, her fingers pale against the condensation on the tempered glass. She didn't look away from Danny until Cole stepped up beside her.

Inside the iron cylinder, Danny’s face was small, waxen, framed by the dark rubber collar of the seal. But his eyes were wide open. He wasn't asleep; he hadn't slept since the grid began to wobble. His gaze locked onto Cole, tracking the faint, unnatural frost tracing the edge of Cole’s jawline.

The external speaker mounted to the cylinder’s rusted chassis hissed with a spit of static, followed by Danny’s voice—thin, metallic, and hitched to the tempo of the pneumatic pump.

"Give 'em hell, Cole."

Cole didn’t flinch. He pressed his broad palm against the outside of the glass, right over the boy’s reflection. The cold radiating off him was real now; tiny needles of frost-cobalt crystallized on the depot air between them, drifting down like frozen ash. His irises flared—a sudden, blinding surge of high-voltage blue that drowned out the yellow halogen glare overhead.

"Count on it, kid," Cole said. His voice was a low, grinding rumble, deep as an idling Peterbilt. "Rest up. Next time I see you, you're walking out of that can under your own steam."

Elena wiped her nose with the sleeve of her grease-spotted thermal, her knuckles brushing Cole's arm. "Go," she said softly, though the word sounded like it was torn straight out of her marrow. "Before the bridges drop. Go."

"Time's burned," Bram barked from the depot floor.

The sound of the hydraulic winches groaned through the vault as the depot’s primary steel blast doors began their slow, screeching crawl upward. Rust flaked down from the overhead rollers like dead skin, falling onto the roof of the armored Ford ambulance idling in the center bay. It was a chopped-up E-350, retrofitted with half-inch ballistic plating, wire-mesh cage glass, and run-flat tires thick enough to roll through an active quarry. The diesel block was rumbling with a throaty, un-muffled roar that vibrated straight through the concrete and into my bad knee.

Grimjaw was already in the driver's cab, his scarred gray bulk crammed behind the steering wheel like an overfed pit bull stuffed into an iron crate. He slammed his flat hand against the horn—two sharp, deafening blasts that echoed off the wet rock walls.

"Move your asses!" Grimjaw bellowed through the sliding partition. "The current’s already surging in the wet-wells! In five minutes, the surface ramp is gonna be a fucking waterfall of boiling sewage!"

Bram grabbed my elbow, his grip like an iron clamp, hauling me toward the rear doors. Every step felt like kicking a curb with broken toes. The synthetic bismuth lattice in my chest pulsed in time with my racing heart, burning cold and sharp, an invasive crystal garden eating its way through soft tissue. Cole was right beside me, moving with that stiff, predatory gait of a man who was using ninety percent of his willpower just to keep from folding in half.

Bram threw Cole up through the open back doors first, then hoisted me up by my vest. The rough, mildewed canvas of the secondary medical gurney caught me hard, the steel frame rattling violently against the diamond-plate floor. Cole collapsed onto the bench opposite me, his back slamming into the aluminum equipment locker with a hollow thud. His breath came in ragged, white plumes that hung in the cab's dead air.

"Doors!" Bram yelled, slamming the heavy steel-sheathed rear portals shut.

The locking bolts engaged with a sound like a guillotine dropping. Darkness clamped down, broken only by the sickly, flickering glow of a single overhead halogen dome light that buzzed like a trapped hornet. The smell inside the rig was suffocating: old rubbing alcohol, stale winter coats, diesel fumes filtering up through the floorboards, and the bitter, coppery tang of the blood-iron leaking from our pores.

I reached into the thigh pocket of my BDUs with numb, shaking fingers and yanked out the silver Motorola Razr. I snapped the clamshell open.

The tiny external screen flashed blue, then illuminated the cracked primary display.

*00:55:00.*

Fifty-five minutes. Fifty-five minutes before the Geas hit terminal density and turned my cardiac muscle into brittle, purple-black slag.

"Fifty-five," I breathed, my voice barely audible over the screaming transmission.

Cole looked up at me from beneath the brim of his greasy watch cap. The cobalt light in his eyes didn't fade; it sharpened, pooling in the corners like liquid mercury. "More than enough time to burn Kearny to the waterline."

Before I could answer, Grimjaw slammed the Ford into low gear.

The transmission didn't just engage—it kicked like an angry mule. The ambulance leaped forward, tires barking on the wet depot concrete, and the violent lurch sent a searing lance of agony straight through my sternum. I doubled over, my teeth sinking into my lower lip until the hot, salty taste of my own blood flooded my mouth. Cole let out a low, strangled hiss through his teeth, his fingers digging gouges into the vinyl of the bench as the g-force smashed us back against the bulkheads.

The engine screamed as Grimjaw pinned the pedal, hauling four tons of steel up the sixty-degree access incline. The blast doors cleared the roof rack with inches to spare. Water from the surface runoff slammed against the windshield like thrown buckets of dirty gravel. We crested the apron, bouncing hard on the heavy-duty leaf springs, and the yellow gloom of the underground died, replaced by the violent, neon-smeared darkness of a North Jersey midnight in the middle of a grid-collapse.

We blew through the rusted perimeter gates of the scrap yard and hit the surface asphalt of Neon Hollow running fifty miles an hour. Rain was sheeting sideways across the cracked pavement, lit purple and bilious orange by the dying sodium-vapor streetlights and the stuttering emergency beacons of Kearny Avenue.

I pulled myself up toward the small, wire-reinforced observation port behind the driver's cab.

"Grimjaw! Stay off the lower turnpike!" I shouted through the grill. "The marshes are already—"

A hundred yards ahead, the wet blacktop didn't just buckle—it detonated.

A geyser of thick, oily, pitch-black magic roared forty feet straight into the night sky, tearing the asphalt into jagged, flying slabs as the telluric vein beneath the street ruptured like an over-pressurized gas main.


---

## CHAPTER 13: THE ISFET HIGHWAY

The 7.3-liter Power Stroke diesel under the doghouse didn’t just roar; it screamed like an iron beast being flayed alive. Grimjaw had bypassed the wastegate with a rusty pair of vice-grips and a strip of baling wire, and every time he kicked the floorboards, raw, unburnt sulfur and black soot blasted past the cracked seals of the firewall, choking the cab in a haze of burnt oil and grease.

We were sideways before I could get my boots planted.

The heavy E-450 trauma-ambulance bucked violently over a collapsed storm drain, tossing me hard against the stainless steel cabinets. Racks of sterile gauze, expired saline bags, and surgical shears rattled in their trays like machine-gun fire. Outside the rear tinted glass, Neon Hollow was bleeding to death under the sick amber hum of broken sodium-vapor lamps. It was 2008, but out there on the avenue, civilization looked like it had stalled out and decomposed twenty years prior. Abandoned ’99 Crown Vics—half of them stripped of their catalytic converters, the other half torched down to their blackened steel ribs—cluttered the asphalt, their anti-theft horns blaring in broken, discordant wails that vibrated right through my molars.

"Grim!" I hauled myself up by the ceiling grab-rail, my shoulder screaming where the shrapnel had carved a trench through my coat. "Keep her off the curbs! The suspension's already riding on the bump stops!"

"Tell that to the goddamn sinkhole that just tried to swallow my front axle, Reyes!" Grimjaw barked back through the open partition, his massive, scarred hands wrestling the worn vinyl steering wheel like he was choking a bull to death. "Floor’s dropping out from under the whole fucking ward! Sit down and hold on!"

I dropped back to my knees beside the gurney. 

Mara was shivering so violently the aluminum frame shrieked against its floor latches. Her skin was the color of skim milk left out in an alley puddle, her dark hair plastered to her temple by sweat and dried river mud. Her combat vest was half-unbuckled, dark arterial stains soaking through the gray weave of her undershirt where the puncture wounds refused to close. Her pulse was a runaway engine—three hundred beats a minute, fluttering behind her collarbone like a trapped starling choking on its own blood.

I caught her right hand in both of mine. Her fingers were ice, the nails blackened with dried carbon.
"Look at me, Vance," I muttered, my voice scraping out like a rasp against rusted iron. "Focus on the rhythm. Don't look at the ceiling."

Her eyes cracked open, pupils dilated until there was barely a sliver of hazel left. When she saw me, her cracked lips parted, drawing in a jagged, rattling breath that smelled faintly of scorched ozone and spent brass. 

I didn't wait for permission. I reached deep into the well behind my ribs, dragging up the frost-cobalt that lived in the marrow of my bones. It burned going down my arms—not a clean, sterile heat, but a numbing, subterranean freeze that bit like a January draft blowing off the Passaic. I forced the cold out through my calloused palms, driving the pale blue arcana straight through the thin skin of her wrists and into the radial artery. 

The frost hit her bloodstream like a shockwave. A sharp gasp tore from her throat as the azure light spread beneath her skin, branching out like delicate, frozen fern leaves across her forearms, forcing the frantic gallop of her heart to drop. Three hundred down to two-twenty. Two-twenty down to one-forty. I was cooling the engine before she threw a rod, turning her blood to cold sludge just to keep the pump from tearing itself apart.

In return, she squeezed my knuckles with a grip that threatened to fracture bone. 

Her magic bled back into me—not frost, but white-lilac. It didn't belong in an oil-stained North Jersey butcher-box of an ambulance, but it flooded my senses anyway, thick and heavy with the scent of wet spring loam and crushed flower petals. It seeped into the raw, ragged nerves of my torn shoulder, deadening the white-hot throb, washing out the iron-tasting bile in the back of my throat. It was an agonizing, suffocating mercy, binding us together on the blood-slick diamond plate floor while the world outside tore itself to pieces.

The glass behind my head frosted over, crystallization racing across the safety panes in jagged web-patterns from the bleed-off of my cobalt chill.

Outside, the street exploded in violence. 

A crew of Syndicate runners had broken through the steel roll-down gates of a pawn shop on the corner of 4th, their jackets soaked in mud and road grime. Half of them were firing cheap snub-nosed revolvers into the air while three more dragged an ancient console television across the sidewalk. Before Grimjaw could clear the intersection, a BATC light tactical squad swung out from an alley in an armored Suburban. They didn’t bother with sirens. They didn't bother with megaphones. They just racked back their short-barreled carbines and opened up, laying down a scything sweep of lead that shredded the looters, the storefronts, and the parked sedans in a single, deafening roar.

Rounds skipped off the reinforced steel flank of our ambulance with high-pitched *pings* that sent flakes of white enamel showering down over my back. Through the frosty glass, I saw bodies dropping into the gutters, their Nextel chirp phones clipped to their web belts vibrating violently, screens glowing neon green against the dark pavement as unread alerts chirped unanswered into the blood-slicked rain.

Grimjaw slammed the horn—a dual-air blast that parted the smoke—and violently hooked the wheel hard to the starboard side. The rear tires broke loose, sliding across a smear of spilled hydraulic fluid, clipping the rear quarter-panel of an abandoned Crown Vic. Plastic tail-lights shattered in a burst of red sparks, the cruiser's horn blaring a continuous, dying drone as we spun past.

"Hold onto your asses!" Grimjaw yelled from the cab, his knuckles white against the wheel as the bypassed turbo whistled a deafening, tea-kettle shriek over the engine roar. "We got BATC barricades up ahead! Concrete barriers and heavy gunners!"

I looked down at Mara. Her eyes were locked on mine, the pale lilac glow in her veins trembling under the sheer pressure of keeping my pain at bay while my cobalt kept her heart from bursting. She swallowed hard, her bloody fingers digging deeper into the meat of my forearm.

"Don't stop, Grim!" I yelled through the partition, my teeth bared in a snarl. "Ram right through the bastards!"

"Hang on to your teeth, then!" Grimjaw roared back.

Instead of hitting the concrete, Grimjaw cut the wheel hard to the left, mounting the sidewalk and taking down a light pole with a sickening crunch of sheet metal. We plowed straight off the road, the heavy steel push-bumper of the Ford smashing through a ten-foot chain-link fence topped with concertina wire. The heavy galvanized mesh shrieked, wrapping around the hood like a shroud before the sheer inertia of five tons of Detroit iron snapped the posts at the welds, dragging us into the labyrinth of the old Kearny industrial train yard.

The ambulance bounced hard across the ballast rock and rotting cross-ties, the shocks bottoming out with bone-jarring violence that threw Mara against my chest. Rows of rusted shipping containers and idle, graffiti-scarred boxcars loomed on either side like the walls of a canyon, cutting off the gunfire from the avenue.

Grimjaw let off the throttle, wrestling the rig down a corridor between two tracks of dead locomotives, the diesel idling with a wet, loping growl.

Then, the earth beneath the tracks began to hum.

It wasn't the low rumble of a passing freight train. It was an abyssal, throat-tearing vibration that shook the rust loose from the boxcar undercarriages, vibrating the fillings in my mouth. 

Fifty yards ahead, between two sets of rusted rails, a heavy cast-iron manhole cover began to rattle violently against its rim. Then another. Then six more in rapid succession, tracing a line straight down the rail spur toward our bumper.

Before Grimjaw could hit the brakes, the iron lids blew sky-high, blasting sixty feet into the night air on violent, geysering pillars of Liquid Isfet—thick, churning plumes of pitch-black, iridescent shadow-magic tearing up from the deep earth, smelling of rot, static electricity, and the ancient, sunless tombs of the Duat.

* * *
The suspension of the stolen rig groaned as we tore under the blackened iron underbelly of the freight trestles out by the Kearny marsh cut. Every pothole on this forgotten stretch of Route 7 sent a fresh, white-hot spike straight through my sternum, grinding broken cartilage against cracked ribs until I could taste copper on the back of my tongue. Outside, the November rain was coming down in sleeting sheets, beating against the ambulance’s fiberglass body like handfuls of buckshot. Inside, it smelled like stale antiseptic, sour sweat, and the sharp, dead-battery stink of fried arcana.

Above the scream of the turbo-diesel, something hit the roof.

It wasn’t gravel. It was a heavy, deliberate *clang*—the kind of dead-weight thud that only came from boots dropping eighty feet out of the iron girders above. Then came another. And another. Steel grapples punched through the gutters with a wet, tearing screech, biting into the frame with the high-torque whine of pneumatic winches. 

"Company on the lid!" Bram Kovacs barked from the jump seat. The dwarf didn’t hesitate. He was already moving with that low-center-of-gravity velocity that made five feet of solid bone and muscle feel like an incoming freight train. He hauled a nylon harness out from under the bench, snapping the forged carabiner into the heavy steel anchor loop of the floor gurney mount with a single, practiced *clack*. 

Above our heads, the ceiling began to bleed fire. 

A high-pitched, tooth-drilling whine tore through the cabin as a pair of plasma-torches bit into the thin metal shell. The paint bubbled, blistering black, and then the blue-white teeth of the arc breached the skin, dripping white-hot slag onto the linoleum floor tiles between my boots. The stench hit instantly—scorched rubber, melting galvanized steel, and the heavy, sweet reek of high-yield ozone. Through the glowing fissures, I caught the stuttering, pixelated flicker of optical-camo cloaks glitching out in the downpour. Syndicate Wire-Runners. Twitchy, speed-burned street-elves who worked the high bridges and turnpike spurs, strung out on bootleg amphetamines and wirehead arcana, looking for salvage or BATC bounties.

"Fucking roaches," Bram growled, hauling a matte-black MP5 from a canvas duffel between his feet. The receiver was hand-chiseled with deep, jagged dwarven wards that swallowed the dim amber light of the cabin interior. He racked the charging handle back, letting it slam home with a definitive, mechanical snap. "Hold on to your dick, Reyes. We’re taking the door off."

Before I could drag enough air into my lungs to curse, Bram hit the emergency latch and kicked the side sliding door outward into the seventy-mile-an-hour gale.

The storm tore into the ambulance like a physical blow. Rain, road grit, and the rank, rotten-egg stench of the Hackensack marshes flooded the box, instantly drenching us in freezing spray. Outside, the black ribbon of asphalt was blurring past under the yellow sodium glare of the distant Turnpike overpass, tires throwing up roostertails of oily spray that choked the mirrors. 

Bram leaned right out into the hurricane, braced against the door jamb, his harness cable going taut as a piano wire. 

Above the roofline, hooked on by magnetic pitons and knee-clamps, two figures hung upside down like spiders in frayed cloaks. The camo weave was dying in the cold rain, shorting out in erratic bursts of static-blue digital interference that exposed skeletal, needle-scarred limbs, leather flight vests, and sharp, angular faces framed by greasy dreadlocks and wired chrome goggles. 

Bram didn’t offer a warning. He leaned out into the slipstream, pulled the stock tight against his shoulder, and leveled the submachine gun upward at a sixty-degree angle.

"Eat lead, you pointy-eared wire-trash!" he roared over the howl of the wind.

The MP5 barked in a deafening, rhythmic drumbeat—a flat, concussive stutter of depleted-bismuth slugs that carved blue-white tracer lines into the sheeting rain. The rounds chewed through the lip of the roof, spitting chunks of aluminum and insulation into the night. One of the runners took three bismuth slugs straight through his exposed bicep and shoulder; the heavy, dense metal shattered the joint on impact, spraying black, chemically treated blood across the exterior pane of the window before the elf lost his grip on his harness and ripped away into the void, tumbling head-over-heels into the dark until his skull met the asphalt with a sickening, distant crack.

Up on the roof, the second torch didn’t stop. The seam was widening. A foot-wide disc of glowing steel began to cave inward right above my stretcher, shower after shower of molten sparks raining down on my canvas coat. Through the opening, I saw a pair of yellow-tinted targeting reticles glowing in the dark, and the snub snout of an automatic machine pistol dipping down, pointing straight at my face.

Pain ripped through my chest like a dull saw as I hauled my right arm up. My ribs felt like they were splintering into my lungs, but the muscle memory was already there, cold and automatic, forged in twenty years of union brawls and back-alley executions. I pulled the heavy, long-barreled .454 Casull revolver from my underarm holster, thumbing the hammer back. The cylinder locked into battery with a heavy, iron click that resonated through my jaw.

I didn't aim for the gap. I aimed three inches ahead of it, right where his center of mass had to be braced against the ambulance's roof-ribbing.
I squeezed the trigger.

The hand cannon went off like a stick of dynamite inside the tin can of the ambulance. The deafening report blew out what little hearing I had left, filling the cabin with a dense fog of burning cordite and gray sulfur. The three-hundred-grain hard-cast round tore through the double-walled steel ceiling as if it were parchment paper, striking the elf through the lower abdomen before exiting out between his shoulder blades.

A spray of hot arterial blood and shredded Gore-Tex erupted across the ceiling breach, immediately followed by a wet, strangled howl that cut through the engine roar. The weight on the roof shifted violently. The runner didn’t fall cleanly. He slid down the curved rear slope of the ambulance, his boots drumming frantically against the back glass, his clawed hands scraping twin gouges through the white paint.

Bram swung his weapon around, tracking the slide, but the elf was already hanging by a single frayed tether off the right rear fender, swinging like a pendulum against the screaming dual rear tires. His goggles were shattered, one eye a ruined socket of black gore, but his jaw was working with rabid, dying fury. 

"Frag the tires!" the elf shrieked into the rain, spitting red froth into the wind, his voice rising in a jagged, metahuman warble that pierced the storm. "Frag the fucking tires!"

His remaining hand—twitching, half-severed from the bismuth spray—dove into the chest pocket of his rig. He didn't come out with a gun. He dragged free a strung cluster of magnetic micro-mines, the arming diodes strobing an angry, high-frequency scarlet.

Bram saw it a split second before I did. "Look out!" the dwarf yelled, lunging back inside the frame as he brought the butt of the MP5 up to shield his face.

The dying runner let go of the tether. He didn't drop behind us. As the ambulance swayed hard into a rut, his body swung forward under the wheel well, and with the last ounce of twitching adrenaline in his nervous system, he hurled the cluster of primed ordnance straight down into the black water pooling directly beneath our front axle.

* * *

The smell of boiling 10W-40 and scorched brake lining was thick enough to chew, drowning out the sour stink of the marsh muck we’d dragged in on our boots. We were tearing down the industrial spur out of Kearny, running without headlights along a cracked two-lane that skirted the dead chemical yards. Overhead, the sagging power lines weren't just humming—they were screaming, vibrating with an unnatural high-voltage shrillness that set my teeth on edge and turned my fillings cold.

Grimjaw was hunched over the Ford’s cracked steering wheel like a gargoyle cast in grease and scar tissue, his massive forearms knotting as the heavy Local 405 ambulance fought him for every inch of pavement. The chassis groaned, burdened under hundreds of pounds of quarter-inch rolled steel our boys at the yard had welded over the quarter-panels and cab doors. 

"Tripwire!" Grimjaw barked, his voice scraping out like a dull rasp across rusted pipe. "Look at the culvert—BATC bastards laid a daisy-chain!"

Fifty yards ahead, half-hidden beneath a tangle of dead sumac and municipal trash, three telluric-laced shaped charges were wired into the guardrail, their arming diodes winking an oily, insectoid amber in the darkness. They didn't want to search us; they wanted to vaporize the front axle and let the Passaic swallow the pieces.

"Brace!" Grimjaw bellowed.

He didn't hit the brakes. Instead, the bastard threw his whole two-hundred-and-sixty-pound frame into the wheel, wrenching the column hard to the left and locking the emergency brake in a single, brutal motion. The five-ton ambulance broke traction on the salt-slicked asphalt, slewing sideways. The center of gravity hitched, violent and sickening, and the passenger-side tires lifted clean off the deck. For two heart-stopping seconds, we rode the knife-edge on two wheels, defying gravity through sheer kinetic momentum as Grimjaw feathered the throttle to carry us wide of the blast cone.

The detonators tripped.

The shockwave hit us like a swinging crane hook. A wall of blue-white concussive heat slammed the driver’s side, flipping the world into a deafening flash of blinding magnesium. The tempered safety glass in the rear double-doors shattered into ten thousand stinging crystals, blowing inward like buckshot. But the Local 405 armor held. The plate flexed with a sickening shriek of tortured weld-beads, deflecting the primary blast upward into the salt-crusted belly of the sky.

The ambulance slammed back down onto all four tires with an impact that hammered my spine straight down into my tailbone. An old Nokia brick phone—taped together at the battery seam—went clattering frantically across the ribbed diamond-plate floor, spinning through glass shards and empty brass casings until it wedged dead against my boot heel. Overhead, three sodium-vapor lamps on the utility poles burst in sympathy with the arc-flash, raining blistering amber glass down onto our armored hood like hot hail.

Ahead of us, the industrial spur bottlenecked into the main security cut leading toward the causeway. 

BATC had set their choke point thick: two portable concrete Jersey barriers staggered across the lanes, backed by a pair of idling Suburbans and four corporate rent-a-cops in tactical black, their assault rifles raised, aiming dead-center for our windshield.

"They think those curbs are gonna save 'em!" Grimjaw yelled, spitting a dark wad of tobacco against the dash.
Grimjaw buried the gas pedal straight through the floorboards. The rebuilt diesel V8 roared—a guttural, smoke-belching bellow that spat black unburnt fuel out the side exhaust. We hit the barricade doing fifty-five. 

The reinforced cow-catcher we’d fabricated from structural I-beams struck the first concrete block dead center. The impact didn't stop us; it pulverized the barrier, sending fifty-pound chunks of aggregate and twisted rebar spinning through the air like cannon shot. One of the BATC shooters fired a panicked, wild burst that stitched empty sparks across our steel cowl before the shockwave of shattering concrete knocked him clean off his boots, sending him tumbling violently down the gravel embankment into the black water of the drainage canal. The other three broke discipline, throwing themselves flat onto the oil-stained shoulder as our front bumper clipped the rear quarter of a Suburban, spinning the heavy SUV around like a toy top and showering the night in red taillight plastic and torn sheet metal.

We blew through the wreckage like a freight train jumping a spur line, tires shrieking as they hooked into fresh asphalt, spitting chunks of pulverized stone into the darkness behind us.

The bottleneck broke wide open. The industrial gloom snapped back, and suddenly we were out on the flat, exposed spine of the main causeway, crossing the salt flats toward the belly of the county.

Grimjaw grabbed the floor-mounted Hurst shifter, fighting the clutch with a heavy boot. The transmission answered with a hideous, metal-on-metal scream as the synchros stripped away.

"Block's getting hot, Cole!" Grimjaw roared over the dying whine of the gearbox, the temperature gauge needle already buried deep into the red hash-marks. "Coolant line’s pissing somewhere underneath! We got maybe twenty miles before she melts down to a paperweight!"

I braced myself against the passenger grab-handle, wiped a streak of greasy condensation from my cheek, and checked the scratched crystal of my mechanical field watch. The second hand swept with cruel, indifferent precision.

"Thirty-five minutes left," I said, my voice dead and steady against the rattle of the dying engine. "Just keep the pedal down."

I turned and looked out the jagged hole where the side window used to be. 

The wind whipping off the flats didn't smell like winter salt or diesel anymore. It smelled like dry pennies, ancient rot, and scorched mica. High above the skyline, over the jagged, oil-rigged horizon of Neon Hollow, the night sky was curdling. It wasn't the charcoal-black of a North Jersey December; it was an unnatural, bruised purple, the color of a fresh contusion on dead flesh, pulsing with an internal, subterranean fever. Along the edges of the causeway, the municipal transformer boxes were violently misfiring, belching green-hot electrical fire into the damp fog every three seconds as the Telluric grid groaned under an impossible, titanic load. 

The earth beneath the blacktop was humming a note so low you couldn't hear it with your ears—you felt it in your marrow, a heavy, sick vibration that made the hearth-coal resonance inside my chest flare like a hot cinder caught in a draft. 

Apep was turning in his grave. The cage was coming apart at the rivets.

Then the world cracked.

It didn't come from the sky. It came from the bedrock, five miles deep beneath the silt and the ancient basalt fault lines of the valley. A deafening, seismic *CRACK* tore through the night, a sound so vast and violent it seemed to swallow every engine noise, every breath, every scream in a twenty-mile radius. The concussion blasted through the air like an atmospheric hammer, blowing inward what was left of the ambulance’s cracked safety glass, showering my lap in powdery white dust.

Out across the flats, through the toxic purple haze, a blinding pillar of white-hot geodetic lightning erupted toward the clouds, tearing open the horizon.

The first Pylon had fallen.


---

## CHAPTER 14: THE SERPENT WAKES

The interior of the rig smelled like scorched copper, dry saline, and the rot-gut sulfur rolling off the Hackensack Meadowlands.
