Every pothole on the lower causeway shuddered up through the ambulance’s worn leaf springs, sending an erratic, tooth-jarring rattle through the aluminum cabinets. Ampules of lidocaine and rolls of sterile gauze clicked against the doors like nervous teeth. 

On the metal tray beside my hip, my silver Motorola Razr was vibrating so hard against the stainless steel it skittered in tiny, frantic circles. No ringtone. No Nextel chirp. Just raw, unmodulated radio-frequency trash humming through the speaker coil—a flat, psychotic buzz that made the small hairs on my forearms stand up straight under the ballistic nylon of my BATC tactical vest.

"Keep your eyes on the road, Jimmy!" Cole barked toward the partition, his voice cutting through the engine roar like a cold chisel through soft iron. 

He didn’t look back at the driver. He didn't look at anything except me. 

Cole sat on the jump seat directly across from me, his knees nearly brushing mine in the narrow aisle. His flannel shirt was gray with stone dust from the Kearny substation, smelling of machine grease, cheap diner coffee, and the iron-sweet sting of spent arc-weld. His knuckles were split across the middle joints, black-rimmed where motor oil had permanently stained the creases of his skin. In the sickly dome light of the ambulance ceiling, the shadows carved into his face looked deep enough to hide a razor blade.

Then the marrow of the earth broke.

It wasn't a sound at first. Sound was too slow, too merciful. It was an instantaneous, catastrophic vacuum in the Weave, the psychic equivalent of a deep-sea diver’s suit imploding under four hundred atmospheres of pressure. 

Ten miles to the east, anchored in the black tidal muck of the marshes, Pylon #1 cracked like a frozen spine. A millisecond later, Pylon #2 folded into itself, its reinforced tungsten-jacketed core shearing apart under an impossible surge of entropic torque.

The backlash didn't travel through the air; it rode the bedrock and the copper grounding cables buried beneath the Turnpike. It hit the rig like a broadside from a freight train.

The breath was violently sucked out of my lungs. My spine snapped backward against the vinyl backrest, my heels locking into the rubber floor mat as the psychogenic bleed flooded into the cabin. The smell of sulfur vanished, instantly replaced by the rancid, synthetic stench of Liquid Isfet—burnt wiring, curdled milk, and the sweet, suffocating odor of embalming fluid.

*Static.* 

Ash-gray, blinding static tore across the backs of my retinas. 

Suddenly I wasn't just sitting in an ambulance careening through Kearny. My nervous system was dragged backward into the dark, into the screams of three hundred and fourteen commuters trapped on the lower level of the transit junction when the seal had failed three years ago. Three hundred and fourteen voices clawing at my skull, their lungs full of black water and burning insulation, begging me to pull the breaker, begging me to shut the gate, screaming that the Commander had left them to drown in the dark. 

*You failed them, Mara. You locked the doors.*

The static surged, thick as grease, threatening to snuff out my lungs. In the center of my chest, just behind my sternum, the fragment of black bismuth embedded in my tissue didn't just hurt—it *woke up*. It began to vibrate at the exact, horrifying resonant frequency of the falling pylons. It twisted in my flesh like an auger, cold as dry ice, feeding on the dying pulses of the ward grid. The Geas didn't merely control me; it was tethered to the infrastructure of North Jersey itself. Every time the city’s bones broke, the parasite inside me gorged itself on the trauma, swelling larger, sinking its crystal taproots deeper into the muscle of my heart.

I couldn't draw air. My throat locked into a dry, shuddering sob.
"Mara."

A hand slammed down over mine. Not a gentle touch—a hard, calloused clamp of flesh, bone, and working-man's leverage. Cole’s palm locked over the back of my trembling fingers, crushing them against the cold armrest, his skin rough and scorched with the residual heat of his own metahuman core. 

His eyes locked directly into mine, hazel and furious, refusing to blink, refusing to yield an inch of ground to the nightmare bleeding through my skull. 

"Look at me," he commanded, his voice dropping an octave into a low, terrifyingly calm rumble that vibrated straight through his forearm into my wrist. "Right here. Look at the furnace, Vance."

The moment his skin pressed fully against mine, the conduit opened. 

It wasn't gentle. It was the brutal, desperate heat of two people who had spent their entire lives surviving industrial fires. From the center of my core, fighting against the suffocating pull of the bismuth shard, my white-lilac flame erupted. It didn't burn outward to scorch the cabin; it surged through my arterial network, rushing straight toward the point of contact where Cole held me. 

His grip tightened until my knuckles ground together, but I welcomed the pain. The pain was real. The pain wasn't three years ago; it was November in Hudson County, raw and sharp and alive. 

The white-lilac light flared behind my eyes, searing and brilliant, burning away the ash-gray static of the 314 ghosts like kerosene poured over dry rot. The phantom screams dissolved into the low, steady rumble of the ambulance’s diesel engine. The suffocating weight peeled back, stripped away by the absolute, immovable mass of Cole’s presence. He was an anvil; the psychic storm was just iron striking him, and he didn't give a single damn millimeter.

I gasped, a jagged, tearing intake of air that burned all the way down to my diaphragm. My left hand came up, digging my fingernails into the thick flannel of his sleeve, clinging to him as if the floorboards had fallen away into the void.

"The first two are gone," I choked out, the words tasting like wet zinc and battery acid on my tongue. "Cole... the first two are gone. The grid is open."

Inside my ribs, the black bismuth gave another sluggish, heavy throb. It felt heavier now, saturated with the necrotic arcana released by the pylons' collapse. It was growing. The ward grid wasn't just falling—it was being harvested, and my chest was the slaughterhouse floor.

Cole didn't flinch. His jaw set into a slab of granite, his thumb stroking hard across the tendons of my wrist, anchoring me, keeping the lilac fire burning steady against the dark.

"Focus on the hearth, Mara," he said, his voice a dead-silent, grounding anchor against the howling wind outside. "Don't let the shadow in. We hold the line."

"Cole, the parasite—it’s feeding on the—"

Before I could finish the sentence, the road vanished.

There was no sound of an explosion. Only a violent, upward hydraulic heave as the tectonic plate beneath the causeway tore itself open along the ward-line fault. The asphalt buckled into a five-foot ridge of shattered macadam. 

The front bumper of the ambulance hit the rise at fifty miles an hour. 

Metal shrieked in agony as the front suspension disintegrated. The entire ten-ton rig was kicked violently upward, tearing loose from gravity, airborne three feet above the smoking, ruptured deck of the highway. Metal cabinets exploded open, showering us in glass and needles, as Cole lunged across the aisle to wrap his arms around my shoulders before we hit the sky.

* * *
The ambulance hit the deck with the kind of bone-rattling violence that rewired your teeth. 

The suspension bottomed out on raw iron, tires biting back into the chewed-up asphalt of the causeway with a shriek that burned rubber straight through the floorboards. Sparks sprayed off the sheared undercarriage like a blown grinder wheel, sheeting bright orange against the black, curdled sky of the Meadowlands. I slammed against the interior bulkhead, my left shoulder taking the brunt of the steel ribbing, my boots sliding in a cocktail of spilled saline, transmission fluid, and ditch water.

"Stay down!" I barked, grabbing a hand-hold near the blown-out rear doors. 

The sheet metal back there was gone, peeled open like a can of sardines from an earlier scrape, giving me an unobstructed view of the hell we were leaving behind. Cold salt air, heavy with the stench of low-tide muck, diesel exhaust, and chemical rot, whipped into the cabin. 

Then the horizon snapped.

Two miles back, through the haze of burning marsh grass and high-tension wire corridors, Pylon #3 went first. It didn’t just collapse; it detonated from the inside out. A blinding bloom of violent, bruised-violet fire punched through the concrete sleeve, followed a split-second later by Pylon #4. The dual shockwaves didn't roll—they cracked across the mudflats like a whip made of compressed lead. 

The blast hit the ambulance an instant later. The entire rig fish-tailed hard to the right, three tons of Detroit steel skittering sideways toward the guardrail before Grimjaw caught the skid with a snarling twist of the wheel. The acoustic wallop caved in my eardrums, turning the world into a high-pitched ring that tasted like copper pennies under my tongue.

Behind us, the skyline of industrial North Jersey was coming unstitched.

"Toughbook’s losing the satellite array!" Bram Kovacs shouted from the bench seat across from me. He was clutching a Panasonic Toughbook, the heavy-duty magnesium-cased brick bolted to a swing arm, its thick rubber bumpers rattling in the mount. The green-and-amber raster display was glitching violently, the GPS topo-map fracturing into serrated jagged lines. "Look at the telemetry! The substrate isn't settling—it's pushing up! Christ, it's pushing *up*!"

I didn't need the screen. I could see it with my own eyes.

The causeway roadbed behind us didn't just crack. It tore open along the expansion joints, the three-inch steel rebar snapping with deafening reports like high-caliber rifle fire. Chunks of Jersey barrier were hurled fifty feet into the brackish marsh water, sending up geysers of foul, black mud. 

And then the ground lifted.

It started as a ridge of dark, jagged stone tearing through four lanes of elevated highway, but it wasn't stone. As the roadbed shattered and peeled back like wet cardboard, the light caught the edges. It was obsidian. Colossal, overlapping scutes of black volcanic glass, each one the size of a two-family house in Bayonne, rising out of the primordial silt of the Newark Basin. 

Dripping from the seams between the scales was Liquid Isfet—a vile, light-drinking pitch that didn't flow like water; it crept like hot tar, sizzling as it touched the air, turning the marsh reeds to ash and the salt water to boiling grease.

Apep. The Great Shadow Serpent of the Duat. Waking up beneath two centuries of industrial runoff and union-laid rebar.

I’d spent my life around heavy machinery—drop-forges, six-axis milling beds, stamping presses that could flatten a die-cast engine block with thirty thousand tons of hydraulic force. None of it compared to the sheer, indifferent physics of what was sliding up through the earth. 

An abandoned 1999 Crown Victoria, an old unmarked cruiser parked near a maintenance spur, was caught under the rising curve of a single ventral plate. There wasn't even a crash. Just a sickening, wet crunch of glass and pressed sheet metal as the sedan was flattened down to an inch-thick pancake, its fuel tank rupturing in a pathetic flash that was smothered in Isfet before the flame could even breathe. A steel-truss high-voltage tower snapped at its concrete footings, dragged down into the fissure like a dropped matchstick. The sound was a continuous, bone-vibrating grind of rock against unholy chitin that made the fillings in my jaw ache.

Bram Kovacs stood frozen in the center of the ambulance bay, his knuckles dead-white where he gripped the stretcher rail. The half-smoked Dutch Masters cigar clamped in his jaw went slack, slipping from his lips and tumbling into the puddle of saline at his boots. His bloodhound eyes were wide, bloodshot, reflecting the void-black shine of the rising scales.

"Mother of God..." Kovacs whispered, his gravelly voice cracked down the middle. "The myths were real. It's... it's the size of a fragging skyscraper."

"Bram! Brace!" I yelled.

From the driver’s cab, separated from us by the shattered plexiglass partition, Grimjaw slammed his foot through the floorboards. The ambulance’s turbo-diesel screamed, spitting black soot from the wheel wells as the big orc hauled on the wheel, fighting the violent lateral tremors that were turning the asphalt into rolling waves. 

"I ain't getting eaten by no ancient giant snake today!" Grimjaw roared, his tusked jaw jutting out, veins bulging along his corded, greenish-gray neck like radiator hoses. "Hold onto your fragging dicks back there! Hold on!"

The rig surged forward, its tires bouncing over widening fissures that vented thick, sulfurous steam. The whole causeway was listing five degrees to the port side, the brackish marshland swallowing the concrete pilings below as the serpent's bulk displaced hundreds of thousands of tons of river silt. Out in the bay, the water receded in a sudden, unnatural low tide, exposing centuries of rusted shipping containers, scuttled barges, and mob hits entombed in oil drums, before rushing back in as a foaming, black-scum surge.

I leaned out the torn rear threshold, wrapping my forearms tight around the interior frame, wind tearing at my leather jacket. The obsidian monster was still surfacing, an endless, undulating wall of jagged, razored plates that blotted out the refineries, blotted out the Skyway, blotted out the faint orange glow of the Newark basin. It wasn't just big; it had a gravitational pull, an aura of rot and cosmic entropy that made my lungs feel like they were coating in grease.

"Pylon #5 is our only vector!" I yelled back through the partition, shouting over the howl of the over-revved diesel and the grinding earth. "Grim, keep her straight! If we lose the approach to the substation, we lose the grid!"

"I'm giving her everything this piece of shit's got!" Grimjaw bellowed back, slamming his palm against the horn as if warning the crumbling world to get out of his way.

Up ahead, through the cracked front windshield, the silhouette of Pylon #5 loomed half a mile off—the last standing monolith of the arcano-containment ring, sparking erratically with desperate blue arcs of static. The road toward it was an open straightaway, flanked by dead reeds and rusted chain-link.

Then the concrete two hundred yards in front of our bumper erupted.

It didn't buckle slowly. It exploded upward in a fountain of pulverized gravel and sheared rebar as another colossal coil of black glass breached the surface, rising like a jagged, impenetrable wall sixty feet into the air, cutting the causeway in half and dead-ending our path in a wall of suffocating shadow.

* * *

The Turnpike didn’t end; it was eaten. A jagged, three-story ridge of raw obsidian had ruptured straight through the northbound lanes like the spine of a prehistoric leviathan, heaving slabs of steel-reinforced concrete into the dead air and severing the overpass ahead into crushed rebar teeth.

"Hold onto your goddamn teeth!" Grimjaw bellowed.

He hauled the wheel of the gutted Ford E-350 with both hands, his heavy orc forearms corded like mooring cables beneath gray hide. The ambulance slammed sideways into a four-wheel slide, rubber howling against the disintegrating shoulder before the front bumper sheared through a line of rusted orange construction barrels. We plummeted down the embankment, hitting an overgrown frontage road that ran parallel to the dead drainage canals of the Kearny marshland. The shocks bottomed out with an iron shriek that rattled through the base of my skull.

My sternum flared with blinding agony. I choked, gripping the dash, my fingernails digging into sun-cracked vinyl. Beneath my torn tactical jacket, the bismuth infection had crawled up past my floating ribs, creeping steadily toward my collarbones. It wasn't skin anymore. It was an iridescent, geometric carapace of violet-black crystal that tightened with every heartbeat, pinning my lungs in a vise. Breathing didn't bring oxygen; it brought the sensation of inhaling ground mason jars, jagged grains of silica scraping the inside of my bronchial tubes until I tasted copper on the back of my tongue.

I checked the digital countdown taped to the dash beside the emergency siren toggle.

*00:25:14.*

Twenty-five minutes until the Geas reached our ventricles and turned our hearts into solid, crystalline paperweights.

"Cole!" I wheezed, throwing a glance into the stripped patient compartment behind us.

Cole was braced against the steel wheel-well, his knuckles white around the grip of his slug-thrower, his own chest heaving in shallow, staccato hitches. The black crystal crawled beneath the neck of his flannel, glittering in the gloom like spilled oil on wet pavement. His eyes met mine—irises rimmed with that brittle frost-cobalt mana he’d been redlining since the substation blew. He gave a single, tight nod, his jaw clenched so hard his molars audibly clicked. He was holding the rear door seals together with sheer spite, frost creeping across the rusted hinges to keep the vacuum from blowing the back out.

Outside, the darkness began to curdle.

It wasn't night falling; it was Apep’s aura bleeding over the meadowlands, dragging the abyss into the physical plane. The smog rolling off the reed beds turned curdled and oily, drowning the yellow beam of the flickering halogen headlights. Then the glass started to sing.

Not from the engine vibration, but from fingers.

Dozens of them. Translucent, ink-stained shadows detached from the vapor, flattening their palms against the windshield and the side glass. They didn’t have faces, only hollow depressions where eyes and jaws should have been, but their voices bypassed my ears entirely, drilling directly into the base of my brain stem with the wet, buzzing rasp of a jammed Nextel chirp.

*You left the second squad in the vault, Vance.*

*You smelled the diesel burning on Route 21 and you didn't turn back.*

*Court-martial coward. Burned-out desk jockey. Dead girl walking.*

"Get out of my head," I ground out, my teeth coated in bloody saliva.

A blackened limb ripped clean through the passenger-side ventilation vent, freezing vapor swirling around cold, desiccated knuckles that reached for my throat. The smell hit me—not marsh gas, but the charred pork and scorched insulation of the Kearny substation fire three years ago, the smell of men I had ordered into an unshielded transformer bay while I stayed behind the blast shield.

"Mara!" Grimjaw yelled, the Ford fishtailing as the tires hit a pool of liquefied road-sludge. The windshield was going completely black, choked with grasping, psychogenic phantoms that smeared phantom frost across the glass. The wipers dragged uselessly across the muck, whining in protest. "I can't see the fucking markers! We’re gonna dump into the canal!"

I didn't answer with words. I couldn't spare the air.

I dug deep into the reservoir beneath my cracked sternum, ignoring the jagged fire that flared along the bismuth-choked meridians of my nervous system, and yanked my weave to the surface. It didn't come easily. The corruption resisted, drinking my mana like dry soil drinks oil, but I forced the current through my forearms until the skin along my wrists split into micro-fissures of pure, searing white-lilac light.

I thrust both hands flat against the inside of the windshield.

The mana punched through the safety glass without shattering it, blooming outward across the Ford's snub nose in a brutal, prow-shaped wedge of fourth-law kinetic radiation. The light was blinding—not the sterile amber of municipal sodium lights, but a sharp, clinical violet-white that smelled of ozone and fresh hospital linen.

The wedge hit the psychogenic swarm like a locomotive snowplow hitting wet drift.

The shadows didn't just scatter; they flash-fried. The whispering voices peaked into high-pitched radio static before detonating into showers of harmless violet sparks that streaked over the cab roof. The reaching hands withered to cinders, their oily residue scouring off the hood in long, sizzling plumes of ash.

"Keep it on the road, Grimjaw!" I shouted over the screaming 7.3-liter diesel engine, my voice vibrating with dual-layered arcane resonance that shook the rusted metal plates under our boots. "I'll keep the shadows off the glass!"

"You just keep breathing, Doc!" Grimjaw roared back, his tusks bared as he sawed the wheel against the slush, his boot stomping the accelerator flat to the rusted firewall. "We're almost at the gates!"

The white-lilac prow cleaved through the curdled mist, illuminating the post-industrial graveyard flanking the frontage road: collapsed chemical shipping containers, drowned utility poles dangling severed copper lines like dead vines, and the black, oily surface of the Hackensack tributary churning with unnatural, counter-clockwise eddies.

Every yard forward cost a piece of my ribs. The bismuth grew thicker with every pulse of mana I fed into the shield, the geometric edges biting into the soft tissue of my pectoral muscles. I could feel the cold encroaching on my pericardium, rhythmic and mathematical, counting down my pulse like a metronome built by a sadist.

*00:23:40.*

We hit a stretch of broken asphalt where the swamp had reclaimed the roadbed. The Ford launched three feet into the air, the undercarriage smacking down with a sickening metallic crunch that tore half the exhaust system free. A shower of yellow sparks chased us through the rear-view mirror, lighting up Cole’s grim, shadowed silhouette as he kept the rear doors locked down against the howling pressure gradient outside.

Ahead, the frontage road curved sharply around the concrete revetment of an abandoned sewage treatment plant.

Grimjaw drifted the ambulance hard to the left, the rear tires catching the lip of the embankment and kicking up a roostertail of black mud and marsh reeds. My shield sheared through a knot of hovering shadow-entities waiting in the apex of the turn, dissolving them into blinding violet vapor that painted the wet concrete walls with our passage.

Then the curve opened up, and the mist broke against a perimeter of blinding, halogen-white glare.

"Mother of God," Grimjaw muttered, his foot easing off the pedal just enough to stop the engine from blowing its gaskets.

Rising out of the brine fog five hundred yards ahead was the base of Pylon #5—a massive, hexagonal monolith of reinforced basalt and cold-rolled steel that anchored the southern spine of the containment grid. But the approach wasn't open road.

The blast-gates were down: three tiers of hydraulic armor-plate sealed shut with glowing orange mag-locks. Sandbag redoubts flanked the primary approach, illuminated by the sweep of high-intensity carbon-arc spotlights mounted on the concrete parapets. And between us and the steel stood the line.

Fifty High-Spire heavy-orcs in full matte-black tactical plate, their shock-halberds humming with ambient lightning, formed a staggered wall across the asphalt. Above them, perched on the reinforced corners of the pillboxes, the twin barrels of automated 30mm arc-turrets swung down from the darkness, their targeting lasers painting two blood-red dots directly across the center of our cracked windshield.


---

## CHAPTER 15: THE BLAST-GATES

The floorboards of the '98 Ford E-350 were vibrating hard enough to loosen fillings. Every five seconds, another volley of heavy tungsten-jacketed rounds chewed into the ambulance’s box body, the impacts sounding like sledgehammers dropped onto empty oil drums. Through the rusted seams of the cab, the Kearny marshlands reeked of sulfur, dying reeds, and the sharp, coppery tang of high-voltage capacitors charging up for a kill shot.

High above the perimeter road, twin arc-turrets mounted on the scaffolding of Pylon #5 hissed as they tracked our approach. A blue-white beam clipped the driver’s side mirror, vaporizing the glass and peeling the door skin back in a strip of molten red slag. 

The old ambulance wasn't going to make the gate. Steel has limits, and whoever built this rig out in a chop shop behind the Pulaski Skyway had welded the push-bumper to dry-rotted frame horns with sloppy flux-core. Thirty more yards under that turret fire and the front suspension would shear clean off, turning us into an eighty-mile-an-hour ball of fire tumbling into the brackish ditch.

I dragged myself up from between the jump seats in the back. My knees slid over spent brass and a greasy spread of dropped wrenches, the stink of scorched 15W-40 thick enough to coat my teeth. My ribs screamed where a High-Spire shock-lance had cracked them two nights ago in Passaic, but pain was just noise. 

I wedged myself between the bucket seats, throwing my weight forward, and planted both palms flat against the sun-baked, cracked plastic of the dashboard.

Grimjaw didn’t look at me. The orc had both ham-fisted hands locked onto the tape-wrapped steering wheel, his bottom tusks jutting out over his lower lip, flecked with gray spit. His left eye was swollen shut from an earlier breach, but the right was wide, bloodshot, and locked on the road ahead.

"Arc-gunners on the gantry!" Grimjaw roared over the deafening clatter of the diesel. "They're dialing the frequency, Cole! Next one blows the axle straight to hell!"

"Hold the line," I told him. My voice sounded flat, scraped raw from breathing burned transformer oil.

I closed my eyes and pulled from the marrow.

Deep in my chest, behind the scar tissue and the soot of twenty years on Newark machine shop floors, the blood-iron reservoir answered. It wasn't clean magic. It was the heavy, cold, unforgiving weight of pig iron and slag, dragged down through negative forty degrees until the cobalt hue of it flooded the backs of my retinas. 

My skin dropped temperature instantly. Frost bloomed out from beneath my calloused palms, racing across the brittle dashboard vinyl like a spiderweb of cyan needles. The plastic didn't just freeze—it bonded with the metal bulkhead underneath. 

I pushed harder, driving the arcane current down through the firewall, through the motor mounts, and into the twin C-channel rails of the chassis. I could feel every bolt, every stress fracture, every fatigue point where Jersey road salt had eaten the undercarriage down to flakes. I flooded the vacancies with cobalt-tempered iron, transmuting the brittle rust into dense, cryo-forged alloy. 

The dashboard went dead silent under a crust of solid, translucent blue ice. My fingers went numb, then my wrists, the cold climbing up into my biceps like liquid nitrogen pumped through the arteries.

Out on the hood, the paint blistered and peeled away as the metal underneath froze down to absolute zero. The frost surged forward in a roaring wave, encasing the warped radiator shell and wrapping the crude, spiked ram-bar welded to the snout in a jagged, eight-hundred-pound sheath of cobalt ice. It didn't look like frozen water; it looked like tempered tool steel grown out of a glacier, faceted with diamond-sharp edges that drank the ambient light.

"Incoming!" Grimjaw yelled, leaning his bulk over the wheel.

A heavy-caliber machine gun opened up from the sandbag redoubt just inside the gate. High-Spire heavy-orcs—eight-foot brutes wrapped in corporate-issue ceramic plate—raked the grille. 

The rounds hit with deafening, metallic clangs. Instead of shredding the radiator, the heavy-caliber slugs shattered against the ice-clad prow like lead thrown against an anvil. The ricochets shrieked off into the dark, whistling through the marsh grass, sparking violently against the road. A stray round caught the center of the bulletproof windshield, blowing a white rosette across the safety glass, but the frost followed instantly, sealing the fissure, knitting the cracked laminate with veins of solid blue rime.

The twin arc-turrets on the overhead gantry fired simultaneously. 

Two lances of pure, ionizing lightning hammered into the front bumper. The air inside the cab tasted like an electrical fire in an elevator shaft. My fillings ached so hard I thought my jaw would split. But the cobalt-iron metallurgy didn't yield; it grounded the immense charge, bleeding the lightning across the frozen frame and discharging it into the wet asphalt below in a cascade of blue sparks.

"Engine's cooking, boss!" Grimjaw shouted.

The temperature gauge on the cluster had snapped off against the right-hand peg. Steam wasn't venting anymore because the lines were crimped shut by my frost, but the block was screaming. The 7.3-liter Powerstroke was running on pure adrenaline and compressed misery. The cylinder heads were warping under the boost, the oil inside the crankcase burning into tar, the pistons expanding so fast they were practically shaving the cylinder walls with every stroke. The whole front end shrieked like an industrial lathe chewing through hardened carbide.

Eighty-five miles per hour. The speedo needle twitched, bounced, and buried itself in the black plastic bezel. 

Through the frost-webbed glass, the blast-gates of Pylon #5 filled the world. Twelve inches of reinforced, hydraulic-sealed naval plate, painted industrial safety yellow and streaked with the soot of a thousand illegal arc-burns. Behind those gates lay the high-spire relay that was bleeding the Newark grid dry, feeding whatever nightmare they were building out in the Meadowlands.

The heavy-orcs behind the concrete barricades finally saw what was coming. Two of them dropped their rifles and broke for the catwalk stairs. The third stood his ground, emptying an entire drum into our front end, his muzzle flashes illuminating the snarling, ice-sheathed monster the Ford had become.

My eyes burned with solid, uninterrupted blue fire. The frost had climbed past my throat now, stiffening the muscles in my neck, turning every breath into a draft of crushed glass.

"Don't lift, Grimjaw," I ground out, my teeth clicking against each other like dice. "Drive it through their teeth."

Grimjaw laughed—a barking, guttural sound full of spit and slaughter—and drove his work boot flat against the floorboards, bending the accelerator pedal into the firewall.

"See you on the other side, boss!"

The smell of melting aluminum block, vaporized transmission fluid, and bitter salt air peaked in a single suffocating instant. The road ran out.
The cobalt-armored battering ram met the dead center of the blast-gates at ninety miles an hour. 

The sound wasn't an explosion; it was the planetary crack of an armor-plate weld shearing under ten thousand tons of kinetic force, an ear-splitting scream of cold metal ripping hot iron in half as the world folded inward into a blinding flash of blue-white light.

* * *
The blast-gates didn’t just give way; they disintegrated under the weight of three tons of reinforced Ford chassis and pure, suicidal momentum. 

When the frost-caked ram-bar struck the threshold, the noise ripped through my skull like a freight car derailing on the high line over Kearny. The iron-gall wards painted into the steel flash-fried instantly, bursting into a blinding arc of blue-black sparks that smelled of scorched vinegar and ozone. Then the momentum took us. The front axle snapped with a hollow, sickening crunch. All four heavy-duty tires blew in rapid, deafening succession—*bam-bam-bam-bam*—shredding rubber across the threshold. The ambulance caught an edge on the buckled track, tripped over its own front end, and flipped violently onto its passenger side.

The world went sideways, then inverted, then violently flat.

I was airborne before my brain could register the roll. The front cabin’s steering-column airbag blew outward with a powdery chemical crack, only to shred itself against the splintered dash a fraction of a second later. My body hammered backward through the bulkhead, colliding ribs-first with the bolted-down aluminum medical cabinets in the rear box. Steel met flesh and bone. The impact drove the air straight out of my lungs in a raw, wet wheeze, stars bursting behind my retinas like phosphorus flares dropping over the Hackensack River. 

We skidded across the courtyard of Pylon #5 on sixty feet of raw, scraping sheet metal. The sound was unbearable—an agonizing, ear-splitting scream of galvanized panels peeling away against coarse, salt-rotted concrete, throwing a trailing rooster-tail of orange sparks into the freezing night. It felt like it would never stop. 

Then came the pillar. 

The roof of the rig slammed flush into an octagonal column of dressed brownstone. The deceleration hit me like a physical hammer. The remaining glass in the side windows didn't just shatter; it pulverized, raining across the interior in a diamond spray of tempered safety glass that cut through my BATC utility fatigues and bit deep into the skin of my forearms. 

Silence followed, heavy and suffocating, punctuated only by the manic, rhythmic *tink-tink-tink* of contracting exhaust metal and the furious, high-pitched hiss of punctured radiator lines bleeding boiling coolant onto the frozen stones. 

I lay there for three seconds, pinned beneath a dislodged oxygen tank, trying to remember how to pull oxygen into lungs that felt entirely flat. 

My mouth tasted like battery terminals and wet pennies. I rolled to my stomach, pushing against a floor that was now a wall, and coughed. A thick gob of dark, coppery spit splattered across the diamond-plate paneling. Every rib along my left flank screamed in unison, sharp and jagged, but nothing felt loose enough to pierce a lung. Not yet.

*Move, Vance. Get the fuck up.*

I dragged myself toward the blown-out opening where the windshield had been, my combat boots scrabbling for purchase in the slick mix of transmission fluid and road brine. My fingers hooked into the jagged frame, pulling my torso through. Outside, the night air of the Meadowlands hit my face like an open freezer door, smelling of low tide, burning synthetic oil, and the sulfurous stench of ancient iron.

Tumbling out onto the cracked concrete, my knee took the brunt of the fall. Right beside my hand, half-buried under a drift of shattered safety glass, lay the magnesium-cased Panasonic Toughbook. 

It had survived the roll, thrown clear through the crushed windshield. The heavy rubber bumper on the corner was gouged raw, and a web of hairline fractures spiderwebbed across the glare-resistant screen, but the LCD back-light was still burning with stubborn, sickly green persistence. 

In the center of the cracked display, the digital counter mocked me:

`[GEAS PROTOCOL: ACTIVE]`  
`[TIME TO HEMOLYTIC COLLAPSE: 00:18:14]`  
`[00:18:13]`  
`[00:18:12]`

Eighteen minutes. 

A sharp, rhythmic throbbing spiked behind my jaw, pulling my attention inward. I reached up with a gloved, trembling hand, peeling back the collar of my tactical jacket. Beneath the sweat-soaked skin of my throat, the bismuth curse was awake. I could feel it through my fingertips—raised, rigid tendrils, hard as pencil lead, pulsing in sync with the erratic beat of my heart. In the faint amber wash of the courtyard lights, the skin over my carotid looked iridescent and bruised, an oily sheen of geometric black-and-violet lines branching upward toward my jawline. The rot was running out of leash.

A violent, metallic thud echoed from the guts of the overturned rig. 

"Son of a *bitch*!" 

A heavy combat boot kicked outward against the crumpled rear doors. The latch held for a beat, then the steel warped under a second, metahuman-strength boot heel. The doors groaned and burst open with a screech of shearing hinges. 

Bram Kovacs tumbled out onto the grit-covered concrete, rolling onto his shoulder before hauling himself up against the undercarriage. His face was a mask of soot, dried road grit, and a jagged scalp laceration leaking dark red down into his graying beard, but his grip was already clamped tight around the receiver of his Benelli shotgun. 

He coughed, spitting a mouthful of black dust onto the pavement, his chest heaving under his Kevlar. "Everyone in one piece? Speak up!"

"I'm here," I rasped, my voice sounding like gravel grinding in a cement mixer. I forced myself to my feet, leaning heavily against the ambulance’s sheared front wheel well. The pain in my side flared hot, but I locked my knees. "Cole. Where is he?"

"Driver's side," Bram grunted, already moving around the crushed hood. "He took the pillar closest."

I didn't wait for him. I scrambled over the twisted hood, sliding across the dented metal to the driver’s side. The cab was collapsed inward, the A-pillar folded down like an accordion against the steering wheel. Cole was wedged between the collapsed dash and the sheared steel of the doorframe, his head slumped forward against his chest, dark hair matted with sweat and glass dust. His heavy canvas work jacket was shredded across the shoulder, showing the bruised, ink-stained skin beneath.

"Cole," I barked, grabbing the collar of his jacket with both hands. "Reyes, wake up!"

He groaned, a low, guttural sound that rattled deep in his sternum. His eyelids fluttered open, dark eyes wild and disoriented for half a second before snapping into hard, lethal focus as he recognized my face. He sucked in a breath, hissing through clenched teeth as he tested his legs against the crushed footwell. 

"Frame's pinned my boot," he muttered, voice thick with road dust. 

I braced my foot against the twisted door hinge and hauled backward with everything left in my arms, ignoring the white-hot fire lancing through my fractured ribs. Bram reached in over my shoulder, his thick, calloused hands gripping the mangled steel of the dash and pulling with metahuman leverage until the sheet metal groaned and tore free with a sharp *twang*. 

Together, we dragged Cole out of the cab, tumbling backward onto the frozen concrete. 

Cole hit the ground, rolled, and immediately came up onto one knee, shaking the glass shards from his knuckles like a dog shedding rain. He looked at me, taking in the blood smeared across my cheek, the way I was clutching my side, and the black, geometric veins visibly crawling above my collar. 

"We're alive," I said before he could ask. I held up the Toughbook, pointing a shaking finger at the green numbers ticking ruthlessly down into oblivion. "Eighteen minutes, Cole. We have to do this now."

Cole looked at the countdown, then down at his own bruised, grease-stained hands. His jaw tightened, the stubborn union machinist in him locking into place beneath the arcana. "Then we don't waste one."

He reached for the heavy iron-jacketed wrench strapped to his thigh, but the sound of slow, rhythmic clapping cut through the courtyard, freezing us in place.

Across the cracked concrete, the heavy white smoke venting from the ambulance’s burst radiator began to drift, caught in the frigid cross-breeze coming off the salt marshes. As the gray haze parted, two figures emerged from the deep shadow beneath the pylon’s primary archway. 

They wore tailored, charcoal-wool overcoats that hadn't caught a speck of dust from our violent entry. Their silk ties were pinned with obsidian clips, their shoes polished to an unyielding, mirror shine against the filthy pavement. They stood shoulder to shoulder, entirely relaxed, watching us like corporate executives observing a late-shift accident on a factory floor.

And behind them, rising out of the subterranean access trench that cleaved the courtyard in two, the darkness began to heave. 

It didn't climb; it uncoiled. A colossal silhouette, vast and armored in overlapping scales the color of dried arterial blood, lifted its head thirty feet into the freezing Jersey air. The ambient light died around it, sucked into the cold void of its hide. Two slit-pupil eyes, burning with the sulfurous, unblinking hatred of an unmade world, locked down onto the three of us. 

Apep had arrived to collect.

* * *

The steering column had crushed against my ribs like a dull guillotine, and for three long, agonizing seconds all I could hear was the hiss of punctured radiator coils spraying scalding antifreeze onto the freezing mud. 

My mouth was full of salt, copper, and powdered safety glass. Every breath tasted like the turnpike after a five-car pileup—burnt transmission fluid, scorched rubber, and the sulfurous rot blowing off the Hackensack marshlands. Behind my eyelids, the Geas pulsed with a sickening, rhythmic heat. It wasn't just pain; it was a digital chronometer etched in caustic violet fire against the back of my retinas, eating its way inward toward my heart valves.

*18:14.*
*18:13.*

Eighteen goddamn minutes until my blood turned to battery acid and my lungs collapsed into ash.

"Cole." 

Mara’s voice was a ragged scrape. She was already dragging herself through the shattered passenger frame, her standard-issue BATC tactical vest shredded along the left shoulder, revealing scorched dermal weaves and raw, bleeding skin. Her service weapon was gone, lost somewhere in the violent rollover that had left our cruiser folded around a sheared steel stanchion, but her eyes were wide, black-rimmed, and entirely lucid. She didn't check her wounds. She just grabbed the rim of the twisted dashboard and pulled herself into a crouch, her boots crunching down on the frosted gravel of the courtyard.

I reached down into the crumpled footwell behind the driver's seat. My fingers brushed cold, checkered walnut and oil-slicked ordnance steel. I hauled it out by the barrel: a heavy Remington 870 Wingmaster, modified in my shop back in Kearny, stripped of its duck-hunting pretensions and fitted with an extended mag tube packed to the muzzle with depleted-bismuth slugs. 

I hauled myself through the frame, boots hitting the cracked macadam. My left knee screamed—torn meniscus or cracked patella, it didn't matter anymore. Nothing south of eighteen minutes had any right to complain.

I brought the fore-end back. The heavy, mechanical *clack-clack* of the pump echoed across the expanse of concrete, chambering a custom three-inch hull with a snap that sounded like a dry bone breaking.

Fifty yards away, the sodium-vapor floodlights of the marshland relay terminal flickered with a dull, jaundiced buzz. 

Standing beneath that sickly yellow wash, untouched by the dirt or the freezing river fog, were Elias Morvain and Lord Malvourne.

They looked like they’d just stepped out of a private dining room at the High-Spire club in Weehawken. Morvain wore a charcoal double-breasted overcoat tailored from spun gossamer-wool, hands resting casually atop an ebony walking cane tipped with cold-forged aurichalcum. Beside him, Lord Malvourne stood tall, slender, and nauseatingly immaculate. The corporate elf’s platinum hair was swept back from his razor-sharp ears without a single strand out of place, and beneath the fine weave of his midnight-blue suit, I could see the pale, opalescent shimmer of kinetic-ward threads tracing geometric lattices across his chest and shoulders.

And behind them—rising out of the toxic black soup of the Passaic like an apocalyptic continental shelf—was the Serpent.

Apep blotted out the western horizon. The beast didn't merely occupy physical space; it displaced reality itself. Its scales were the color of stagnant oil on a wet asphalt highway, each plate the size of a suburban tract house, grinding together with the subterranean groan of tectonic plates shifting beneath Newark Bay. The creature’s head hung suspended in the freezing fog three hundred feet above the substation, massive and terrible, casting a shadow so absolute it swallowed the distant glow of the Manhattan skyline. Its slit pupils didn't reflect the sodium lamps. They burned with a thick, viscous luminescence—Liquid Isfet, churning in the sockets like boiling pitch, leaking trails of black-violet smoke that drifted down across the courtyard and withered the dead weeds clinging to the fence lines.

The ambient mana in the air was so dense it set my fillings to vibrating. My skin crawled with static; every hair on my arms stood straight up under my blood-stiffened flannel shirt.

Malvourne smiled. It wasn't a grin of fear, or even of caution. It was the condescending smirk of a mid-level executive watching a line-cook drop a tray of dirty glasses.

"Look at you," Malvourne called out. His voice carried an unnatural, resonant chime that cut through the low-frequency thrum of the Serpent's breathing. It was elven arrogance distilled into pure High-Spire cadence, smooth as single-malt Scotch and just as hollow. "Broken street-rats dragging yourselves from the debris. You have eighteen minutes to live, Reyes. What could you possibly hope to achieve?"

Beside him, Morvain checked the gold watch pinned to his lapel, his thin, bureaucratic lips barely twitching. He didn't even bother to unbutton his coat. They looked at us like an administrative error that was about to correct itself through simple attrition.

My ribs clicked as I pulled air into my chest. The cold air hit my raw throat like ground glass. I didn't look up at the mountain of scales looming in the clouds. I didn't look at the cosmic god of oblivion ready to drag the tri-state area into an endless void of uncreation.

I looked right at the two men standing on the concrete.

I looked at Morvain, who had signed the acquisition requisitions that turned Sub-Station Seven into a slaughterhouse. I looked at Malvourne, who had authorized the hit squads that pumped caustic Isfet into the water mains, the bastards who had stood in their high-rise penthouses while Danny choked his lungs out on an iron cot in the basement of our shop, dying for twenty-six dollars an hour and a lapsed union health plan.

They thought the ticking clock was theirs. They thought because they lived in towers of reinforced glass and warded silk, the dirt under our fingernails didn't have teeth.

I turned my head and spat a thick wad of blood and road grit onto the cracked concrete between my boots.

"A sliver of justice, you son of a bitch," I said. 

My voice didn't echo. It didn't have magic in it. It was just flat, gravel-hard, and cold as an open grave in the Kearny marshes in January.

"And eighteen minutes is all I need to put you in the ground."

*17:48.*

Mara didn't say a word. She drew an iron-jacked trench knife from her boot with her left hand, her knuckles whitening as she adjusted her grip, the cold blue light of a BATC ward-breaker spark dancing across her bruised knuckles. She met my glance for half a second. There were no grand speeches left. No union contracts. No oath to the state. Just the raw, red accounting of debts that were overdue.

The ward-mesh on Malvourne’s lapels flared bright azure as his smile finally thinned into something predatory and sharp. Apep lowered its colossal snout behind them, a hiss like a steam turbine blowing its seals washing across the gravel, freezing the air into sharp needles of rime.
I seated the shotgun’s buttstock hard into the pocket of my shoulder, pushed off my good leg, and broke into a dead, tearing sprint across the open courtyard straight into the dark.
