## CHAPTER 6: THE DEFIBRILLATOR RESURRECTION (PART 2

The void stretches infinite.

Not darkness—I've seen darkness in the Kearny Marshes when the fog rolls thick over the rust-caked pilings. This is something else. Something hollow. Empty space where my heartbeat should be drumming against my ribs like a machinist's hammer on forged steel.

I float in it.

Fifty-nine seconds.

I count them because counting is all I can do. Each second a frozen moment. My breath doesn't move. Time doesn't flow. Just me suspended in this silent expanse while somewhere outside my body, reality continues its brutal march forward.

The collar around my heart—the Lead-Bismuth Geas that's been choking me since I signed with Pylon #5—finally gives way. Not with fanfare or dramatic shattering. It just... dissolves. Blue-black iron-gall residue flaking off into nothingness, each fragment carrying away pieces of their contracts, their governance, their control.

Gone.

The weight lifts from my chest cavity.

And then—

The void *explodes*.

Lightning lances through neural pathways that haven't fired in nearly a minute. My spine snaps rigid as a steel I-beam. Every muscle in my body seizes at once, tendons pulling taut enough to snap. The world slams back into being with such force that I taste copper and cedar on my tongue—burning metallic sweetness.

My eyes fly open.

Overhead halogen dome lights of the ambulance blur into twin suns. The vinyl gurney beneath me creaks under the force of my convulsions. Somewhere in the periphery, Mara's voice cuts through the white noise screaming in my ears: *"CLEAR!"*

Her hands press defibrillator paddles against my bare chest—still slick with conductive gel that smells like ozone and singed cotton. The LifePak 12 capacitor charges with a high-pitched whine that climbs octaves until it becomes physical, vibrating in my teeth.

White-lilac magic crackling between the paddles.

Another jolt.

This one different. This one *real*. My heart stutters—*thump-thump-pause-thump*—then slams into motion like a stalled engine finally catching. Brutal. Agonizing. Each beat sends shockwaves through my ribcage, hammering against my sternum like someone trying to break down a door.

I gasp.

Air floods my lungs. Not gentle. Violent. Filling spaces that have been empty too long. I choke on it, coughing up what feels like frost and broken glass. My throat raw.

*"Hold the fragging line! The Ogre breachers need three more minutes to clear the slag!"*

Bram Kovacs's voice crashes through the cracked Motorola dash-radio mounted above the windshield. Static laces every word, making him sound like he's broadcasting from the bottom of a well. Behind his shout, I catch the wet crunch of flesh on steel—gunfire somewhere close outside the ambulance. Too close.

The world swims back into focus.

Mara looms over me, tactical vest still spattered with the gray dust of my dissolved collar. Her white-lilac eyes are wide, pupils dilated to pinpricks. She sees me seeing her and her shoulders drop half an inch—relief or exhaustion, maybe both.

"Welcome back," she says. Voice hoarse. "You were dead for fifty-nine seconds."

My hand moves before thought catches up. Fingers closing around the front of her vest, pulling myself upright despite muscles screaming protest. The movement makes something crack in my left shoulder—not bad, just loose. Will heal.

"Fifty-nine seconds." My own voice sounds wrong. Raspy. Like I've inhaled ground glass. "Long enough."

Through the ambulance's rear windows, I can see the industrial sprawl of Pylon #5's perimeter. Slag-heaps glowing orange under floodlights. Shadow-figures moving between shipping containers—the Ogre breachers Bram mentioned, their silhouettes massive even at distance. They're holding the line against whatever shitstorm is pouring out of the Crown Vault breach.

"My turn."

* * *

The air reeks of burnt oil and ozone. My hands move without thought—muscle memory forged in a hundred midnight repairs on rust-bucket sedans along the South Side. The IV drip hissing into Mara's arm, that pale blue paralytic solution, goes first. I yank the tubing free and watch droplets scatter across her tactical jacket like mercury.

"Fuck," she gasps, voice raw. "Thought... thought he'd already..."

"Not yet." My fingers find the LifePak paddles, still warm in their charging cradle. The weight feels right. Solid. Real.

She's already tearing at her own gear, fingers fumbling with Velcro straps, ripping apart Kevlar layers. There it is—the Sterling-Voss Geas, pulsing beneath her skin like a parasitic sun. That sickly violet glow spreading through the vessels of her chest, tendrils creeping toward her heart. The thing is *breathing*, expanding and contracting with her panicked breaths.

"I can see it, Cole." Her eyes are wide, pupils blown so dark only a thin rim of amber remains. "Can feel it... eating from the inside out."

The rotary dial on the LifePak catches my thumb. Cold metal, notched positions marked in degrees. Each click echoes in the cramped ambulance cabin like a hammer strike. The monitor beside us blips steady. Too steady. Her heart racing against the poison Vane Thorne fed her.

"Sixty seconds, Cole." She collapses back onto the gurney, arms spread, exposing everything. The glowing parasite crawls higher, seeking purchase around her sternum. "If you miss the window, Vane Thorne's estate gets my soul. Don't frag this up."

My hand doesn't shake. Won't allow it. I've rewired ignition systems while bullets chewed through windshields. I've replaced transmissions under fire. This is just mechanics—different kind of engine, same principles.

"You're a mechanic," she whispers, reading my silence. "You know how to jumpstart a battery."

"Battery that might explode in my face? Sure." I force the words flat, deadpan. Humor or something like it. My other hand finds the syringe prepped with the cocktail—potassium chloride, epinephrine, lidocaine, all measured to push a healthy heart into cardiac arrest. Push her over the edge.

She flinches as I press the needle against her arm.

"Do it," Mara says. "Do it now before—"

The world lurches. The Panasonic Toughbook slides off the dashboard, clattering against the floor mat. Another explosion rocks the ambulance, closer this time. The crucible outside—the massive sludge-filled cauldron that's been simmering since before any of us were born—throbs brighter. Heat radiates through the shattered windshield, a wave of sickly warmth that turns my stomach.

I depress the plunger.

Mara arches her back, a silent scream tearing from her throat as her body convulses. Her hand claws at my wrist, fingers digging crescents into flesh. The parasite on her chest flares brilliant violet, responding to the assault.

Her monitor spikes—a jagged mountain range of electrical activity—and then...

Flatline.

A solid green line across the screen. Screaming static where her heartbeat should be. Sixty seconds starts now.

My hands are already moving. Conductive gel from the foil packets, smearing across her sternum, conducting paths around the glowing Geas. Can't have the electricity arcing through the parasite instead of her heart. That would finish her for sure. Would give Vane Thorne exactly what he wants.

"Come on, Little Halo," I mutter, positioning the paddles. One above her left breast, one below her right rib cage. "Don't you fucking die on me now."

I look up. Mara's eyes are open but empty, staring past me at the ceiling. The light is already fading from them, replaced by something else. Something wrong.

*Thirty seconds.*

The LifePak charges with a rising whine.

* * *

I count the seconds like a prayer to something I stopped believing in years ago.

"Thirty-one... thirty-two..."

The flatline monitor screams its single, deafening tone—steady, merciless, the sound of death that never takes a breath. My palms press against Mara's chest, feeling nothing but the cold certainty of absence. No heartbeat. No life. Just flesh cooling under my fingers while outside this metal cocoon, the world bleeds itself to pieces.

"Forty... forty-one..."

Blood spatters across the reinforced glass behind me. A Street-Elf— Razor-Wire gang, by the bone-white markings—and he's thrown sideways by something kinetic and violent enough to leave his silhouette smeared crimson against the window before he disappears from view. The Pulaski Skyway has become a meat-grinder, all shrieking engines and bodies breaking against concrete, but none of it matters.

Only her matters.

"Forty-five..."

The corporate Geas on her chest does something impossible. It turns black—not gray, not dark, but *black*—like obsidian caught in starlight. Then it crystallizes. I watch the contract fragment into geometric shards, each one refracting the ambulance's emergency lights until they scatter across her skin like dying fireflies. The thing that owned her, that turned her into a weapon, that made her forget what she was before the corporations got their hooks in—it's shattering.

Fifty-seconds.

My frost-cobalt blood is singing now, iron-hot beneath my skin. The defibrillator charges with a rising whine that competes with the flatline's monotone wail. Sixty joules. One hundred twenty. Two hundred forty. Three hundred sixty. The numbers blur together as my vision tunnels down to the paddles in my hands—their rubberized grips slick with sweat or blood, I can't tell which.

"Fifty-five..."

Grimjaw's voice erupts through the Nextel i1000plus clipped to my belt: *"Reyes! The suit-suckers are pushing the gantry! We can't hold this choke-point forever!"*

I don't respond. Can't respond. My entire universe has compressed itself into the space between Mara's ribs where life should be.

Sixty seconds.

I slam the paddles into her chest with both fists.

Everything goes white.

Not the sterile medical white of hospital fluorescent bulbs, but something *alive*—blazing, incandescent, the color of stars being born and dying simultaneously. Frost explodes outward from the contact points, crystallizing on her skin in intricate fractals while the ozone smell hits me like a physical wall. My blood-iron pours through the electrodes, 360 joules of pure electrical agony, and I feel it travel through every circuit of her body.

*Clear!*

The word doesn't come from any machine. It comes from somewhere deeper—a place inside my bones where the frost-coal burns brightest.

---

## CHAPTER 7: THE HEARTH-COAL & WHITE-ASH SUN

The flash cleared like a camera shutter snapping shut on reality itself. I blinked hard against the afterimage burned into my retinas—a negative space where the world used to be solid.

"Cole."

Mara's voice cut through before I could process anything else. My hand was already moving, fingers closing around her wrist where she lay sprawled across the tilted gurney. The metal frame groaned beneath us both as I hauled her up and over, setting her feet on what used to be the floor but was now an angle of shattered glass and buckled steel plating.

I didn't feel the weight anymore.

My chest—where the Lead-Bismuth coil had crushed my ribs for nine years straight, where every breath came weighted down with the phantom mass of corporate governance and magical regulation—was *empty*. Not just light, but genuinely, physically absent of that suffocating pressure. I could actually expand my lungs fully for the first time since 2000.

"What...?" Mara steadied herself against me, her eyes wide and reflecting something I'd never seen before. Not the sickly green of her old shadow-magic, but something brighter. Cleaner.

I looked at my hands spread before me on instinct. The blue-black residue of iron-gall that had always coated my skin like industrial grime was burning away in threads of pure light. No smoke, no chemical reaction—I watched particles of my own essence transfigure into glowing embers that dissipated into the air like sparks from a forge.

"No more governors," I said, tasting the words for their truth. "No more corporate leashes."

The platform stretched out around us. Sodium-vapor lamps flickered overhead, their dying orange glow barely competing with the way the very atmosphere seemed to shimmer now. Each breath drew in not just air but something else—electricity without pain, magic without limitation. My frost-cobalt power hummed along my spine like it had finally been unplugged from a faulty outlet and was running on its own clean current for the first time.

Mara raised one hand experimentally. Tendrils of her shadow-work extended outward, but they weren't the diseased gray-green of before. They moved like liquid starlight, pooling and dispersing across the grating beneath our feet where blood and oil had stained the metal just minutes ago. Wherever her magic touched down, the filth simply *vanished*, revealing pristine steel underneath.

"Jesus Christ," someone whispered.

A Gnome frequency-broker sat slumped against a concrete pylon twenty feet away, one leg twisted at an angle that should have knocked him unconscious from pain alone. He clutched a modified PalmPilot in both hands, the screen cracked spiderweb-style across its surface. But his eyes weren't on his broken equipment—they were locked on us.

"Mother of circuits..." The device slipped from his grasp, hitting the grating with a metallic ping that echoed across the empty platform. "You guys are... you're actually *glowing*."

I glanced down at myself. He wasn't wrong. My coveralls hung loose on my frame, but beneath them I could see the outline of my body traced in faint blue-white light. Not the cold, mechanical luminescence of machinery, but something warmer. Alive in a way that felt fundamentally different from anything I'd experienced during all those years of working the South Side machine shops.

The air itself tasted different now. No more sulfur, no more copper tang of ozone burning. Instead—cedar? Fresh cut wood and the smell of charcoal fresh from a forge, smoldering with controlled heat rather than wildfire destruction.

Behind us, the ambulance cab was a total wreck. Metal folded like paper around the space where we'd been moments ago. Sparks still dripped from severed cables, hissing as they hit pools of hydraulic fluid spreading across the platform. But none of it mattered because we were standing here, upright, unchained.

The crucible far below in the Industrial Abyss began to roar.

* * *

My lungs expand for the first time in three years.

The weight that's been crushing my sternum—that wool-thick, ash-gray suffocation I've carried since Sub-Station Seven—it *lifts*. Not gradually, not slowly, but like someone cut the cables holding me underwater and I'm rocketing toward the surface.

"Fuck," I gasp, and the word tears through my throat raw.

Cole's hand finds mine in the dark between the Pylon's spinning gyroscopic cores. His fingers are solid. Real. Warm in a way that shouldn't be possible when the temperature has dropped to where breath crystallizes before it leaves your lips. The hearth-coal smell—that impossible, *impossible* smell—fills the space between us, burning away the static.

I see it happening.

The gray wool that's clung to my aura since 2005—the memory of those 314 souls screaming as my wild magic consumed the train, turning flesh to carbon and bone to powder, saving twelve Orphans by murdering hundreds—I watch it *flake apart*. Like dead skin. Like ash in wind. Each fragment catches fire from Cole's strange warmth and dissolves into brilliant white particles that scatter and vanish.

"Mara." His voice is steady even as our combined frequencies send harmonic vibrations through the Crown Vault floor. "Look at me."

I do. Can't not. Those amber-fire eyes hold something older than the Jersey City docks, older than the tunnels beneath Newark, older than the first time magic tore its way into this world through the rift we call the Breach.

"The static..." My words come easier now. Cleaner. "It's gone, Cole. It's just us now."

Over the comms, Vane Thorne's voice cuts through the Pylon's ambient hum like a blade. Panicked. Elvish accent sharpened with terror: *"Their telemetry is dark! Malvourne, they broke the vows! Kill them!"*

Malvourne doesn't respond with words. I feel him instead—a pressure against my mind like trying to push through water made of broken glass. He's coming for us. Corporate Aegis. High-Spire justice. The penalty for breaking binding oaths is usually death.

Good. Let him try.

My flame responds to my will without hesitation for the first time since before Sub-Station Seven. White-lilac fire blooms along my arms, pure and uncorrupted, burning hot enough to make the air shimmer but cool enough that it doesn't consume. The color is brighter now. Brighter than it was three years ago. Like someone turned up the saturation on reality itself.

Cole's frost-cobalt answer spirals around mine, each strand of his power so cold it should freeze everything it touches, yet somehow it only makes my flames burn cleaner. Together we're creating something new—not white-lilac or frost-cobalt anymore, but both at once. Opposites that don't cancel out but amplify each other.

The Telluric busbars lining the Crown Vault walls begin to vibrate in sympathy. Their deep thrumming frequency harmonizes with our combined magic until the entire space feels alive, resonant, *aware*. The Pylon #5 recognizes what we've become.

I raise my hands between us, watching as the ambient magic—*our* magic—begins to physically manifest in the space. White-lilac and frost-cobalt weaving together, interlacing like DNA strands or railroad tracks diverging into infinity. The light grows brighter.

Brighter still.

Until it becomes blinding.

* * *

The world went white.

Not the gentle white of snow or clouds, but the screaming white of forge-hearts and dying stars colliding inside my chest. I felt Cole's presence like a second heartbeat, his pain and power flooding through where our shadows had merged. The Hearth-Coal burned in my left side—a sun of crimson-gold fury that tasted of gunpowder and desperation. The White-Ash churned in my right—Mara's legacy, cool as winter wind and twice as deadly, smelling of lilacs growing through concrete cracks.

Together we were impossible. Together we were inevitable.

"I can't—" Cole started to say, but his voice cracked mid-sentence, swallowed by the sound of our own existence. The toxic rain from Apep's Venom didn't just stop when it hit our combined aura—it *screamed*. Each droplet struck our field and simply ceased to be, vaporizing into nothing but memory and heat-shimmer. Where Cole's crimson magic touched it, the venom boiled away in angry red bursts. Where mine engaged, the droplets froze into crystalline fragments before shattering into harmless dust.

We walked forward.

The steel grating beneath our feet rang out like a war drum, each synchronized step driving the beat of our approach. My boot came down. Cole's followed. Mine again. His. The rhythm was perfect because we were perfect together—the cracked detective who'd lost everything and the student who'd never had anything worth losing except her mentor's trust.

Lord Malvourne stood at the far end of the gantry, his aristocratic Elf features twisted into something ugly and afraid. Even at this distance, I could see the way his fingers trembled around the black-iron staff he'd summoned. Behind him, Elias Morvain maintained his composure better, though I caught the telltale flicker of uncertainty in his eyes as he watched us approach.

"This is impossible!" Malvourne's voice echoed across the gap between us, desperate and shrill. "Street-trash cannot generate this yield! You're nothing! Less than nothing!"

Cole racked his shotgun—*thunk*—the sound sharp and final. Even that mundane action carried weight now, backed by the Hearth-Coal burning through his veins. The weapon glowed white-hot in his hands, the polymer frame smoking, but it held. Didn't melt. Wouldn't break.

"Check your math, suit," Cole said calmly. Too calm for someone holding an incandescent weapon.

I extended my hand toward Elias Morvain.

The whip materialized instantly—a thing of terrible beauty, coiling and crackling with power that shifted between white-lilac cold and crimson-gold heat. It sang as it formed, a high-pitched harmonic that made the air shimmer. The lash stretched twenty feet from my outstretched palm, each inch of its length writhing with barely-contained annihilation.

Aimed directly at Elias Morvain's throat.

Behind them both, the corporate mercenaries who'd tried to flank our position weren't even screaming anymore—they were just... gone. Blinded by our light. Their rune-etched MP5s had melted into puddles of slag on the gantry floor, tactical polymer turned to worthless scrap in seconds. The smell hit me then: burning plastic and seared metal mixing with ozone and cedar smoke.

The High-Spire soldiers themselves staggered back from the edge of our aura, their combat spells failing before they could complete formation. One of them clawed at his faceplate, his scream muffled behind the melting polymer. Another simply collapsed, his neural implant overloading from proximity to what we had become.

But I didn't watch them fall. My eyes stayed locked on Elias Morvain.

On the man who'd stood beside Malvourne when my mentor burned.

---

## CHAPTER 8: DROWNING THE FOUR HEADS

The fusion strike catches Malvourne mid-step, the combined weight of our magics slamming into the suspended platform like God's own fist. Eight hundred thousand gallons of boiling industrial sludge suddenly *pauses*—not stops, just... hesitates—creating a shimmering dome of distorted reality above the crucible below.

Mara moves through the light like she owns it now. Her fingers trace arcane geometries that make my eyes water when I try to follow their patterns. The air pressure drops another ten pounds per square inch.

"Elias!" She doesn't look at him, but he responds anyway, his blood-work glowing faint with reactive power as he begins weaving supplementary runes in the space behind us. The heat from below is crushing now—a physical thing pressing against my skin, making sweat bead instantly and roll down my spine.

Malvourne stumbles back toward the control station, one hand already reaching for what looks like an emergency kill switch. His other hand comes up fast, mouth opening to speak words of binding and curse. But Mara's already there—or her magic is. The wards around him don't even slow her down.

They *shatter*.

Not break. Shatter. Like glass dropped on concrete, the protective hexes surrounding Malvourne explode outward in a flash of violet sparks that rain across the steel mesh flooring. Somewhere in the wreckage, I hear copper wiring start to pop and hiss as it overloads, smell burning plastic and ozone thick enough to taste.

"You slit Dr. Halcyon's throat to hide the Sub-Station Seven bypass." Mara's voice is flat, emotionless. Deadly. "You traded 314 lives for a promotion."

Malvourne's composure cracks. His High-Spire accent slips, sliding into something gutter-trash desperate: "It was corporate restructuring, you naive little wire-rat! Those people were—"

"They were *people*." Another step forward. Mara's right hand opens, palm up, and suddenly every Telluric conduit on this platform lights up like Christmas morning. The control panels spark violently—they're not just shorting out, they're actively fighting her presence, trying to redirect power through safety systems designed to prevent exactly this kind of magical intrusion.

She crushes them anyway.

Metal shrieks. Transformers groan in agony as their casings split along stress fractures. A Sony MiniDisc data-drive—old tech, but Malvourne always did have a fetish for analog backups—explodes in a shower of molten plastic and corrupted memory chips. Sparks scatter across the floor like dying fireflies.

Elias shifts behind me, ancestral warding staff coming up slowly. I can feel him gathering mass, preparing to tear space itself open if he needs to. The air starts tasting wrong—that metallic tang that means reality's getting thin somewhere nearby.

"Mara." Just her name. Warning.

She ignores me, eyes locked on Malvourne as he presses himself against the emergency console. There's panic in his face now. Real panic. His fingers fumble over switches labeled in languages even I can't read—not English, not Spanish, something older written in glyphs that hurt to look at directly.

"You don't understand what you're doing here," he gasps. "The Council will—"

"The Council is already dead," Mara says softly. "Or they will be by sunrise."

Then she raises both hands together, palms forward, and the air between us and Malvourne *compresses*. Not into a solid wall—into something worse. Something that exists in all dimensions simultaneously, pressing inward from every angle at once until there's nowhere left for him to go except through it or into it or—

The gantry groans.

* * *

The air crackled with wrongness as Morvain's lips moved through the final syllables of whatever foul geas he was weaving. I saw it happening in slow motion—the way his good hand tightened around that sickly glowing staff, how the shadows coalesced into something almost tangible between him and Mara.

Then she *moved*.

No spell. No incantation. Just pure, primal fury channeled through flesh and bone.

Mara closed the distance in three strides, her boots slamming against the rust-streaked floor hard enough to send up sprays of red-tinged water. The Hearth-Coal burned white-hot in her chest now, visible through the tattered remains of her jacket, casting everything in that hellish amber glow. She didn't grab the staff like someone trying to disarm an opponent—she seized it like a woman crushing a snake.

The obsidian shrieked.

It was a sound beyond hearing, a violation of physics that made my teeth ache and brought blood from my nose. That staff had been drinking souls for three millennia, and it knew exactly what it was doing: trying to pull Mara apart molecule by molecule, to suck her down into its endless hunger.

She just kept squeezing.

"NO!" Morvain's composure shattered completely. "You cannot—you're mortal—YOU'RE NOTHING—"

Mara's answer was to yank the staff toward herself with impossible strength, forcing him to stumble forward. In the same motion, she pivoted, bringing the obsidian pole down across her raised knee.

*CRACK.*

The sound was deafening. Not the satisfying snap of wood—that was something else entirely. Something ancient giving way. Three thousand years of accumulated darkness compressed into a single point of catastrophic failure.

The staff exploded.

Not magically. Physically. The obsidian shattered into fragments that sprayed outward like bullets, each one trailing threads of corrupted energy that hissed where they struck wet metal. But worse—the magical feedback loop that had sustained itself for centuries suddenly found itself unmoored, all that stolen power having nowhere to go except *backward*.

Morvain threw up his remaining hand as if that could stop anything. It didn't. The blast caught him center mass, and I saw his left arm detach at the elbow in a spray of red that immediately began evaporating in Mara's heat, turning to a fine pink mist before it hit the ground.

He screamed—a high, thin sound that cut through the cacophony of failing enchantments and tearing reality. His aristocratic mask was gone utterly, replaced by raw agony as he collapsed to both knees, clutching the stump of his severed limb while blood pumped between his fingers in steady rhythmic spurts.

"The fuck did you do?" Mara's voice came out wrong, too deep, edged with something not quite human. She stood over him, chest heaving, flames licking around her hands. "You wanted to play with forces beyond mortal comprehension? Let me show you what happens when you break toys you can't fix."

I stepped up beside her, my voice coming out as that low mechanical rumble even I barely recognized anymore: "Warranty voided."

Behind Morvain, Malvourne had stopped trying to channel power. He just stared at his brother—at the bleeding ruin on the floor—and I saw the exact moment calculation replaced panic in those cold eyes. He turned on his heel and ran, boots slapping against wet concrete as he sprinted toward the emergency blast-hatch leading down to the lower crucible.

Mara made a move to follow, but I caught her shoulder.

"Let him run," I said. "We've got bigger problems."

The water at our feet had started boiling without any visible heat source. And from somewhere below us—in the depths where we'd never thought to look—the earth itself began to *throat*.

* * *

The air tastes like copper and ozone as I step past Mara's trembling form. She's still catching her breath, that white-lilac fire dying down to embers in her pupils. Her hands shake—adrenaline, not fear. Never fear.

Below us, the emergency blast-hatch yawns open like a throat swallowing screams.

I hear them down there. Morvain and Malvourne. Their voices echo off the crucible walls—wet sounds, pained and desperate. The clang of metal on metal as they try to climb the maintenance ladder, their expensive suits torn and bloodied. Good. Let them suffer.

"Scratch two suits! The board is gonna need a new pair of executives!" A Goblin splice-tech's voice crackles through my comms. Someone's watching on security feeds. Smart. They'll want to see how this ends.

*Restructuring complete.* Mara's words hang in the recycled air. She means the facility's systems—the overclocked fusion cores she just rewired through sheer willpower and spite. But I know what she really means.

Eight years. Eight fucking years since they took my sister.

I pull the rune-etched welding torch from my tactical harness. Its weight feels right in my grip—familiar, final. The blue-white flame sparks to life at its tip, casting dancing shadows across the steel grating beneath our feet.

Mara looks up at me, sweat beading on her forehead. "You sure about this?"

My jaw tightens. "They made me into something I'm not. Might as well finish it."

The torch hums—a low, hungry vibration that resonates in my bones. Below, the screaming stops abruptly. A body hits water with a tremendous splash. Then another.

"One more for the road," I mutter, and step toward the edge of the hatch.

The crucible stretches away into darkness below. Somewhere down there, in the ruptured lower chamber, Morvain and Malvourne are drowning in their own blood and the alkaline slurry that used to fuel Pylon #5's reactors. The same reactors they poisoned to frame me.

Heat builds in my chest—not magical, not arcane. Just pure, unadulterated rage finally finding its target.

I crouch at the hatch's edge, torch ready.

---

## CHAPTER 9: THE SLIVER OF JUSTICE

The blast-hatch comes down like God's own hammer.

Cole doesn't hesitate. Doesn't measure. Two tons of military-grade steel crashes into place over the maintenance shaft with a *CLANG* that reverberates through my ribcage like a shotgun blast in an elevator. The sound is final. Absolute.

"Seal it," I tell him. My voice sounds hollow even to me, bouncing off the Crown Vault's curved walls.

He's already moving to the welding station, thick gloves pulling on like a second skin. The industrial torch spits blue-white flame—no, not flame. Something colder. His frost-cobalt blood-iron magic makes the arc-welder look like a child's sparkler, each bead of molten metal crystalline and sharp-edged as broken glass.

Through the viewport—a six-inch circle of reinforced glass set dead-center in the hatch—I see Morvain first. He's pressed against the far wall of the chamber below, his perpetual sneer finally wiped clean by panic. Malvourne slams against the door from inside, fists hammering the steel in rhythmic desperation. Their voices come through the intercom system as muffled, distorted buzzes, like insects trapped in amber.

*"Reyes! We can make a deal!"* Malvourne's face presses flat against the glass, eyes wide and wet. *"I can give you the Syndicate's offshore accounts!"*

Cole doesn't look up. The welder's mask obscures his features, but I know he's smiling behind it. That same cruel curve of lip I saw when we burned down the Pylon #3 substation last month.

*"Keep it,"* Cole says, his voice strangely calm over the sizzle-and-pop of molecularly-recombined steel. *"You're gonna need it for the toll across the river."*

The weld-beads cascade down the seam where door meets frame. Each one is perfect, geometric, fusing the steel at an atomic level. Not just locked. Become one substance. Unbreakable without thermite charges and enough time to evacuate three city blocks.

Morvain's face appears beside Malvourne's now, both men shoulder-to-shoulder in their desperate display. Through the distorted glass they look like museum specimens, already fossilized. Already forgotten.

*"Commander Vance!"* Morvain's deeper voice cuts through the static. *"Think about this! You execute us here, the BATC will never accept—"*

"The BATC accepts results." My finger finds the trigger of my sidearm, but I don't aim. Don't need to. They know what comes next. "And you two are going to be very, very dead."

But death isn't coming from my gun. Death is already sealed in that chamber with them, ticking down in increments of seconds rather than minutes.

Cole moves to the manual override panel, still welding as he walks, creating a continuous bead of frozen light around the entire perimeter of the hatch. The smell hits me then—that acrid burn of vaporized steel mixing with ozone sharp enough to make my eyes water. It's the scent of things being made permanent.

He reaches out—doesn't even break stride—and *rips* the crucible's primary sludge-valve lever into the OPEN position.

The metal shrieks. Rivets pop. Something massive shifts in the machinery below our feet, and for a moment the whole Crown Vault groans like a dying whale. Then silence, broken only by Cole's welder and the frantic pounding on the other side of that glass circle.

"What did you just do?" I ask, though I'm not sure I want the answer.

Cole finally looks up, sliding his mask back. His eyes are black as oil slicks in moonlight. "Pulled the plug on their air recirculation system. The crucible's main purge cycle runs every ninety seconds when the valves are open. First cycle will vent atmospheric pressure to compensate. Second cycle..." He shrugs. "Pressure equalization. The reinforced glass can take maybe five PSI differential before it becomes decorative rather than structural."

I watch the viewport. Morvain has gone pale. Malvourne keeps hammering, but there's something mechanical about it now, reflexive rather than desperate. They're already calculating how long they have. Experienced men know the mathematics of suffocation.

*"Vance!"* Malvourne's voice cracks through the speaker. *"Please! I have information about the Kearny Marshes operation! The Aegis can't afford to lose this intel!"*

"Already lost it," I tell him. And it's true. Whatever he knows dies with him in approximately... forty-five seconds, if Cole's estimate is accurate.

The Commander in me wants to feel something. Guilt. Doubt. The weight of taking lives without trial or judgment.

But the sliver of justice I've carried since my daughter's death in the Pulaski Skyway collapse? That feels warm. Almost comfortable. Like coming home after too many years away.

Cole completes the final weld-seam and steps back. The hatch might as well be part of the floor now, welded so deep into the frame that even industrial cutting equipment would need hours to breach it. We have minutes at most.

"Let's go," I say, turning toward the Crown Vault's exit.

Behind us, the pounding on the glass continues for exactly fifteen more seconds. Then stops. Abruptly. Finally.

The intercom crackles once—static from ruptured lung tissue hitting open air—and goes silent.

We leave them there, sealed like secrets in a tomb they helped build brick by brick over decades of betrayal. The Millennium Breach is still out there, still bleeding through the gaps in reality like water finding cracks in concrete. But here, in Pylon #5's heart, we've made one thing certain.

Some things get welded shut. Forever.

* * *

The pressure gauge above the crucible spikes into red territory. I watch it climb—twenty million PSI and still climbing—and then there's no more thinking.

"Bram! Open those fucking valves NOW!"

Static crackles across the comm line for one infinite heartbeat. Then: "Valve array—rotating to open position. This is gonna get loud, Commander."

It gets louder than loud. It gets deafening.

The massive black-iron valves above the lower crucible—each one the size of a suburban house—begin to shear open with the sound of a thousand trains derailing at once. Metal screams as hydraulic pistons the width of telephone poles force the gears apart. The grinding is so intense my teeth ache. 

Morvain looks up at the opening valves. His face goes slack with realization.

Then the tidal wave hits.

Eight hundred thousand gallons of boiling Apep's Venom comes crashing down into the sealed chamber like the wrath of God Himself, all liquid hellfire and chemical rage. The impact on the far wall creates a shockwave that rattles the viewport in its frame. The glass spiderwebs with hairline fractures—reinforced steel-reinforced glass, and it's *cracking*.

Through the glass, I see Morvain and Malvourne caught in the flood.

They don't even have time to scream.

The sludge slams into them like a freight train made of liquid poison. Morvain's head snaps back from the impact, his body lifted off its feet by the sheer force of the waterfall. Malvourne tries to raise his hands, but the wave is already over him, washing him away like a rag doll.

I can see their mouths open. Can see them inhaling—because even drowning men need air—but instead of air, they're pulling in superheated experimental sludge laced with enough arcane shit to power a small city.

The magic in the room—I can feel it now, Cole's residual signature still hanging in the air like static electricity after a lightning strike—and the venom in the sludge begin to react.

It happens fast. Too fast.

Malvourne's chest swells, then convulses as something begins growing inside him. Through the clear glass of the viewport, I watch black-iron crystals explode outward from his trachea. They erupt from his mouth in a shower of jagged metallic spikes, each one gleaming with an oily sheen that catches the red emergency lights. His eyes bulge, veins popping across the whites like cracked rivers on a map.

Morvain's turn comes next. He makes it maybe two seconds longer than his brother before his lungs betray him completely. The crystallization starts deep in his chest cavity—the sound doesn't carry through the sealed glass, but I can see his body twitching, muscles spasming as his respiratory system fills with solid metal. Then his throat tears open from the inside out. Black-iron shards punch through skin and muscle like they were made of paper. Blood sprays in an arc, misting the interior of the chamber.

Both men freeze mid-drown, mid-scream. Their bodies locked in place by the rapid crystallization spreading through their systems. I can see it moving under their skin—dark networks branching through their torsos like tree roots made of obsidian, replacing flesh and bone with something hard and dead and utterly permanent.

They're drowning. And freezing. At the same time.

Cole stands over the viewport, one hand resting against the reinforced glass. His face is unreadable. Not triumphant. Not satisfied. Just... detached. Like he's watching a test tube reaction instead of two men dying in the most horrific way imaginable.

The sludge continues to fill the chamber past their frozen bodies, rising higher, covering them completely. Soon there are just two shapes visible beneath the surface—a pair of silhouettes encased in black iron, suspended in toxic water like exhibits in some hellish museum.

"Reyes? Status on the execs?"

Bram's voice crackles through my comm unit. I almost forget to answer.

"The threat is neutralized," I say quietly.

Over in his control booth, Cole lifts his head slightly at Bram's question. His frost-cobalt eyes reflect the red emergency lighting for a moment before he speaks into his own mic.

"They caught a bad case of the black lung," he says. His voice is flat. Emotionless as a weather report. "We're clear."

The valves above begin to grind shut again, sealing off the flow. The roar diminishes gradually until all that's left is the sound of my own breathing inside my helmet and the faint sloshing of eight hundred thousand gallons settling in the sealed chamber below.

Cole steps back from the viewport.

And for the first time since this whole nightmare began, I see something flicker across his face. Something that looks almost like regret.

He killed them. Not with a weapon or a spell or any conventional means—but by drowning them in poison and magic combined, crystallizing their lungs from the inside out while they still had enough consciousness to feel every second of it.

And he did it without hesitation. Without remorse.

I look at those two frozen shapes suspended in black sludge beneath reinforced glass—what used to be Morvain and Malvourne now nothing more than ornate tombstones—and wonder what kind of man can do something like that and just... walk away.

The realization settles over me like ash:

Cole's already walked away. And he'll never come back from whatever place he just went to do it.

"Secure the area," I tell my team. My voice sounds hollow even to myself. "Lock down Pylon Five. No one gets in here until we figure out how to dispose of what's left."

But I'm not looking at what's left. I'm watching Cole turn away from the glass, his coat swirling around him as he heads toward the exit.

He doesn't look back.

* * *

The platform shuddered beneath my feet like a dying god taking its last breath.

Cole's hand tightened around mine—iron grip, trembling slightly. Not from fear. From exhaustion. From the weight of what we'd just witnessed crystallize in those two hollow shells. The architects of suffering, locked forever in their own poisoned perfection.

"It's not enough," he said, voice raw sandpaper over broken glass. His eyes stayed fixed on the cooling metal where those bodies had been moments ago. "It's never enough."

I knew that tone. Had heard it in my own voice during the hours after Kearny, when the adrenaline bled out and left nothing but the aching truth: some wounds don't heal. They just scar deeper.

I squeezed back, feeling the calluses on his palm—that mechanic's hands that had held wrenches while holding together a city that kept trying to fall apart. "I know. But it's a start. We closed the ledger, Cole."

A lie I told myself as much as him. You can't balance an account against infinity. Can't make cosmic scales tip toward justice when one side holds every child who ever screamed in darkness, every name forgotten in the marsh's hungry mud.

The distant thrum of Pylon #5's power grid had stabilized—steady heartbeat of something massive waking up from anesthesia. The white-lilac glow of my magic cast long shadows across the platform, illuminating nothing but our breathing figures and the black water still lapping at the welded hatch below.

Cole shifted his weight, steel-toed boots scraping against the deck with a sound like bones settling into final rest positions. "Danny's still dead. The sewer trials didn't un-happen. This doesn't scrape the iron out of his lungs."

"No," I agreed quietly. "But they can't hurt anyone else. That counts for something."

The temperature plummeted without warning.

My breath became visible clouds in air that suddenly tasted of tombs and venom—not fresh decay, but ancient. Old. Older than Neon Hollow. Older than the marshes. Something that had been waiting in darkness so deep it had forgotten what light meant.

Cole's head snapped up first—survival instincts honed by years of surviving things that shouldn't exist. His eyes caught mine, wide with recognition of wrongness so profound it defied description.

Then the entire cavern *heaved*.

Metal groaned like a throat screaming. The platform lurched sideways—we staggered, still connected, and I felt Cole's muscles coil beneath his coat as he automatically positioned himself between whatever was coming and me.

From directly beneath the flooded crucible came a sound.

Not an explosion. Not machinery failing.

A sound like a continent tearing in half. Like the sky splitting open over Giza when something too hungry to name finally decided it wanted more than its allotted portion of darkness.

---

## CHAPTER 10: THE ABYSSAL LUNGE

The silence lasted exactly three seconds.

Then the world began screaming.

I felt it through my boots first—a deep, resonant hum that vibrated up through my shins and into my bones. Not the mechanical thrum of machinery, but something older. Something hungry. The telluric groan of stressed metal pushed beyond its limits.

"Cole—" Mara started, but I was already moving.

The heavy steel decking beneath us twisted like tinfoil. Rivets the size of my fist popped free with sounds like gunshots, pinging off the cavern walls. The platform tilted five degrees. Ten. My stomach lurched as the angle steepened.

"GRIMJAW!" I screamed into my radio, grabbing Mara's wrist and yanking her behind the reinforced concrete housing of the primary generator. "WHAT THE FUCK IS HAPPENING?!"

The response came back frantic, all traces of the Orc's swagger burned away by panic. "*Reyes! The whole fragging foundation is dropping! Get out of there! The meters are off the charts!*"

My Nextel pager—a Gnome seismological emergency device they'd practically glued to me before we entered—was screaming a continuous tone that made my teeth ache. I ripped it free from my belt, read the display once, then hurled it against the concrete wall. The numbers didn't matter. The red flashing light said everything.

"It wasn't just sludge," Mara breathed, her face pale in the dying amber glow of the crucible. "It was solvent. The final piece."

The massive Telluric busbars—that network of ancient power conduits we'd been using for leverage—snapped like guitar strings. One whiplashed across the space where we'd been standing moments before, the sound a deafening metallic shriek that echoed through the cavern like the death cry of some mechanical god.

Another snapped. Then another. Each one tearing free from their anchor points, each release sending fresh tremors through the failing structure.

"Hold the causeway!" I shouted back at Grimjaw, even though he couldn't possibly hear me over the cacophony. "We have to set the Anchor!"

But how? How do you perform rituals when reality itself is coming apart?

Beneath our feet, the platform lurched violently. I slammed into Mara, both of us crashing against the generator housing as a section of decking buckled downward with a groan of tortured steel. Through the gap, I could see into the lower crucible—the one we'd thought was dead and buried under tons of crystallized nightmare.

A fissure cracked across its floor.

Not small. Not cautious. A yawning, glowing gash that split the crystallized bodies of Morvain and Malvourne directly down the middle. Their frozen forms fractured cleanly, each half sliding away from the other as the floor beneath them fell into darkness deeper than any shadow had a right to be.

The telluric energy surging up through the breach hit my eyes like looking directly at the sun—not light, but pure force made visible. It washed over everything in waves of sickly luminescence, making the air shimmer and stink of ozone and burning copper.

"The Fifth Nail," Mara whispered. "The physical anchor. Cole, it's failing."

I knew. God help me, I could feel it in every fiber of my being. The seal that had held this thing—this entity, this wound in spacetime—for millennia wasn't just weakening. It was shattering.

And beneath the Pylon #5 Crown Vault, two million tons of concrete and steel were about to follow it down into whatever abyss had been festering there since before the first human crawled out of the mud.

"Grimjaw!" I roared into the radio again. "We need more time!"

No response. Just static filled with the sounds of tearing metal and screaming wind.

I looked at Mara. She looked back at me, and for the first time since I'd met her, I saw something close to fear in those calculating eyes.

"How much time?" she asked quietly, already knowing the answer wouldn't matter.

The platform bucked violently beneath us.

* * *

The seal broke like bone.

I felt it split before I heard it—the ancient Telluric ward that had held for three millennia simply... *cracked*. The sensation hit me behind my eyes, then drove downward through my skull like a spike of pure, undifferentiated dread. My knees buckled on the catwalk grating. Blood spilled from my nostrils, hot and copper-bright, splattering across my tactical vest.

"Commander!" Cole's voice cut through the rising static.

Not now. Couldn't respond. The magic was *wrong*—so fundamentally broken that my metasenses couldn't parse it. Where there should have been structure, there was only hunger. Where there should have been containment, there was *nothing*, and nothing was eating everything around it.

The white-lilac flame—my anchor, my tether to this reality—flickered.

We were standing on top of a corpse whose mouth had just opened.

The temperature plummeted. Not Cole's controlled frost-cobalt, but something older, wetter. The chill of the Duat itself, carrying with it the smell of ancient dust and rotting papyrus. The air grew thick, viscous. Each breath tasted like breathing through grave dirt.

The harmonic whine started low, then climbed past human hearing into frequencies that made my teeth ache. It was the sound of 3,500 years of enforced silence finally screaming its last.

"Cole! It's not just a breach!" I screamed over the noise, clutching my head as blood ran freely down my face. "The entire gate is gone! She's coming through!"

The cavern lights flickered, died, came back half-strength. In that stuttering illumination, I looked down at the crucible. The black sludge wasn't settling anymore. It was *moving*, churning in patterns too complex for simple convection currents. Something underneath, displacing volume. Something big.

Vane Thorne's abandoned corporate comm-channel crackled to life—automated Elven evacuation protocols, their soothing synthetic voices completely disconnected from the apocalypse unfolding beneath the Kearny Marshes:

*...PROCEDURE VERDANT SHIELD INITIATED...ALL PERSONNEL PROCEED TO DESIGNATED SHELTER ZONES...THIS IS NOT A DRILL...*

"Shut it off," I snarled, swiping at the bleeding mess that was my nose. "Thorne's dead. His fucking corporation is dead. We need—"

The catwalk groaned under us.

Not from our weight. From something moving below—the massive displacement of material as whatever had been pressing against the seal for three thousand years finally found purchase on this side. The sludge in the crucible erupted upward in a geyser of obsidian filth, and in the spray, lit by our dying worklights, I saw them.

Scales.

Writhing, overlapping plates of absolute darkness that drank the light around them rather than reflected it. Each one the size of a door. Moving with impossible, serpentine fluidity beneath the surface of that primal ooze.

"Mara!" Cole grabbed my arm, his frost-cobalt flaring bright blue-white around his hands. "We have to retreat! Command needs to know—"

"They already know." My voice was raw. I could taste more blood. "Did you feel that? Every metahuman in North Jersey just felt the seal go. They're all feeling it now."

The high-pitched whine reached a crescendo, then shattered like glass. Silence crashed down in its wake—deeper, heavier than any quiet had a right to be.

And in that sudden silence, I heard it breathing.

Slow, wet exhalations that moved air across distances that should have muted them into nothingness, but instead carried perfectly clear through the cavern. Each breath preceded the sound of scales dragging across stone, the grinding scrape of something built for crushing entire cities shifting its weight.

The sludge erupted again, this time violently displaced upward by mass. Something moving underneath. Something big enough to affect the entire volume of that crucible—which held ten thousand gallons, minimum.

"Oh God," Cole whispered. "Commander, what *is* that?"

I watched the black water explode skyward, and in the momentary arc of displacement, I caught a glimpse of an eye. Not mammalian. Not reptilian. Something older, with a pupil shaped like a keyhole and irises that spiraled inward into depths where geometry itself went mad.

"That," I said, my voice barely audible even to myself, "is what we were never supposed to wake up."

The temperature dropped another twenty degrees.

My white-lilac flame guttered once, twice, and in the third pulse, I saw the true shape of it—the thing beneath the Kearny Marshes, beneath Pylon #5, beneath three millennia of carefully maintained wards.

It was not dying. It was not sleeping.

It was simply patient.

And its patience had finally expired.

* * *

## The Sheared Fang

---

The sound hits me first—a thunderclap wrapped in silk that tears through my skull and rattles every bone in my body. Then comes the heat. Not fire-heat. Something older. Something that remembers when the world was molten and screaming.

*Oh, fuck.*

I see her rising through the crack in reality like a fist punching through wet cardboard. Except this isn't cardboard. This is everything we thought we knew about how things work, and she's shattering it.

Apep.

The name tastes like copper and regret on my tongue as I force myself to watch. To *look* at what's clawing its way up from the Duat into our world.

She's—

There are no words for what she is.

Obsidian scales the size of freight cars slide against each other with sounds like grinding tectonic plates. Each one catches the light wrong—not reflecting it, but *consuming* it, pulling darkness around itself like a living void. Black venom drips from her form in ropes thick enough to crush buildings, hissing where it hits the steel floor of the vault, eating through inches of reinforced metal like tissue paper.

Those fangs.

God, those *fangs*.

Thirty feet of crystalline death curve downward from jaws that could swallow a subway train whole. They scrape along the cavern walls as she ascends, spark-showers erupting where they contact steel—sparks the size of sedan automobiles tumbling away into the darkness, still glowing white-hot.

"Cole!" Mara's voice cuts through the apocalyptic din. "COLE!"

I feel her grab my arm, fingers burning even through my jacket. Her magic blazes between us now—a fusion of frost-cobalt and white-lilac that has somehow crystallized into something new. Something pure. The Hearth-Coal & White-Ash Sun pulses between us both, casting sharp-edged shadows across the rising nightmare.

"We need to move!" She drags me backward toward the platform, toward the Anchor mechanism we'd prepped before all this went sideways. Her eyes are wide, pupils blown with fear and determination. "Now, Cole! NOW!"

The shotgun in my hands feels absurdly light, absurdly small, absurdly *useless*. But muscle memory is a bitch—my thumb racks the pump action anyway, the sound swallowed by Apep's emergence. Shell casings ping against the floor, forgotten.

"Well," I say because saying nothing would be worse, "that's a big fragging snake."

Apep clears the final threshold of the seal.

The crucible beneath her ruptures completely. Steam billows upward—not water-steam but something thicker, more malevolent. Boiling sludge cascades across the vault floor in a torrent, flooding outward from ground zero. Where it touches, metal shrieks and dissolves. Pipes buckle and burst. Fire suppression systems trigger automatically, their jets of pressurized foam meeting the acidic deluge and creating clouds of noxious vapor.

And she just keeps *rising*.

Her neck extends impossibly, scales overlapping like armor plating on some ancient warship. Multiple eyes open along her length—glowing orbs of radioactive intensity that pulse in sequence, each one locking onto our position. They're not just seeing us. They're measuring. Calculating. Deciding how best to unmake us from existence.

The largest eye—easily twenty feet across, set in a skull the size of a house—swivels to face us directly.

I feel its gaze like physical pressure. Like being pressed between mill stones.

Then she opens that jaw.

---

**Shift: Mara Vance POV**

---

His blood runs cold—I can feel it through the fusion, through the shared magic burning between our hearts. Cole Reyes, who has stared down angels and demons both, who has walked through hell and come back laughing, is genuinely afraid right now.

Which means we are so far past fucked it isn't even funny.

"Get the Anchor ready, Cole." My voice sounds steady. I make it sound steady because if I let the terror in, if I let myself feel what's really happening here, I'll shatter. "We're slamming the door on her neck."

I push more power into the Hearth-Coal & White-Ash Sun, feeling it flare brighter. The fusion-point where our magics meet burns white-gold at the center of my chest—so bright it should be blinding but instead cuts through the noir shadows of this place like a scalpel through darkness. Illuminates everything. Shows me the truth.

Apep is preparing to breathe.

That maw—the cavernous space behind those fangs—is drawing inward. A vortex of *nothing* building there, compression turning potential energy into pure annihilation. I can see dark magic coalescing, ancient Egyptian sorcery older than the pyramids, older than written language, older than humanity itself. This is god-stuff. First-principle reality-warping bullshit we have no business being anywhere near.

And she's aiming it right at us.

"Mara!" Cole's shouting over the rising wind—a hurricane-force gale emanating from Apep's throat as she prepares to exhale. His shotgun fires, fires again, useless shots that spark harmlessly off scales thick enough to stop tanks. But he keeps firing anyway because stopping means accepting defeat and Cole Reyes doesn't do acceptance. "The platform! We need to get to the—"

The clock tower in the distance chimes.

Eleven fifty-nine.

One minute until midnight. One minute until New Year's Eve becomes New Year's Day 2009. One minute until whatever's supposed to happen next *happens*, whether we're ready or not.

Apep's eyes narrow.

Her jaw unhinges further—I didn't think that was physically possible, but physics clearly don't apply to cosmic serpent deities bent on eating the sun.

The vortex in her throat reaches critical mass.

I throw my hands forward, pushing every last erg of merged power into a barrier. Frost-cobalt chains intertwine with white-lilac flames, creating something like a crystalline shield between us and inevitable obliteration. It won't hold. I know it won't hold. But maybe, just maybe, it'll buy us the three seconds we need to reach the Anchor mechanism and—

Cole grabs me, yanks me backward with strength born of pure adrenaline. We stumble across the crumbling platform edge, sliding on sludge-slick steel as the entire vault shakes with seismic force. Behind us—or rather below us now, because we've reached the precipice—the Anchor glows soft-blue, waiting for activation.

Waiting for someone brave or stupid enough to pull the lever.

Apep inhales.

And the world goes dark around her mouth as she prepares to breathe out all our tomorrows at once.
